- the only place we need to update an issue file when the issue is partially complete is the "current behavior" section. We don't need to add append-logs to the end, it's better to update the main body to align with the current design, and the current behavior with the current status.

```

### feedback_comprehensive_first_pass.md

```markdown
---
name: Don't tier work into cheap / medium / expensive
description: For new features, do every fold of the work in one comprehensive slice rather than splitting into easy-now / hard-later tiers
type: feedback
originSessionId: 1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa
---
When scoping a new feature, resist the instinct to propose a
"slice 1 covers cheap fields; slice 2 covers expensive fields"
split unless the user explicitly asks for it.

**Why:** The user's framing: "they should all be configurable
with the same interface, so... don't split up the work in that
way. Just do it comprehensively the first time so we don't
forget anything on the return trip." Tiered work means coming
back, and round-trips are where details get forgotten —
especially the cross-cutting plumbing that connects the easy
and hard paths.

**How to apply:** When writing an issue file, if a feature
spans cheap-and-hard variations of the same surface (e.g. all
fields of a schema, all kinds of a polymorphic type), describe
slice 1 as covering the whole surface. The implementation may
still ship incrementally on a per-commit basis, but the issue
should not encode a "we'll do the rest later" plan unless the
user has explicitly asked for that staging.

```

### feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language design pitfalls
description: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format
type: feedback
originSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb
---
When designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.

**1. Don't propose runtime "handles" that route operations back to the originating spec.**

**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.

**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The "phone home" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says "operations on this value cross back to the source."

**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**

**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.

**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.

**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**

**Why:** The user pointed out that "discriminator" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt "which param is the length?" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.

**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message ("destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here").

**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.

```

### project_cross_language_wire.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language wire format
description: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.
type: project
originSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c
---
Design corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older "JSON always" framing.

**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.

**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.

**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.

**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.

**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.

**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque` ("these bytes are language-X-internal"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.

**`$function_pointer` reconstruction — wrapper binary + persistent subprocess (issue 318, amended 2026-05-22).** Earlier design had the consumer's spec FFI-cast the raw process-local address. Rejected: FFI is language-pair-specific, biases SoraMech toward the Lua↔C corner, breaks the N-not-N² rule. Replacement: at map-compile time the compiler asks the *producing* spec to compile the referenced function + its enumerable dependencies into a standalone wrapper binary on disk that speaks a small line protocol on stdio. The consumer spec spawns one persistent subprocess per `$function_pointer` it receives and talks to it over the same socket-like channel used for any out-of-process spec. Every language pays the same price; new languages only implement "compile a function to a wrapper binary" — no pair-wise FFI knowledge required.

**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.

**Two compile-time layers stack:**
- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.
- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.

**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):
1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.
2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's "two rings per slot" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.
3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask "is param 2 the length?" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.

**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.

```

### project_custom_translation_specs.md

```markdown
---
name: Custom translation specs per port
description: Users can override the default native/JSON wire path on any input port for any reason — a knob in the wire format vocabulary (issue 246)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Per-port custom translation specs** let the user intervene at a specific input port and replace the default dual-ring decode path with user-written code. The override applies to that one port; the rest of the graph uses the default native-or-JSON path from issue 312.

**Motivating cases (any reason qualifies, not just cross-language):**
- Cross-language ambiguity the default specs can't infer: a C++ class with methods landing at a C box (drop methods? expose as fn pointers? restructure?), a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a union whose discriminator is on a separate wire.
- Same-language reshape: massaging a value into a different shape on its way in (rename fields, drop a layer, project a subset) without adding a transform box on the canvas.
- Validation / coercion: clamp a number, enforce a schema, fail loudly on unexpected shapes.

**How it composes with the dual-ring design:**
- The custom spec runs at *pop* time on the consumer side, after the ordering ring has been consulted and the cell has been read from the appropriate ring. The user's code receives the decoded value (native or JSON-decoded) and produces whatever the consumer's `invoke` will see.
- A port with a custom translation gets its own wire color in the editor (issue 245) — visible signal that this port doesn't use the default path.

**Why:** The default native/JSON contract covers the cases JSON's structure handles cleanly. Everything outside that needs a user escape hatch — *and* the same hatch is useful for purely-local "I want this input shaped differently" cases. One mechanism, many uses.

**How to apply:** When the design needs an override knob on the cross-language path, propose "custom translation spec on the destination port" rather than inventing per-function annotations, type discriminator metadata, or producer-side conversion hints (all three were rejected — see feedback_cross_language_pitfalls). The port is the unit of override; the spec is user code; the rest stays default.

```

### project_editor_visual_language.md

```markdown
---
name: Editor visual language for wires
description: Wire color in the canvas editor encodes language pairing across the edge, not just routing kind — a UI invariant future work should respect (issue 245)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Wires are colored by language pairing across the edge**, with a separate color for wires whose destination port carries a user-written custom translation (issue 246). Pre-245 wires were colored purely by routing kind (default slate-blue, comparator branches orange/blue/green).

**The pairing-based palette:**
- **Same-language hop** — the wire carries native bytes; default neutral color.
- **Cross-language hop (forest green, ~`#228b22`)** — different producer/consumer languages; runtime translates via JSON at the wire. The color is a standing reminder that encode + decode is happening on that hop.
- **Custom-translation hop** — a third distinct color signaling the destination port has a user-written translation spec overriding the default path.
- Branch-routing colors (orange/blue/green from comparator boxes) compose on top — routing kind and language pairing are orthogonal axes the editor must show simultaneously.

**Why:** The runtime treats same-lang and cross-lang hops very differently (dual-ring slot design, issue 312), but pre-245 the editor gave the box author no visual signal that the JSON translation step existed. It was invisible until someone read the dispatch code. Translation cost should be legible from the canvas.

**How to apply:** Any future editor work that touches wire rendering must preserve "color encodes language pairing." Don't propose recoloring schemes that overload the cross-language signal onto another concept. New routing concepts get new axes (line style, glyphs, animation) rather than stealing color. When discussing wire visuals, name both axes — routing kind AND language pairing — even if only one is changing.

```

### project_encapsulated_map.md

```markdown
---
name: Encapsulated map as box
description: A sub-map opens as a single box on a parent canvas. Data boxes marked externally-supplied become input ports; write boxes marked externally-consumed become output ports. The documented exception to single-output-per-box (issue 248, amended 2026-05-23)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.

**The encapsulation contract — symmetric input and output toggles:**
- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-supplied" in its inspector. Each such box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box.
- **Outputs:** any `write` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-consumed" in its inspector. Each such box surfaces as a **distinct output port** on the encapsulated box. A write box with the toggle on can still write to its `path` if one is set — the file destination and the parent-wire destination are independent.

**Encapsulated maps are the documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule.** They have *N* output ports — one per externally-consumed write box, where *N* may be zero (pure side-effect map), one, or many. Every other box kind still has exactly one output.

**Rejected earlier design (2026-05-21):** packing all write-box outputs into a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, single wire out. Rejected 2026-05-23 because it would have repurposed file-writing machinery to emit strings into wires — substituting one mechanism for another. The symmetric toggle design preserves the `write` box's "terminate a value" semantics and treats the destination kind as a mode toggle.

**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to "user-defined functions" while staying graph-native.

**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or "how do users build libraries of behavior" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, blob-packed outputs) without explicitly weighing them against the symmetric-toggle shape. Both toggles (`externally-supplied` on data boxes, `externally-consumed` on write boxes) are the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate "ports manifest" file.

```

### project_soramech.md

```markdown
---
name: SoraMech project context
description: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.

**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.

**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.
- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).
- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).

**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**
- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.
- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.
- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.
- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.
- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.
- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.

**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.

```

### project_threading.md

```markdown
---
name: threading_model
description: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 SoraMech-owned C thread pool with per-port slots and language specs
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.

**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.

Key phase 3 concepts:
- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.
- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.
- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.
- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.
- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.
- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.
- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.
- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.
- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.
- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.
- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.

**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.

**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.

```

### project_yarq_and_third_ring.md

```markdown
---
name: YARQ and the third input ring (issue 320)
description: Per-port third ring carries box-JSON reconfigure messages; YARQ (yield-and-requeue) is the project name for the cooperative-with-scheduler barrier that protects in-place box mutation
type: project
originSessionId: 1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa
---
Issue 320 introduces two pieces of project vocabulary that
recur in other code-paths:

**YARQ** (yield-and-requeue) — the synchronization primitive
that protects in-place box mutation. Acquire is a CAS from 0
to 1 on a per-box atomic word. On acquire failure, the
contended worker does NOT busy-wait — it re-submits its own
task to the **tail** of the pool queue and returns, letting
the scheduler drain other work first. Same barrier is acquired
by every path that mutates a box's record (reconfigure,
runtime_connect from 319d). The point: synchronization
*cooperative with the scheduler*, not adversarial to it.
The user named it; the joke is that they want to name a dog
YARQ too.

**The third input ring** — every input slot grows a third ring
alongside the native + JSON pair from issue 312. Carries
box-JSON-shaped reconfigure messages. Per-PORT placement (not
per-box) — any input port can receive reconfigure cells, and
the per-cell ring-selector tag from issue 312/318a grows a
third value (`RING_RECONFIGURE`). When the consumer's
input-gather encounters a reconfigure cell, it retains
already-popped values, acquires YARQ, applies the reconfigure,
releases YARQ, and resumes gathering under the new config.

**Why:** Together with issue 319 (create_box / connect),
issue 320 gives the runtime its full "graph as a living
artifact" surface: 319 grows the graph (additive), 320
mutates what's already there (in-place). Many future features
will read or write these primitives — runtime DSLs, planner
boxes, the editor's live-mutation feedback path.

**How to apply:** When other issues touch box mutation,
slot rings, or per-cell ordering, treat YARQ and the third
ring as established vocabulary — don't reinvent the
primitive or the name. When the user mentions "reconfigure,"
"the third ring," or YARQ, they mean these specific pieces
of the design.

```

### reference_strategems.md

```markdown
---
name: Strategems directory

History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.\n\n**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy.       "content":"---\nname: threading_model\ndescription: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 SoraMech-owned C thread pool with per-port slots and language specs\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a\n---\n**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.\n\n**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.\n\nKey phase 3 concepts:\n- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.\n- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.\n- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.\n- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.\n- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.\n- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.\n- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.\n- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.\n- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.\n- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.\n- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.\n",

      "content":"---\nname: Cross-language wire format\ndescription: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c\n---\nDesign corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older \"JSON always\" framing.\n\n**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.\n\n**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.\n\n**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.\n\n**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.\n\n**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.\n\n**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer` (in-process callable address + signature), `$lang_opaque` (\"these bytes are language-X-internal\"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.\n\n**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.\n\n**Two compile-time layers stack:**\n- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.\n- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.\n\n**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):\n1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.\n2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's \"two rings per slot\" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.\n3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask \"is param 2 the length?\" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.\n",

      "content":"---\nname: Cross-language design pitfalls\ndescription: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format\ntype: feedback\noriginSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb\n---\nWhen designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.\n\n**1. Don't propose runtime \"handles\" that route operations back to the originating spec.**\n\n**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.\n\n**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The \"phone home\" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says \"operations on this value cross back to the source.\"\n\n**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**\n\n**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.\n\n**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.\n\n**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**\n\n**Why:** The user pointed out that \"discriminator\" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt \"which param is the length?\" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.\n\n**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message (\"destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here\").\n\n**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.\n",
      "filePath":"/home/ritz/.claude/projects/-mnt-mtwo-programs-sora-soramech/memory/feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md"
    }
  },

Wire color\nencodes routing kind, not language pairing. Two wires leaving the\nsame producer — one to a Lua consumer, one to a C consumer — look\nidentical.\n\nThe runtime treats those wires very differently: the same-language\nhop carries native bytes, the cross-language hop carries JSON\n(issue 312). The editor gives the box author no visual signal that\nthe JSON translation step exists. It's invisible until someone\nreads the dispatch code.\n\n## Concept\n\nWires are colored by **language pairing across the edge**, with a\nthird color for wires whose destination port has a user-written\ncustom translation (issue 246):\n\n- **Forest green** (`#228b22` or similar) — cross-language wire.\n  Producer and consumer are different languages; the runtime\n  translates via JSON at the wire. The default\ncontract is sufficient for primitives, strings, arrays, and\nobjects — the cases JSON's structure covers cleanly and the cases\nnative pass-through covers cleanly.\n\nA custom translation spec lets the user intervene at a specific\ninput port for **any reason** — not just cross-language\nambiguity. Two motivating cases:\n\n**Cross-language ambiguity.** Some translations cannot be\ninferred by the spec because the language constructs don't have\nuniversal mappings:\n\n- A C++ class with both data fields and method functions arrives\n  at a C box. C has no notion of methods; whether to expose them\n  as function pointers, drop them, or restructure into a tagged\n  union is a development-time decision the user has to make.\n- A `void *` arrives carrying a libcurl handle the receiving\n  language's spec has no general way to interpret.\n- A union type whose discriminator lives in a separate input\n\n=== issues/247-debug-build-and-per-box-statistics-lens.md ===\n# 247 — Debug build alternative and per-box statistics lens\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nThe Compile button currently produces one artifact: a release\nbuild of the map. Box authors who want to know which boxes are\nslow, which fire often, or which produce variably-sized outputs\nhave no editor-side way to see it — the run-output JSONL exists\n(`tmp/last-run.jsonl`) but reading it requires leaving the\neditor.\n\nThis issue adds two things that work together:\n\n1. **Compile-button alternatives.** A small dropdown (right-click\n   the button, or a tiny arrow next to it) opens a menu of build\n   modes. The filter is a small\n   panel in the editor — \"color by: run count / speed /\n   consistency / cumulative time\" — and the canvas re-tints as\n   the user picks.\n\n=== issues/248-encapsulated-map-as-box.md ===\n# 248 — Encapsulated map as box\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nA map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the\ntop-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to\nopen a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*\non the currently-edited parent map.     "originalFile":"---\nname: Cross-language wire format\ndescription: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c\n---\nDesign corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older \"JSON always\" framing.\n\n**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.\n\n**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.\n\n**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.\n\n**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.\n\n**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.\n\n**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer` (in-process callable address + signature), `$lang_opaque` (\"these bytes are language-X-internal\"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.\n\n**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.\n\n**Two compile-time layers stack:**\n- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.\n- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.\n\n**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):\n1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.\n2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's \"two rings per slot\" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.\n3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask \"is param 2 the length?\" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.\n",

          "content":"---\nname: Editor visual language for wires\ndescription: Wire color in the canvas editor encodes language pairing across the edge, not just routing kind — a UI invariant future work should respect (issue 245)\ntype: project\n---\n\n**Wires are colored by language pairing across the edge**, with a separate color for wires whose destination port carries a user-written custom translation (issue 246). Pre-245 wires were colored purely by routing kind (default slate-blue, comparator branches orange/blue/green).\n\n**The pairing-based palette:**\n- **Same-language hop** — the wire carries native bytes; default neutral color.\n- **Cross-language hop (forest green, ~`#228b22`)** — different producer/consumer languages; runtime translates via JSON at the wire. The color is a standing reminder that encode + decode is happening on that hop.\n- **Custom-translation hop** — a third distinct color signaling the destination port has a user-written translation spec overriding the default path.\n- Branch-routing colors (orange/blue/green from comparator boxes) compose on top — routing kind and language pairing are orthogonal axes the editor must show simultaneously.\n\n**Why:** The runtime treats same-lang and cross-lang hops very differently (dual-ring slot design, issue 312), but pre-245 the editor gave the box author no visual signal that the JSON translation step existed. It was invisible until someone read the dispatch code. Translation cost should be legible from the canvas.\n\n**How to apply:** Any future editor work that touches wire rendering must preserve \"color encodes language pairing.\" Don't propose recoloring schemes that overload the cross-language signal onto another concept. New routing concepts get new axes (line style, glyphs, animation) rather than stealing color. When discussing wire visuals, name both axes — routing kind AND language pairing — even if only one is changing.\n",

          "content":"---\nname: Encapsulated map as box\ndescription: A sub-map can be opened as a single box on a parent canvas, with externally-supplied data boxes becoming input ports and write boxes packed into one output blob (issue 248)\ntype: project\n---\n\n**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.\n\n**The encapsulation contract:**\n- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map (the existing language-agnostic file-IO source) can be toggled \"externally-supplied\" in its inspector. Toggling declares the value comes from the encapsulating context rather than the box's `path` or `value`. Each externally-supplied data box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box on the parent canvas.\n- **Outputs:** the sub-map's `write` boxes are collected and packed into a single byte-blob output with a leading size index. One wire leaves the encapsulated box; the parent destructures the blob downstream if it wants the pieces.\n\n**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to \"user-defined functions\" while staying graph-native.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or \"how do users build libraries of behavior\" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, etc.) without explicitly weighing them against the encapsulated-map shape. The externally-supplied toggle on `data` boxes is the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate \"ports manifest\" file.\n",

          "content":"---\nname: Custom translation specs per port\ndescription: Users can override the default native/JSON wire path on any input port for any reason — a knob in the wire format vocabulary (issue 246)\ntype: project\n---\n\n**Per-port custom translation specs** let the user intervene at a specific input port and replace the default dual-ring decode path with user-written code. The override applies to that one port; the rest of the graph uses the default native-or-JSON path from issue 312.\n\n**Motivating cases (any reason qualifies, not just cross-language):**\n- Cross-language ambiguity the default specs can't infer: a C++ class with methods landing at a C box (drop methods? expose as fn pointers? restructure?), a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a union whose discriminator is on a separate wire.\n- Same-language reshape: massaging a value into a different shape on its way in (rename fields, drop a layer, project a subset) without adding a transform box on the canvas.\n- Validation / coercion: clamp a number, enforce a schema, fail loudly on unexpected shapes.\n\n**How it composes with the dual-ring design:**\n- The custom spec runs at *pop* time on the consumer side, after the ordering ring has been consulted and the cell has been read from the appropriate ring. The user's code receives the decoded value (native or JSON-decoded) and produces whatever the consumer's `invoke` will see.\n- A port with a custom translation gets its own wire color in the editor (issue 245) — visible signal that this port doesn't use the default path.\n\n**Why:** The default native/JSON contract covers the cases JSON's structure handles cleanly. Everything outside that needs a user escape hatch — *and* the same hatch is useful for purely-local \"I want this input shaped differently\" cases. One mechanism, many uses.\n\n**How to apply:** When the design needs an override knob on the cross-language path, propose \"custom translation spec on the destination port\" rather than inventing per-function annotations, type discriminator metadata, or producer-side conversion hints (all three were rejected — see feedback_cross_language_pitfalls).     "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# 319 — Built-in library for map self-construction\n\n## Status\nopen — planning stub. Several design questions need user resolution\nbefore implementation can begin. See **Open design questions**\nbelow.\n\n## Concept\n\nA map should be able to build more of itself while running.\nTwo built-in primitives, exposed by the runtime to every language\nspec, are enough to bootstrap that capability:\n\n- **`create_box(filepath, function_name) -> box_handle`**\n  Spawn a new box on the currently-running map. The first argument\n  is the file holding the function the box will run; the second is\n  the name of that function inside the file. The runtime does any\n  build-pipeline work that's needed (compile the source, register\n  the spec, allocate the box's input port slots) before returning\n  a handle the caller can use to wire the box up.\n\n- **`connect(from_box, to_box_a, to_box_b, ...) -> bool`**\n  Attach a wire from the single output of `from_box` to each of\n  the destination boxes. Variadic on the destinations, since fan-out\n  from a single producer is the common pattern. Returns true if\n  every connection succeeded, false otherwise.\n\nTogether these let a running map grow new sub-graphs in response\nto runtime conditions: a planner box decides what sub-pipeline to\nbuild, calls `create_box` for each node, calls `connect` to wire\nthem, and the dispatch layer picks up the new region on the next\npush.\n\n## Why this shape works (and the parts that need to be checked)\n\n**Single-output-per-box is already the law.** Issue 218 collapsed\nboxes to one output. Variadic destinations on `connect` is just\nfan-out across that single output — no new concept on the wire\nside. The variadic part of the API matches the data model.\n\n**`filepath + function_name` matches box JSON.** That's already how\nlanguage specs locate the code a box runs. The API takes the same\ntwo strings the box JSON would hold.\n\n**Handle-as-return mirrors `data` boxes' encapsulation contract\n(issue 248).** Encapsulated maps already expose typed handles\nto externally-supplied inputs. A `create_box` handle is the same\nkind of thing — a reference the caller uses to identify the box\nin follow-up calls.\n\n## Open design questions\n\nThese are real forks in the design. Each one changes what the\nimplementation looks like; none have a default answer that's\nobviously right.\n\n### Q1 — When does the new box exist?\n\nPhase 3's runtime assumes input-port slots are **allocated at\ngraph load and durable for the run** (per the threading model:\n\"per-input-port slots, not per-task, allocated at graph load\").\n`create_box` at runtime contradicts this directly. Three shapes\nare possible:\n\n- **(a) Runtime growth.** The slot store gains an `append` primitive;\n  new boxes get fresh slots allocated mid-run. Cheapest API for the\n  user, biggest impact on the slot store invariants.\n- **(b) Build-time only.** `create_box` is a *compile-time* call —\n  it runs during graph load, not during dispatch. A planner box that\n  wants dynamic structure has to declare its sub-graph at build time\n  with conditional connections. Cleanest for the runtime, weakest\n  for the use case.\n- **(c) Sandboxed region.** New boxes go into a separate\n  \"dynamic region\" with its own slot store that grows. The\n  original graph stays frozen. Lets us preserve the load-time\n  invariant for the static portion.\n\nWhich one does the user want?\n\n### Q2 — Which input port does `connect` target?\n\nA box has multiple input ports. `connect(from_box, to_box_a, ...)`\ndoesn't say which port on `to_box_a` receives the wire. Options:\n\n- **(a) Variadic of pairs:** `connect(from_box, {to_a, \"x\"}, {to_b, \"y\"})`\n  — explicit per destination, more typing.\n- **(b) Implicit first-free port:** the runtime picks the lowest-indexed\n  unwired input port on each destination. Cheap, surprising in mixed\n  cases.\n- **(c) Port-on-handle:** the handle returned by `create_box` carries\n  per-port sub-handles; `connect(from_box.output, to_box.input_x)`.\n  Verbose at call sites, unambiguous everywhere.\n\n### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash\n\nCLAUDE.md says \"prefer error messages and breaking functionality\nover fallbacks\" and \"nil checks are just asking for errors.\" A\nbool return on `connect` is exactly the shape that invites silent\nignoring. Two paths:\n\n- **(a) Keep bool.** The caller is expected to branch on it. Matches\n  the user's draft.\n- **(b) Hard-crash with reason.** `connect` returns nothing; on any\n  failure it aborts the program with a plain-English message\n  (\"can't connect box X to box Y: Y has no free input ports\").\n  Matches the project-wide error policy elsewhere.\n\n### Q4 — What is the \"box handle\" actually?\n\nThe user wrote \"pointer to the box.\" In a single-process runner the\nliteral pointer works, but it can't survive wire crossings or be\npassed across the cross-language JSON wire (the wire format forbids\nhandles that back-route to the owning spec). Options:\n\n- **(a) Stable string id** (the existing `box_id` from the JSON\n  schema). Survives serialization. Slower lookup in the dispatch\n  layer.\n- **(b) In-process `$ref` sentinel.** Fast in the calling spec,\n  must be unwrapped before crossing a language boundary.\n- **(c) Both:** the handle is a small struct carrying both the\n  fast pointer and the durable id; the wire layer keeps only the\n  id when it crosses.\n\n### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline?\n\nThe user said \"compile it (if necessary) and other map-wide tasks.\"\nThe build pipeline (issues 217–222) currently lives on the server /\ncompile-button side. If `create_box` runs at runtime, the runner\ngains a dependency on the compiler. That crosses the program-\nseparation boundary documented in `project_soramech`:\n\"Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server.\nMap directory format is the only shared contract.\"\n\nEither the runner gains the compiler as a library (changing the\nthree-program separation), or `create_box` requires the source to\nbe pre-compiled and merely *registers* the resulting artifact\n(simpler, but the user has to do the build step separately).\n\n## Suggested implementation steps (after Q1–Q5 are resolved)\n\n1. Resolve the open design questions; update this issue with the\n   chosen shape before any code is written.\n2. Add the two built-ins to the language-spec contract\n   (`lang_spec_t` — the runtime exposes them via the spec's\n   built-in table; each language spec wraps them in its native\n   calling convention).\n3. Extend the slot store with the growth primitive Q1 selects\n   (if Q1 picks (a) or (c)).\n4. Add dispatch-layer logic for newly-created boxes — they need to\n   participate in the same push-on-arrival mechanism as static\n   boxes.\n5. Tests under `tests/`: a small map whose first box uses\n   `create_box` + `connect` to build a downstream pipeline, then\n   runs end-to-end and validates outputs.\n6. Update `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` to describe the\n   self-construction contract and the slot-store growth shape.\n7. Update phase-3-progress.md.\n\n## Related issues and documents\n\n- 248 — encapsulated map as box (the function-like abstraction\n  these primitives could be used to construct ad-hoc).\n- 302 — wire value slot store (the structure that needs the growth\n  primitive in Q1).\n- 218 — single output per box (justifies the variadic-on-destinations\n  shape).\n- 217–222 — compile pipeline (relevant to Q5).\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — current threading model these\n  primitives must fit inside.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/319-builtin-library-for-map-self-construction.md"
        },

At runtime: a small durable record holding its language handle (e.g. a `lua_State` slot), its input port slot indices, and its output edge list.\n\n- **Input port** — a named position on a box where values arrive. A box may have many. Each port owns exactly one **slot**.\n\n- **Output** — a single value-producing position. **One per box** (issue 218). Fan-out is achieved by having multiple wires *leave* the one output.\n\n- **Slot** — a ring buffer (or atomic counter) belonging to one input port. The receptacle a producer's value lands in when a wire is \"pushed.\" Five variants per the header you just saw: 1-cell peek, N-cell pop, N-cell pop tagged, atomic counter, large-value.\n\n- **Slot store** — the pool that holds all slots for the whole graph. Allocated once at **graph load**. Per-slot locks on the hot path; **no allocator-wide lock**. That last clause is the load-bearing one for Q1.\n\n- **Graph load** — the moment, before any task runs, when the C runner reads every `boxes/<id>.json`, builds the in-memory box records, counts how many slots each box's input ports need, and asks the slot store to allocate them all at once. After this finishes, the slot store's size is frozen.\n\n- **Dispatch layer** — the worker-side state machine. When a value lands in a box's last empty input slot, the dispatcher spawns a **task** for that box. The task pops its inputs, invokes the spec, pushes the output into downstream slots, ends. Tasks carry just `box_id` + a counter snapshot; everything else lives in the durable box record and the durable slots.\n\n- **Worker** — a thread in the C pool. Every \"push into downstream input slot\" is a write into the store; every \"pop\" is a read. Allocation happened once, at load.\n\nNow drop `create_box` into a running spec:\n\n```\n            [BOX A]\n           .─────.\n           │ run │  ◀── spec is executing, calls:\n           '─────'      handle = create_box(\"foo.lua\", \"bar\")\n              │\n              ▼\n   ┌──────────────────────────────────┐\n   │ runtime built-in implementation  │\n   │                                  │\n   │  1. resolve foo.lua : bar        │\n   │  2. The header literally encodes this: \"Lifetime is the run. Slots are freed when the store is destroyed at the end of the run.\" There is no `slot_grow` primitive, and the per-slot locking strategy was chosen *because* the slot **array** itself never moves — once a slot's index is handed out, the pointer to it is stable forever, so readers can cache the address.\n\nIf the array can grow, two things go wrong:\n- **Reallocation moves slots.** A `realloc`-style grow invalidates every cached slot pointer that any worker is mid-write on.\n- **The lock-free hot path becomes lockful.** Adding even a single rwlock around the slot array to protect grow-vs-access kills the \"no allocator-wide lock\" property the header is bragging about.\n\n## The three options, against the break\n\n**(a) Runtime growth — let the slot store grow in place.** Means redesigning the slot store's storage so slot pointers stay stable across growth (e.g. a two-level table: chunks of N slots each, append a new chunk to grow; old chunks never move; readers index by `chunk_idx, slot_in_chunk`). The hot path stays lock-free *if* you accept that \"what slots exist\" is observed via an atomic counter that workers re-read. Implementation cost is real but bounded; conceptual cost is that *every* runtime structure that the dispatcher walks (edge lists, box records) needs the same treatment. The user pays nothing at the API; the system grows a lot of concurrency machinery.\n\n**(b) Build-time only — `create_box` runs during graph load, not during dispatch.** The built-in is callable, but only from a special \"graph build\" phase before any task runs. A planner box that wants dynamic structure has to declare every possible sub-graph statically with conditional connections (which already exists via comparator branching). Cheapest for the runtime; effectively says **self-construction isn't really self-construction** — it's just code-driven graph authoring at startup. The user loses \"the planner box decides what to build at runtime\" entirely.\n\n**(c) Sandboxed dynamic region — a second slot store for new boxes.** Original graph's store stays frozen, lock-free, untouched. New boxes from `create_box` go into a separate growable store. Edges from static-into-dynamic and dynamic-into-dynamic are allowed; edges from dynamic-into-static are forbidden (because that would require pushing into a static box's slot from an unknown-at-load-time producer, which breaks compile-time slot sizing). The dispatcher gains a \"which region?\" lookup before every push, paying a small constant cost. Conceptually clean: the part of the graph that knew about itself at compile time stays the way it was; the part that grew at runtime lives in its own world.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThe split between (a) and (c) is the same split you see in OS kernels between \"monolithic allocator\" and \"per-arena allocator.\" (a) generalizes the existing thing to handle the new case; (c) puts the new case in its own room so the old thing stays simple. Soramech's existing rule \"boxes are durable, tasks are ephemeral\" already chose the per-arena flavor at the *task* level — (c) extends that same philosophy one level up to the *box* level.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n**The way the three options frame the use case:**\n\n- (a) says *the runtime adapts to dynamic structure.*\n- (b) says *dynamic structure isn't really runtime; bring it back to load time.*\n- (c) says *static and dynamic are different beasts; let them live in different houses.*\n\n## My read (yours to override)\n\nI'd lean (c). The lock-free hot-path invariant in the slot store is load-bearing — it's the reason phase 3's throughput story works at all. Option (a) preserves the user API but pays for it by complicating the runtime structure that's already the most concurrency-sensitive code in the project. Option (b) is the cheapest to build but seems to defeat the use case you actually want (a planner box building sub-pipelines in response to LLM output is a runtime decision, not a load-time one). Option (c) gives you the runtime decision while letting the existing slot store stay exactly as it is.\n\nWhich way do you want it? Once you decide, I'll fold the resolution into the issue file's Open Design Questions section (Q1 collapses to a chosen answer plus a short \"why\")."

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Great answers in your question — let me take the three terms first, then your design, then a side observation that just emerged that I want you to confirm before I memorize it.\n\n## \"Allocator-wide lock\" — the thing we are *not* paying for\n\nImagine the slot store had **one mutex** at the top, and every `push` and every `pop` from any worker on any slot had to grab it. Worker A pushing to slot 5 would block worker B popping from slot 99 — totally unrelated operations, serialized. That's an allocator-wide lock. The slot store explicitly avoids it by giving each slot its own tiny lock (a one-byte `atomic_flag` spinlock) for header mutation; the global pool has no lock at all on the read/write path. Throughput therefore scales with the *number of slots being touched at once*, not the number of workers, which is the property that makes the C pool worth building. Anything we add for dynamic growth has to preserve this — that's the constraint Q1 was really probing.\n\n## \"Counter snapshot\" — the iterator-ordering tag\n\nWhen an **iterator box** spawns tasks (it's the kind that fires repeatedly, once per element of some sequence), every task gets the iterator's counter value frozen at spawn time. Two reasons it travels with the task:\n\n1. **The dispatch layer needs to know which \"iteration\" this task represents** when it pushes the output downstream. If the consumer slot is in `SLOT_TAGGED` mode (from the header), the push attaches this counter as the cell's tag, and the consumer pops in iterator-counter order rather than arrival order. This is how parallel iterator tasks can run out-of-order across workers but the downstream box still sees them in iteration order.\n2. **For comparator/randomizer routing decisions**, the counter snapshot lets the task make a deterministic per-iteration choice (e.g. randomizer with a seeded PRNG keyed off the counter).\n\nSo it's not just an integer — it's the **task's identity within its parent box's iteration sequence**, used both for downstream ordering tags and for any per-iteration routing the dispatcher does.\n\n## Your two-level table design — does it solve Q1? Mostly yes, with one subtlety\n\nYour intuition is exactly right: hold pointers in an index table, and the slots themselves never move. The thing I want to make explicit is that **the table itself also needs to grow without moving**, or readers cache a stale table pointer:\n\n```\n [ index table — chunked, append-only ]\n   chunk 0: [ s0* | s1* | s2* | ... | s63* ]\n   chunk 1: [ s64* | s65* | ... | s127* ]\n   chunk 2: [ s128* | ... ]                   ← new chunk appended on growth\n       ▲\n       │ slot_idx 5 lives at chunk[0][5]\n       │ slot_idx 200 lives at chunk[3][8]\n       │\n   workers read this concurrently while writers append new chunks\n```\n\nThe two-level shape is what makes this safe lock-free:\n\n- **Slots themselves**: never move, ever. Once allocated, the pointer is stable for the run.\n- **Index table top level**: a small array of chunk pointers. Adding a chunk writes a single pointer slot at the next free top-level index, then bumps an atomic \"chunks in use\" counter. Readers re-read the counter on lookup. No realloc, no copy, no movement.\n- **Within a chunk**: also append-only. Workers atomic-increment a per-chunk \"next free slot index\" to claim a slot during `create_box`, then publish the slot pointer at that index.\n\nCost per access: one extra indirection (read the chunk pointer, then the slot pointer). One extra cache line if the chunk pointer isn't already in L1. That's the price for collapsing static and dynamic into one mechanism, and it's small enough to pipeline away.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThis is the **same shape Linux uses for its file descriptor table** (per-process FD table, grows as new FDs are opened, FD numbers stay stable forever, lookups are O(1) with one indirection). The pattern is general because it satisfies one specific requirement: \"handles must stay stable under concurrent growth.\" Anywhere that requirement appears, this two-level chunked-append structure is a reliable answer.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n## Removal (the 315-style box breakdown)\n\nIf a box is destroyed mid-run, its slots' table entries can't be reused without an **ABA hazard** — worker A reads \"slot 17 points to X,\" sleeps, slot 17 gets freed and reallocated to point at Y, worker A wakes up and writes to Y thinking it's still X. Two clean ways out:\n\n- **Tombstone the index** — mark dead, never reuse the slot index. Wastes a slot of address space per destroyed box but is cheapest to implement and safest.\n- **Generation counter on the handle** — handles become `(index, generation)`; reuse bumps the generation; readers compare and abort if stale.\n\nRecommend tombstoning unless 315 expects so much churn that wasted indices accumulate. Worth deferring the decision to whenever 315 actually lands.\n\n## Side observation — the \"encapsulated maps are the only multi-output boxes\" thing\n\nYou dropped a load-bearing fact: **encapsulated maps (248) and possibly 313 produce multiple outputs**, breaking the \"single output per box\" rule from issue 218. Before I write that into memory or update 248's design, I want to confirm what you mean:\n\n- **Option A:** Encapsulation in 248 *stays* single-output (one byte-blob with size index, as the issue currently says), and your comment is about the **unzipped runtime view** — inside, the unzipped sub-graph has multiple `write` boxes, each of which is itself a single-output box. From the outside-of-the-wrapper view, it's still one output (the blob).\n- **Option B:** You're **amending 248**: encapsulated maps in their wrapper form actually have multiple distinct outputs (one per `write` box), not a packed blob. This would update 248 and require a corresponding update to memory.\n\nWhich one? It changes whether I touch 248 or just note the unzipping behavior.\n\n## Q1 resolution — written into the issue\n\nLet me fold your decision in now.\n</br>"
