```json
    "originalFile":"# 319 — Built-in library for map self-construction\n\n## Status\nopen — planning stub. Several design questions need user resolution\nbefore implementation can begin. See **Open design questions**\nbelow.\n\n## Concept\n\nA map should be able to build more of itself while running.\nTwo built-in primitives, exposed by the runtime to every language\nspec, are enough to bootstrap that capability:\n\n- **`create_box(filepath, function_name) -> box_handle`**\n  Spawn a new box on the currently-running map. The first argument\n  is the file holding the function the box will run; the second is\n  the name of that function inside the file. The runtime does any\n  build-pipeline work that's needed (compile the source, register\n  the spec, allocate the box's input port slots) before returning\n  a handle the caller can use to wire the box up.\n\n- **`connect(from_box, to_box_a, to_box_b, ...) -> bool`**\n  Attach a wire from the single output of `from_box` to each of\n  the destination boxes. Variadic on the destinations, since fan-out\n  from a single producer is the common pattern. Returns true if\n  every connection succeeded, false otherwise.\n\nTogether these let a running map grow new sub-graphs in response\nto runtime conditions: a planner box decides what sub-pipeline to\nbuild, calls `create_box` for each node, calls `connect` to wire\nthem, and the dispatch layer picks up the new region on the next\npush.\n\n## Why this shape works (and the parts that need to be checked)\n\n**Single-output-per-box is already the law.** Issue 218 collapsed\nboxes to one output. Variadic destinations on `connect` is just\nfan-out across that single output — no new concept on the wire\nside. The variadic part of the API matches the data model.\n\n**`filepath + function_name` matches box JSON.** That's already how\nlanguage specs locate the code a box runs. The API takes the same\ntwo strings the box JSON would hold.\n\n**Handle-as-return mirrors `data` boxes' encapsulation contract\n(issue 248).** Encapsulated maps already expose typed handles\nto externally-supplied inputs. A `create_box` handle is the same\nkind of thing — a reference the caller uses to identify the box\nin follow-up calls.\n\n## Open design questions\n\nThese are real forks in the design. Each one changes what the\nimplementation looks like; none have a default answer that's\nobviously right.\n\n### Q1 — When does the new box exist?\n\nPhase 3's runtime assumes input-port slots are **allocated at\ngraph load and durable for the run** (per the threading model:\n\"per-input-port slots, not per-task, allocated at graph load\").\n`create_box` at runtime contradicts this directly. Three shapes\nare possible:\n\n- **(a) Runtime growth.** The slot store gains an `append` primitive;\n  new boxes get fresh slots allocated mid-run. Cheapest API for the\n  user, biggest impact on the slot store invariants.\n- **(b) Build-time only.** `create_box` is a *compile-time* call —\n  it runs during graph load, not during dispatch. A planner box that\n  wants dynamic structure has to declare its sub-graph at build time\n  with conditional connections. Cleanest for the runtime, weakest\n  for the use case.\n- **(c) Sandboxed region.** New boxes go into a separate\n  \"dynamic region\" with its own slot store that grows. The\n  original graph stays frozen. Lets us preserve the load-time\n  invariant for the static portion.\n\nWhich one does the user want?\n\n### Q2 — Which input port does `connect` target?\n\nA box has multiple input ports. `connect(from_box, to_box_a, ...)`\ndoesn't say which port on `to_box_a` receives the wire. Options:\n\n- **(a) Variadic of pairs:** `connect(from_box, {to_a, \"x\"}, {to_b, \"y\"})`\n  — explicit per destination, more typing.\n- **(b) Implicit first-free port:** the runtime picks the lowest-indexed\n  unwired input port on each destination. Cheap, surprising in mixed\n  cases.\n- **(c) Port-on-handle:** the handle returned by `create_box` carries\n  per-port sub-handles; `connect(from_box.output, to_box.input_x)`.\n  Verbose at call sites, unambiguous everywhere.\n\n### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash\n\nCLAUDE.md says \"prefer error messages and breaking functionality\nover fallbacks\" and \"nil checks are just asking for errors.\" A\nbool return on `connect` is exactly the shape that invites silent\nignoring. Two paths:\n\n- **(a) Keep bool.** The caller is expected to branch on it. Matches\n  the user's draft.\n- **(b) Hard-crash with reason.** `connect` returns nothing; on any\n  failure it aborts the program with a plain-English message\n  (\"can't connect box X to box Y: Y has no free input ports\").\n  Matches the project-wide error policy elsewhere.\n\n### Q4 — What is the \"box handle\" actually?\n\nThe user wrote \"pointer to the box.\" In a single-process runner the\nliteral pointer works, but it can't survive wire crossings or be\npassed across the cross-language JSON wire (the wire format forbids\nhandles that back-route to the owning spec). Options:\n\n- **(a) Stable string id** (the existing `box_id` from the JSON\n  schema). Survives serialization. Slower lookup in the dispatch\n  layer.\n- **(b) In-process `$ref` sentinel.** Fast in the calling spec,\n  must be unwrapped before crossing a language boundary.\n- **(c) Both:** the handle is a small struct carrying both the\n  fast pointer and the durable id; the wire layer keeps only the\n  id when it crosses.\n\n### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline?\n\nThe user said \"compile it (if necessary) and other map-wide tasks.\"\nThe build pipeline (issues 217–222) currently lives on the server /\ncompile-button side. If `create_box` runs at runtime, the runner\ngains a dependency on the compiler. That crosses the program-\nseparation boundary documented in `project_soramech`:\n\"Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server.\nMap directory format is the only shared contract.\"\n\nEither the runner gains the compiler as a library (changing the\nthree-program separation), or `create_box` requires the source to\nbe pre-compiled and merely *registers* the resulting artifact\n(simpler, but the user has to do the build step separately).\n\n## Suggested implementation steps (after Q1–Q5 are resolved)\n\n1. Resolve the open design questions; update this issue with the\n   chosen shape before any code is written.\n2. Add the two built-ins to the language-spec contract\n   (`lang_spec_t` — the runtime exposes them via the spec's\n   built-in table; each language spec wraps them in its native\n   calling convention).\n3. Extend the slot store with the growth primitive Q1 selects\n   (if Q1 picks (a) or (c)).\n4. Add dispatch-layer logic for newly-created boxes — they need to\n   participate in the same push-on-arrival mechanism as static\n   boxes.\n5. Tests under `tests/`: a small map whose first box uses\n   `create_box` + `connect` to build a downstream pipeline, then\n   runs end-to-end and validates outputs.\n6. Update `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` to describe the\n   self-construction contract and the slot-store growth shape.\n7. Update phase-3-progress.md.\n\n## Related issues and documents\n\n- 248 — encapsulated map as box (the function-like abstraction\n  these primitives could be used to construct ad-hoc).\n- 302 — wire value slot store (the structure that needs the growth\n  primitive in Q1).\n- 218 — single output per box (justifies the variadic-on-destinations\n  shape).\n- 217–222 — compile pipeline (relevant to Q5).\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — current threading model these\n  primitives must fit inside.\n",
```

```json
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Three threads to pull on, all interesting. Let me take them in order.\n\n## \"Double-buffered ring-buffer\" for the index table — checking what we're solving\n\nWant to make sure we're talking about the same growth event before picking machinery. Two candidates, very different shapes:\n\n**(A) Index table growth** — the top-level structure that maps \"slot index N\" to \"this slot lives at address X.\" This grows when new boxes are added.\n\n**(B) Individual ring buffer growth** — a single input port's cells, when the user pushes 200 values before the consumer fires.\n\nDouble-buffering — allocate a new larger version, copy contents, atomically swap a pointer, wait for old readers to drain, free the old — is a **real and robust pattern** (it's the core idea behind RCU in the Linux kernel). It's the right answer for **(B)** the individual ring buffer growth, because each slot already has its own lock, and growth happens under that lock: take the lock, allocate new ring, copy cells, swap, release. Old readers can't exist because they couldn't have held the lock concurrently. Clean.\n\nFor **(A)** the index table, double-buffering works but is overkill — we'd be paying for the copy on every growth event when we don't have to copy at all. The chunked-append shape I described skips copying entirely:\n\n```\ntop-level array (sized large at startup, e.g. 1024 slots)\n   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n   │ chunk0* │ chunk1* │ chunk2* │ NULL │ NULL │ ... │   │\n   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n       │         │         │\n       ▼         ▼         ▼\n     [64 slot ptrs]  [64 slot ptrs]  [64 slot ptrs]\n\ngrowth = \"write a chunk pointer to the next NULL top-level slot,\n          bump the atomic chunks-in-use counter\"\nno copy, no swap, no drain.\n```\n\nChunked-append is more robust *for this case* because there's no swap-and-drain race surface at all — readers see either old size or new size, and any size they see is valid. The user pays one pointer indirection per slot lookup forever.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\n\"Most robust\" is context-dependent. Double-buffer-with-swap is the most robust shape **when contents must be copied** (a value-array growing). Chunked-append is the most robust shape **when handles must stay stable** (a pointer-array growing). We need the second; you're suggesting the first. Different tools for different growth patterns.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n**Suggestion:** chunked-append for the index table (A), double-buffer-with-swap under the per-slot lock for individual ring buffer growth (B). Both robust, neither overpaying. Sound right?\n\n## Removal — your refcount intuition is exactly right\n\nYou nailed it. The ABA hazard I described **only exists in a world without proper refcounting**. With 315's refcount discipline:\n\n- A box's refcount drops to zero **only when no other box references it as a producer or consumer** — meaning no future task can ever push to its slots or pop from its outputs.\n- Any worker that needs to access the box must already hold a reference, which keeps the count > 0.\n- So \"refcount went to zero\" is a *proof* that no worker has the pointer.\n- After zero, tearing down and reusing the slot index is safe.\n\nSo scratch tombstoning. **315's refcount is the safety mechanism** — slot reuse is fine once refcount has gone to zero. The simpler design wins. I'll update the issue.\n\n## The encapsulated-map \"no return values\" realization — this is a genuine design unlock\n\nYou're seeing something important. Let me walk it out:\n\nThe model right now: **a box's output is consumed by other boxes via wires. Files/RAM are written by dedicated `write` boxes.** There's no third channel. There's no \"return value to the outside world\" because there's no outside world — every value either flows to another box on a wire, or to a file via a `write` box.\n\nA `.map` file is self-contained under this rule. It has wires inside, `write` boxes inside, and no concept of \"the value the map produces.\" If you encapsulate it into a parent, the question is: **how does any value cross the encapsulation boundary going outward?**\n\nThree shapes — only one feels right to me:\n\n- **(α) Blob output via repurposed write machinery.** Your rejection: re-targeting `write` machinery away from files toward strings/wires is ugly. Agreed.\n- **(β) Multi-output via every `write` box becoming an output port.** Still repurposes `write` boxes. Same ugliness.\n- **(γ) Symmetric to the input side: a *new* opt-in toggle on `write` boxes that emits-to-parent-wire instead of writing to a file.** The `write` box keeps its semantics (\"I terminate a value\"); the toggle just chooses the *destination kind*. Input side already has this exact shape (a `data` box toggled to \"externally-supplied\" gets its value from a parent wire instead of a file). Output side is the mirror: a `write` box toggled to \"externally-consumed\" sends its value to a parent wire instead of a file.\n\nUnder (γ):\n- An encapsulated map has **as many output ports as it has `write` boxes toggled to externally-consumed**. Could be zero (pure side-effect map), one (the common case), or many (the \"this is the only multi-output box kind\" exception you flagged).\n- The single-output-per-box rule (issue 218) gets a footnote: \"exception — encapsulated maps, where each externally-consumed `write` box surfaces as a distinct output port.\"\n- No machinery is repurposed. `write` boxes still terminate values; they just have a destination switch.\n- The encapsulation contract becomes beautifully symmetric: `data` boxes marked one way become inputs; `write` boxes marked one way become outputs.\n\n**This is an amendment to 248** and worth writing into the issue + memory. It rejects the byte-blob design in 248's current text.\n\nBefore I update anything — does (γ) match what you're seeing? Or are you pulling toward \"encapsulated maps simply have no outward outputs at all and parent boxes consume via shared file paths in tmp/\"? That's a fourth option that keeps single-output-per-box pristine but pushes coordination burden onto the user (file paths must agree across encapsulation boundaries).\n\nOnce you pick, I'll:\n1. Update the 319 issue with the refcount-not-tombstone amendment and the chunked-append/double-buffer split.\n2. Either amend 248 (if you pick γ) or just memorize the design rule under your chosen shape.\n\nReady for your call."
```

## [147]

```json
{
  "uuid":"acdb9ea6-2c2f-475e-ac31-d5972d5abcb4",
  "type":"user",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-23T18:01:45.217Z",
  "parentUuid":"501140a0-c343-422e-a8af-9d9716c34690",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "numLines":466,
      "startLine":1,
      "totalLines":466,
      "content":"# 248 — Encapsulated map as box\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nA map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the\ntop-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to\nopen a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*\non the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a\nsingle box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from input\nports inside the sub-map that have been marked as\nexternally-supplied; its outputs come from the sub-map's\n`write` boxes, packed into a single byte-blob with a leading\nsize index.\n\nEncapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.\nThe parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box\nwith declared input ports, declared output ports, and known\nsemantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across\nparent maps, and packaged once for distribution.\n\n## Marked input ports inside the sub-map\n\nA **data** box inside the sub-map (kind: `data`, the existing\nlanguage-agnostic file-IO source) can be marked as\n**externally-supplied** via a small toggle on the box's\ninspector. Toggling declares: \"this data box's value comes from\nthe encapsulating context, not from its `path` or `value`\nfield.\"\n\nThe toggle is intentionally scoped to `data` boxes — those are\nthe natural entry points for external values into a map. Call\nboxes / read boxes / write boxes don't carry the toggle, which\nkeeps the inspector uncluttered for the common cases. Each\nexternal input becomes a small shared-memory chunk seeded by\nthe encapsulating call's invoke; the marked data box reads from\nthat chunk on each fire, treating it identically to a value\nloaded from disk.\n\nThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"sum_input\",\n    \"kind\": \"data\",\n    \"external\": {\n        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n        \"name\": \"count\",            // for named\n        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n    },\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nThree binding kinds capture how the encapsulating box's input\nmaps to this internal port:\n\n- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating\n  box has N input ports; the *k*th port's value flows to the\n  internal box whose `external.index` is *k*. Conceptually\n  matches positional function arguments.\n- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index. Same shape\n  as positional but the user picks the number (so they can leave\n  gaps, reorder freely, etc.).\n- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's\n  input port has a label; the matching internal box's\n  `external.name` is the same string.\n\nA single sub-map can mix kinds across its marked boxes — some\npositional, some named — and the parent map's encapsulated box\nexposes the union as its input ports.\n\n## Output collection from `write` boxes\n\nThe sub-map's `write` boxes (issue 229's file-write kind) become\nthe encapsulating box's output ports. Each `write` box's `value`\ninput feeds an output slot of the encapsulating box. The boxes\nkeep their normal disk-write behaviour (they write the file as a\nside effect) AND emit the value upward as the encapsulating\nbox's output.\n\nIf the sub-map has N write boxes, the encapsulating box has one\noutput wire carrying a packed byte-blob with all N values.\n\n### Packed output format\n\n```\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| size[0] | size[1] | ... | size[N-1] | 0       |   ← size index\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| data[0] (size[0] bytes)                       |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| data[1] (size[1] bytes)                       |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| ...                                           |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| data[N-1] (size[N-1] bytes)                   |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n```\n\nEach `size[i]` is a 4-byte unsigned little-endian integer. The\nsize array is **NULL-terminated** with a trailing zero, so a\nreader can walk it without knowing N up front. Data sections\nimmediately follow the size index, packed end-to-end with no\npadding.\n\nTo read field *i*:\n\n```\nsize_array_bytes = (i_count + 1) * 4     // includes terminator\noffset = size_array_bytes + sum(size[0..i-1])\ndata_i = blob[offset .. offset + size[i]]\n```\n\nThis is a self-describing format. The parent map can pull out\nindividual fields with the offset arithmetic, or pass the whole\nblob downstream and let further consumers slice it. A small\nhelper library (probably `libs/encap-output.{lua,c}`) packages\nthe unpack logic so consumers don't have to write the\narithmetic themselves.\n\n## File layout in the parent map\n\n**The encapsulating box is a normal `call` box.** From the\neditor's perspective it has the same JSON shape as any other\ncall box — `kind: \"call\"`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`,\n`connections`, `routing`. What makes it an encapsulation is\nthat its `lang` is `map` and its `ref` points to a sub-map\ndirectory rather than a source file. The map-language spec\n(`langs/map/spec.so`) is responsible for the \"behind the\nscenes\" processing — running the sub-graph and packing the\noutputs.\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"stats_pipeline\",\n    \"kind\": \"call\",\n    \"lang\": \"map\",\n    \"ref\": \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",\n    \"fn\": null,                                  // unused for map kind\n    \"inputs\": [\n        { \"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"int\" },\n        { \"name\": \"label\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n    ],\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nThe map-language spec is registered in the spec registry the\nsame way `lua` / `c` / `bash` are. Its `file_ext` is `.map`\n(or no extension if the ref points to a directory). The graph\nloader resolves the `ref`, the map spec's `init` (per worker)\nloads the sub-graph, and its `invoke` runs the sub-graph and\npacks the outputs. From the dispatch layer's view, an\nencapsulating call is just another spec invocation.\n\nThe sub-map's input ports (derived from its marked data boxes)\nare exposed on the encapsulating box's JSON as a normal\n`inputs` array. The user doesn't write that array themselves —\nthe editor generates it from the sub-map on first encapsulation\nand re-syncs it when the sub-map changes.\n\n## Editor UI\n\n### File browser\n\nThe file browser (issue 207's source-file-browser, or its\ndescendant) shows map directories with a distinct icon — a\nfolder-like glyph annotated to suggest \"this is a runnable\ngraph, not a source file.\" Clicking opens a small menu:\n\n- **Edit this map** — switches the editor's active map (the\n  existing map-select behaviour).\n- **Encapsulate** — adds the map as a `kind: \"map\"` box to the\n  currently-edited parent map. The new box appears on the\n  canvas at the cursor position; the user wires it in like any\n  other box.\n\n### Input-port slider\n\nThe inspector for any input port (on read / data / write boxes)\ngrows a small toggle next to the port name:\n\n```\n  ┌─────────────────────────────┐\n  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound\n  │   kind:    named            │\n  │   name:    \"count\"          │\n  └─────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nWhen the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector\n(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.\nWhen off, the port behaves normally (wires-in or literal-value).\n\nA map with no marked inputs encapsulates to a no-input box (just\na source of write-box outputs). A map with no write boxes\nencapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting only —\nunusual but legal).\n\n### Visual on the canvas\n\nThe encapsulating box renders distinctly — different border,\nmaybe a small \"sub-map\" badge — so the user sees at a glance\nthat this isn't a leaf call. Hovering shows the sub-map's name\nand a small thumbnail of its graph.\n\n## Runtime model — two paths, needs a decision\n\nTwo implementation paths exist. The encapsulating box being a\nnormal `call` box from the editor's perspective doesn't pick\nbetween them; the choice lives in what the map-language spec\ndoes behind the scenes and what (if anything) the compile\npipeline does at build time.\n\n### Path A — Compile-time inlining\n\nThe compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call\nboxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.\nSteps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:\n\n1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.\n2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:\n   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.\n3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.\n4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with\n   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input\n   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.\n5. For each write box inside the sub-map: route its emitted\n   value into the packed-blob writer that produces the\n   encapsulating box's output (or, alternatively, expose each\n   write box's value as a separate output wire that downstream\n   consumers can wire to individually — see \"Output unpacking\n   under inlining\" below).\n6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph.\n\nAfter expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.\nThe runtime never sees `lang: \"map\"`. The map-language spec\nexists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing\nthe sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector).\n\n**Pros:**\n\n- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec\n  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.\n- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no\n  nested dispatch.\n- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-\n  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions\n  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.\n- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to\n  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.\n\n**Cons:**\n\n- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit\n  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.\n- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to\n  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the\n  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.\n- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of\n  encapsulations.\n- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)\n  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.\n- Output unpacking under inlining is awkward: the packed-blob\n  output format makes sense at a boundary; with no boundary,\n  downstream consumers either wire to individual sub-write-box\n  outputs (more efficient but a different mental model) or get\n  the packer's blob baked in too (the packer is just another\n  inlined function call).\n\n### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch\n\nThe encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat\ngraph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at\ncall time:\n\n1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced\n   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each\n   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,\n   dispatch context).\n2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., out_buf, ...)`** —\n   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk\n   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the\n   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch\n   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished\n   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk the write boxes,\n   read their emitted values, pack them into the size-index +\n   data-section blob, write the blob to `out_buf`.\n\nThe sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the\nparent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the\nparent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is\njust box-id prefix.\n\n**Pros:**\n\n- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent\n  invocations and across many parent maps.\n- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the\n  new version on next run (no parent recompile).\n- The packed-blob output format is the natural shape — the\n  boundary exists, the spec packs at the boundary, downstream\n  consumers unpack with the helper library.\n- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the\n  task's namespace says \"this came from `stats-pipeline`\").\n- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its\n  own spec for a sub-sub-map.\n\n**Cons:**\n\n- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested\n  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy\n  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch\n  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.\n- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —\n  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous\n  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.\n- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the\n  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at\n  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be\n  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's\n  a separate design.)\n- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset\n  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get\n  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a\n  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).\n\n### What to weigh\n\nThe choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time\nabstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**\nor **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared\nlibrary)**.\n\nPath A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is\nhow the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one\nflat program. Best for raw performance and integration with\nthe existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.\n\nPath B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a\nreal boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output\nas the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,\nhot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and\nloss of cross-boundary optimization.\n\nA third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating\nbox** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: \"inline\" |\n\"runtime\"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;\nruntime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per\nencapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost\nbut maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it\nfor later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.\n\nRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under\neither path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or\nload-time, under B) error.\n\n## Relationship to existing issues\n\n- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the\n  entry point for the \"encapsulate\" action.\n- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the\n  external-input slider reuses the same visual idiom on the\n  input-port row.\n- **Issue 229 (data box as language-agnostic file IO)** — the\n  write boxes whose outputs become the encapsulating box's\n  output ports are already specified by that issue. No change\n  needed to the write box itself; the encapsulation observes\n  its emitted value.\n- **Issue 309 (build system / compile pipeline)** — the\n  compile-time inlining path (option A above) extends the\n  pipeline with an \"encapsulation expansion\" step.\n- **Issue 313 (whole-program same-language merge)** — composes\n  with compile-time inlining; the inlined sub-graph's same-\n  language regions merge into the parent's merge as if they\n  were always part of one map.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, the `kind: \"map\"` box,\n  the per-input-port external-binding state.\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — file browser; menu with Edit /\n  Encapsulate actions.\n- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI for the external-binding\n  toggle.\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend; resolving sub-map\n  paths, validating bindings.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — graph loader; recognise\n  `kind: \"map\"`, resolve the sub-map, build the encapsulated\n  shape.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — encapsulating-box dispatch (runtime\n  path) or compile-time expansion (compile path).\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — encapsulation expansion if the\n  compile-time path wins.\n- `libs/encap-output.{lua,c}` — packed-output unpacker library\n  for downstream consumers.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: \"map\"`, the `ref` field, and\n   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a\n   clear error if any field is missing where required.\n2. **External-input slider UI**: inspector toggle on input ports;\n   kind / name / index selectors when on.\n3. **File browser \"Encapsulate\" action**: adds a `kind: \"map\"`\n   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's\n   marked inputs and write boxes to populate the new box's\n   `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.\n4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's\n   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and\n   write-box lists on the parent box record.\n5. **Packed-output format**: implement the size-index +\n   data-section serializer at the encapsulation boundary. Add a\n   small unpacker library for parent-side consumers.\n6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph\n   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a\n   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).\n7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at\n   compile (or load) time.\n8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for\n   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent\n  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later\n  renames or moves `<sub>`? The reference path is brittle.\n  Options: store a stable id in the sub-map's `meta.json` and\n  reference that, plus a path hint; or require the sub-map to\n  live inside the parent's map directory tree.\n- **Re-sync behaviour when the sub-map changes**: if the user\n  edits the sub-map and changes its marked inputs, the parent's\n  encapsulating box's `inputs` array drifts out of date. Likely\n  resolution: on parent map load, the loader re-derives the\n  inputs from the sub-map and warns the user if wiring needs\n  fixing.\n- **`.map` packaging format**: this issue assumes sub-maps are\n  directories. A single-file `.map` archive (tarball / zip)\n  would be more portable for distribution. Out of scope here;\n  separate ticket if it becomes relevant.\n- **Output ordering**: the packed-output format implies an\n  order on the write boxes. The user might want to label\n  outputs (so the parent consumer can pull \"result_a\" by name\n  rather than by index). A named-output variant of the packed\n  format is a follow-on.\n- **Side-effect ordering**: the sub-map's write boxes run as\n  part of the sub-graph and write to disk. The encapsulating\n  box's output emits *after* those side effects complete. If\n  the parent wires the encapsulating box's output forward, the\n  downstream task can rely on the writes having happened. Worth\n  documenting; not a design choice so much as a consequence of\n  the existing dispatch model.\n\n## Quote\n\n> \"the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of\n> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null\n> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index\n> of data. You know that it's i * size_at_index in the size\n> array + the built up total to estimate exactly how far in the\n> array you have to go, so it's really a decent and easy data\n> structure storage place.\" — 2026-05-21\n",

        "content":"1\t# 248 — Encapsulated map as box\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Concept\n7\t\n8\tA map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the\n9\ttop-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to\n10\topen a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*\n11\ton the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a\n12\tsingle box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from input\n13\tports inside the sub-map that have been marked as\n14\texternally-supplied; its outputs come from the sub-map's\n15\t`write` boxes, packed into a single byte-blob with a leading\n16\tsize index.\n17\t\n18\tEncapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.\n19\tThe parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box\n20\twith declared input ports, declared output ports, and known\n21\tsemantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across\n22\tparent maps, and packaged once for distribution.\n23\t\n24\t## Marked input ports inside the sub-map\n25\t\n26\tA **data** box inside the sub-map (kind: `data`, the existing\n27\tlanguage-agnostic file-IO source) can be marked as\n28\t**externally-supplied** via a small toggle on the box's\n29\tinspector. Toggling declares: \"this data box's value comes from\n30\tthe encapsulating context, not from its `path` or `value`\n31\tfield.\"\n32\t\n33\tThe toggle is intentionally scoped to `data` boxes — those are\n34\tthe natural entry points for external values into a map. Call\n35\tboxes / read boxes / write boxes don't carry the toggle, which\n36\tkeeps the inspector uncluttered for the common cases. Each\n37\texternal input becomes a small shared-memory chunk seeded by\n38\tthe encapsulating call's invoke; the marked data box reads from\n39\tthat chunk on each fire, treating it identically to a value\n40\tloaded from disk.\n41\t\n42\tThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:\n43\t\n44\t```json\n45\t{\n46\t    \"id\": \"sum_input\",\n47\t    \"kind\": \"data\",\n48\t    \"external\": {\n49\t        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n50\t        \"name\": \"count\",            // for named\n51\t        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n52\t    },\n53\t    \"...\": \"...\"\n54\t}\n55\t```\n56\t\n57\tThree binding kinds capture how the encapsulating box's input\n58\tmaps to this internal port:\n59\t\n60\t- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating\n61\t  box has N input ports; the *k*th port's value flows to the\n62\t  internal box whose `external.index` is *k*. Conceptually\n63\t  matches positional function arguments.\n64\t- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index. Same shape\n65\t  as positional but the user picks the number (so they can leave\n66\t  gaps, reorder freely, etc.).\n67\t- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's\n68\t  input port has a label; the matching internal box's\n69\t  `external.name` is the same string.\n70\t\n71\tA single sub-map can mix kinds across its marked boxes — some\n72\tpositional, some named — and the parent map's encapsulated box\n73\texposes the union as its input ports.\n74\t\n75\t## Output collection from `write` boxes\n76\t\n77\tThe sub-map's `write` boxes (issue 229's file-write kind) become\n78\tthe encapsulating box's output ports. Each `write` box's `value`\n79\tinput feeds an output slot of the encapsulating box. The boxes\n80\tkeep their normal disk-write behaviour (they write the file as a\n81\tside effect) AND emit the value upward as the encapsulating\n82\tbox's output.\n83\t\n84\tIf the sub-map has N write boxes, the encapsulating box has one\n85\toutput wire carrying a packed byte-blob with all N values.\n86\t\n87\t### Packed output format\n88\t\n89\t```\n90\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n91\t| size[0] | size[1] | ... | size[N-1] | 0       |   ← size index\n92\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n93\t| data[0] (size[0] bytes)                       |\n94\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n95\t| data[1] (size[1] bytes)                       |\n96\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n97\t| ...                                           |\n98\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n99\t| data[N-1] (size[N-1] bytes)                   |\n100\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n101\t```\n102\t\n103\tEach `size[i]` is a 4-byte unsigned little-endian integer. The\n104\tsize array is **NULL-terminated** with a trailing zero, so a\n105\treader can walk it without knowing N up front. Data sections\n106\timmediately follow the size index, packed end-to-end with no\n107\tpadding.\n108\t\n109\tTo read field *i*:\n110\t\n111\t```\n112\tsize_array_bytes = (i_count + 1) * 4     // includes terminator\n113\toffset = size_array_bytes + sum(size[0..i-1])\n114\tdata_i = blob[offset .. offset + size[i]]\n115\t```\n116\t\n117\tThis is a self-describing format. The parent map can pull out\n118\tindividual fields with the offset arithmetic, or pass the whole\n119\tblob downstream and let further consumers slice it. A small\n120\thelper library (probably `libs/encap-output.{lua,c}`) packages\n121\tthe unpack logic so consumers don't have to write the\n122\tarithmetic themselves.\n123\t\n124\t## File layout in the parent map\n125\t\n126\t**The encapsulating box is a normal `call` box.** From the\n127\teditor's perspective it has the same JSON shape as any other\n128\tcall box — `kind: \"call\"`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`,\n129\t`connections`, `routing`. Its `file_ext` is `.map`\n153\t(or no extension if the ref points to a directory). The graph\n154\tloader resolves the `ref`, the map spec's `init` (per worker)\n155\tloads the sub-graph, and its `invoke` runs the sub-graph and\n156\tpacks the outputs. The user doesn't write that array themselves —\n162\tthe editor generates it from the sub-map on first encapsulation\n163\tand re-syncs it when the sub-map changes.\n164\t\n165\t## Editor UI\n166\t\n167\t### File browser\n168\t\n169\tThe file browser (issue 207's source-file-browser, or its\n170\tdescendant) shows map directories with a distinct icon — a\n171\tfolder-like glyph annotated to suggest \"this is a runnable\n172\tgraph, not a source file.\" Clicking opens a small menu:\n173\t\n174\t- **Edit this map** — switches the editor's active map (the\n175\t  existing map-select behaviour).\n176\t- **Encapsulate** — adds the map as a `kind: \"map\"` box to the\n177\t  currently-edited parent map. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy\n316\t  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch\n317\t  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.\n318\t- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —\n319\t  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous\n320\t  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.\n321\t- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the\n322\t  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at\n323\t  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be\n324\t  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's\n325\t  a separate design.)\n326\t- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset\n327\t  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get\n328\t  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a\n329\t  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).\n330\t\n331\t### What to weigh\n332\t\n333\tThe choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time\n334\tabstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**\n335\tor **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared\n336\tlibrary)**.\n337\t\n338\tPath A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is\n339\thow the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one\n340\tflat program. Best for raw performance and integration with\n341\tthe existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.\n342\t\n343\tPath B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a\n344\treal boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output\n345\tas the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,\n346\thot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and\n347\tloss of cross-boundary optimization.\n348\t\n349\tA third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating\n350\tbox** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: \"inline\" |\n351\t\"runtime\"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;\n352\truntime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per\n353\tencapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost\n354\tbut maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it\n355\tfor later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.\n356\t\n357\tRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under\n358\teither path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or\n359\tload-time, under B) error.\n360\t\n361\t## Relationship to existing issues\n362\t\n363\t- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the\n364\t  entry point for the \"encapsulate\" action.\n365\t- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the\n366\t  external-input slider reuses the same visual idiom on the\n367\t  input-port row.\n368\t- **Issue 229 (data box as language-agnostic file IO)** — the\n369\t  write boxes whose outputs become the encapsulating box's\n370\t  output ports are already specified by that issue. No change\n371\t  needed to the write box itself; the encapsulation observes\n372\t  its emitted value.\n373\t- **Issue 309 (build system / compile pipeline)** — the\n374\t  compile-time inlining path (option A above) extends the\n375\t  pipeline with an \"encapsulation expansion\" step.\n376\t- **Issue 313 (whole-program same-language merge)** — composes\n377\t  with compile-time inlining; the inlined sub-graph's same-\n378\t  language regions merge into the parent's merge as if they\n379\t  were always part of one map.\n380\t\n381\t## Relevant files\n382\t\n383\t- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, the `kind: \"map\"` box,\n384\t  the per-input-port external-binding state.\n385\t- `assets/js/005-app.js` — file browser; menu with Edit /\n386\t  Encapsulate actions.\n387\t- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI for the external-binding\n388\t  toggle.\n389\t- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend; resolving sub-map\n390\t  paths, validating bindings.\n391\t- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — graph loader; recognise\n392\t  `kind: \"map\"`, resolve the sub-map, build the encapsulated\n393\t  shape.\n394\t- `src/012-dispatch.c` — encapsulating-box dispatch (runtime\n395\t  path) or compile-time expansion (compile path).\n396\t- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — encapsulation expansion if the\n397\t  compile-time path wins.\n398\t- `libs/encap-output.{lua,c}` — packed-output unpacker library\n399\t  for downstream consumers.\n400\t\n401\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n402\t\n403\t1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: \"map\"`, the `ref` field, and\n404\t   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a\n405\t   clear error if any field is missing where required.\n406\t2. **External-input slider UI**: inspector toggle on input ports;\n407\t   kind / name / index selectors when on.\n408\t3. **File browser \"Encapsulate\" action**: adds a `kind: \"map\"`\n409\t   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's\n410\t   marked inputs and write boxes to populate the new box's\n411\t   `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.\n412\t4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's\n413\t   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and\n414\t   write-box lists on the parent box record.\n415\t5. **Packed-output format**: implement the size-index +\n416\t   data-section serializer at the encapsulation boundary. Add a\n417\t   small unpacker library for parent-side consumers.\n418\t6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph\n419\t   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a\n420\t   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).\n421\t7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at\n422\t   compile (or load) time.\n423\t8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for\n424\t   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.\n425\t\n426\t## Open questions\n427\t\n428\t- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent\n429\t  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later\n430\t  renames or moves `<sub>`? Likely\n437\t  resolution: on parent map load, the loader re-derives the\n438\t  inputs from the sub-map and warns the user if wiring needs\n439\t  fixing.\n440\t- **`.map` packaging format**: this issue assumes sub-maps are\n441\t  directories. A single-file `.map` archive (tarball / zip)\n442\t  would be more portable for distribution. Out of scope here;\n443\t  separate ticket if it becomes relevant.\n444\t- **Output ordering**: the packed-output format implies an\n445\t  order on the write boxes. The user might want to label\n446\t  outputs (so the parent consumer can pull \"result_a\" by name\n447\t  rather than by index). A named-output variant of the packed\n448\t  format is a follow-on.\n449\t- **Side-effect ordering**: the sub-map's write boxes run as\n450\t  part of the sub-graph and write to disk. The encapsulating\n451\t  box's output emits *after* those side effects complete. If\n452\t  the parent wires the encapsulating box's output forward, the\n453\t  downstream task can rely on the writes having happened.           "old_string":"**The structure: two-level chunked-append index table.**\n\nThe slot store keeps a small top-level array of \"chunk pointers.\"\nEach chunk is a fixed-size block of slot pointers. Slot bodies\nthemselves are allocated separately and pointed to from chunk\nentries. Growth means:\n\n- Appending a new slot: atomic-increment the in-use counter on\n  the current chunk; write the slot pointer into the next free\n  chunk index.\n- Adding a new chunk: write a new chunk pointer into the\n  top-level array at the next free top-level index; bump the\n  atomic \"chunks in use\" counter.\n- **Slots themselves never move.** Once allocated, a slot's\n  address is stable for the run. Workers cache slot pointers\n  freely.\n- **The index table itself never moves.** The top-level array\n  is itself append-only (chunks are added, never reallocated).\n  Workers reading the table mid-growth see either the old size\n  or the new size atomically, never garbage.\n\nCost per slot access: one extra indirection (chunk pointer, then\nslot pointer). The allocator-wide-lock-free property of the\nexisting slot store is preserved — only the chunks-in-use counter\nand the per-chunk next-free counter use atomics; everything else\non the hot path stays per-slot.\n\n**Removal (315 territory).** Box destruction during a run will\nexist eventually (per issue 315, compiled artifact reference\ncounting). Reusing a slot index that has been freed creates an\nABA hazard for any worker that read the old pointer before the\nfree. Recommendation: **tombstone freed indices** (mark dead,\nnever reuse) unless 315 expects high enough churn that wasted\nindices accumulate. Defer the final decision until 315 lands.\n\n**What this resolution does NOT decide:** the precise API of the\ngrowth primitive on the slot store, the policy for sizing the\ntop-level chunk array, and whether ring buffer cells grow via\nreallocation-copy or via the same chunked-append shape. Those\nare implementation details for the slot store work itself, not\nthe `create_box` / `connect` design.",
```
```json
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"**The structure: two-level chunked-append index table, no\nstatic ceilings.**\n\nThe slot store keeps a top-level array of \"chunk pointers.\" Each\nchunk is a fixed-size block of slot pointers. Slot bodies\nthemselves are allocated separately and pointed to from chunk\nentries. Three layers of growth, each cheaper than the layer\nabove:\n\n- **Layer 1 — appending a slot inside a chunk** (most common).\n  Atomic-increment the chunk's in-use counter; publish the slot\n  pointer at that index. Lock-free, single-instruction-ish.\n- **Layer 2 — adding a new chunk** (uncommon). Write a new chunk\n  pointer into the top-level array at the next free top-level\n  index; bump the atomic \"chunks in use\" counter. Lock-free.\n- **Layer 3 — growing the top-level array** (rare; logarithmic in\n  total slots across the run). When the top-level array itself\n  fills, use the double-buffer-with-swap pattern: allocate a new\n  top-level array of 2× size, copy existing chunk pointers\n  (pointers only; chunks themselves stay put), atomically swap\n  the top-level array pointer, defer-free the old array via\n  refcount or epoch-based reclamation. Workers caching the old\n  top-level pointer can finish their lookups against it — every\n  chunk and every slot the old array references is still alive.\n\n**No static ceilings anywhere.** Layer 1's chunk capacity is a\ntuning constant (cache-friendly size, e.g. 64), not a limit on\ntotal slots. Layer 2's top-level capacity grows via layer 3.\nLayer 3 has no upper bound. The user pays one extra indirection\non every slot access (top-level → chunk → slot), and a rare\ndouble-buffer swap whose cost amortizes to zero across the run.\n\n**Same machinery serves three callers:** graph load (the first\nbatch of slots), `create_box` (one slot at a time during dispatch),\nand `.map` unzipping for encapsulated maps (a burst of slots when\na sub-map is expanded into the runtime). All three look identical\nto the slot store — append, append, append.\n\nThe allocator-wide-lock-free property is preserved. Only the\nin-use counters and the top-level swap use atomics; everything\non the hot read/write path stays per-slot.\n\n**Removal — refcount, not tombstone.** Issue 315 (compiled\nartifact reference counting) is the safety mechanism. A box's\nrefcount goes to zero only when no other box references it as\nproducer or consumer; any worker about to use the box must hold\na reference that keeps the count positive. ```json
```
```json
{
  "uuid":"4176b567-e49a-4c48-b9de-d4fa9ddcec66",

    "originalFile":"# 319 — Built-in library for map self-construction\n\n## Status\nopen — planning stub. Several design questions need user resolution\nbefore implementation can begin. See **Open design questions**\nbelow.\n\n## Concept\n\nA map should be able to build more of itself while running.\nTwo built-in primitives, exposed by the runtime to every language\nspec, are enough to bootstrap that capability:\n\n- **`create_box(filepath, function_name) -> box_handle`**\n  Spawn a new box on the currently-running map. The first argument\n  is the file holding the function the box will run; the second is\n  the name of that function inside the file. The runtime does any\n  build-pipeline work that's needed (compile the source, register\n  the spec, allocate the box's input port slots) before returning\n  a handle the caller can use to wire the box up.\n\n- **`connect(from_box, to_box_a, to_box_b, ...) -> bool`**\n  Attach a wire from the single output of `from_box` to each of\n  the destination boxes. Variadic on the destinations, since fan-out\n  from a single producer is the common pattern. Returns true if\n  every connection succeeded, false otherwise.\n\nTogether these let a running map grow new sub-graphs in response\nto runtime conditions: a planner box decides what sub-pipeline to\nbuild, calls `create_box` for each node, calls `connect` to wire\nthem, and the dispatch layer picks up the new region on the next\npush.\n\n## Why this shape works (and the parts that need to be checked)\n\n**Single-output-per-box is already the law.** Issue 218 collapsed\nboxes to one output. Variadic destinations on `connect` is just\nfan-out across that single output — no new concept on the wire\nside. The variadic part of the API matches the data model.\n\n**`filepath + function_name` matches box JSON.** That's already how\nlanguage specs locate the code a box runs. The API takes the same\ntwo strings the box JSON would hold.\n\n**Handle-as-return mirrors `data` boxes' encapsulation contract\n(issue 248).** Encapsulated maps already expose typed handles\nto externally-supplied inputs. A `create_box` handle is the same\nkind of thing — a reference the caller uses to identify the box\nin follow-up calls.\n\n## Open design questions\n\nThese are real forks in the design. Each one changes what the\nimplementation looks like; none have a default answer that's\nobviously right.\n\n### Q1 — When does the new box exist? — **RESOLVED: runtime growth, unified store**\n\n**Resolution.** The slot store grows at runtime. There is no\n\"static region\" versus \"dynamic region\" distinction — every box\nis a dynamic box, allocated through the same mechanism, whether\nit was declared in `boxes/<id>.json` at graph load or created\nby a `create_box` built-in call mid-run. Graph load becomes the\nfirst user of the growth primitive rather than a separate code\npath.\n\n**Why this is the right shape (not a compromise).**\n\nThe slot store *already* needs dynamic memory at runtime for an\nunrelated reason: a user may push 200 values into an input slot\nbefore the consuming box has run even once. Ring buffer cells\nhave to be growable on the push path regardless of whether the\ngraph itself is growing. Once dynamic allocation is in the slot\nstore's hot path, gating new *box* allocation behind a separate\n\"static-only\" pathway is artificial — we'd be solving the same\nproblem in two places.\n\nThe encapsulated-map feature (248) and the same-language-merge\nresearch (313) both want to *unzip* a `.map` file into the\nruntime graph at the same level as ordinary boxes — the entire\npoint is that the runtime doesn't spawn a nested thread pool for\nthe inner graph. Unzipping requires growing the box population\nat runtime. A unified growable store covers all three callers\n(graph load, `create_box`, map unzipping) with one mechanism.\n\n**The structure: two-level chunked-append index table.**\n\nThe slot store keeps a small top-level array of \"chunk pointers.\"\nEach chunk is a fixed-size block of slot pointers. Slot bodies\nthemselves are allocated separately and pointed to from chunk\nentries. Growth means:\n\n- Appending a new slot: atomic-increment the in-use counter on\n  the current chunk; write the slot pointer into the next free\n  chunk index.\n- Adding a new chunk: write a new chunk pointer into the\n  top-level array at the next free top-level index; bump the\n  atomic \"chunks in use\" counter.\n- **Slots themselves never move.** Once allocated, a slot's\n  address is stable for the run. Workers cache slot pointers\n  freely.\n- **The index table itself never moves.** The top-level array\n  is itself append-only (chunks are added, never reallocated).\n  Workers reading the table mid-growth see either the old size\n  or the new size atomically, never garbage.\n\nCost per slot access: one extra indirection (chunk pointer, then\nslot pointer). The allocator-wide-lock-free property of the\nexisting slot store is preserved — only the chunks-in-use counter\nand the per-chunk next-free counter use atomics; everything else\non the hot path stays per-slot.\n\n**Removal (315 territory).** Box destruction during a run will\nexist eventually (per issue 315, compiled artifact reference\ncounting). Reusing a slot index that has been freed creates an\nABA hazard for any worker that read the old pointer before the\nfree. Recommendation: **tombstone freed indices** (mark dead,\nnever reuse) unless 315 expects high enough churn that wasted\nindices accumulate. Defer the final decision until 315 lands.\n\n**What this resolution does NOT decide:** the precise API of the\ngrowth primitive on the slot store, the policy for sizing the\ntop-level chunk array, and whether ring buffer cells grow via\nreallocation-copy or via the same chunked-append shape. Those\nare implementation details for the slot store work itself, not\nthe `create_box` / `connect` design.\n\n### Q2 — Which input port does `connect` target?\n\nA box has multiple input ports. `connect(from_box, to_box_a, ...)`\ndoesn't say which port on `to_box_a` receives the wire. Options:\n\n- **(a) Variadic of pairs:** `connect(from_box, {to_a, \"x\"}, {to_b, \"y\"})`\n  — explicit per destination, more typing.\n- **(b) Implicit first-free port:** the runtime picks the lowest-indexed\n  unwired input port on each destination. Cheap, surprising in mixed\n  cases.\n- **(c) Port-on-handle:** the handle returned by `create_box` carries\n  per-port sub-handles; `connect(from_box.output, to_box.input_x)`.\n  Verbose at call sites, unambiguous everywhere.\n\n### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash\n\nCLAUDE.md says \"prefer error messages and breaking functionality\nover fallbacks\" and \"nil checks are just asking for errors.\" A\nbool return on `connect` is exactly the shape that invites silent\nignoring. Two paths:\n\n- **(a) Keep bool.** The caller is expected to branch on it. Matches\n  the user's draft.\n- **(b) Hard-crash with reason.** `connect` returns nothing; on any\n  failure it aborts the program with a plain-English message\n  (\"can't connect box X to box Y: Y has no free input ports\").\n  Matches the project-wide error policy elsewhere.\n\n### Q4 — What is the \"box handle\" actually?\n\nThe user wrote \"pointer to the box.\" In a single-process runner the\nliteral pointer works, but it can't survive wire crossings or be\npassed across the cross-language JSON wire (the wire format forbids\nhandles that back-route to the owning spec). Options:\n\n- **(a) Stable string id** (the existing `box_id` from the JSON\n  schema). Survives serialization. Slower lookup in the dispatch\n  layer.\n- **(b) In-process `$ref` sentinel.** Fast in the calling spec,\n  must be unwrapped before crossing a language boundary.\n- **(c) Both:** the handle is a small struct carrying both the\n  fast pointer and the durable id; the wire layer keeps only the\n  id when it crosses.\n\n### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline?\n\nThe user said \"compile it (if necessary) and other map-wide tasks.\"\nThe build pipeline (issues 217–222) currently lives on the server /\ncompile-button side. If `create_box` runs at runtime, the runner\ngains a dependency on the compiler. That crosses the program-\nseparation boundary documented in `project_soramech`:\n\"Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server.\nMap directory format is the only shared contract.\"\n\nEither the runner gains the compiler as a library (changing the\nthree-program separation), or `create_box` requires the source to\nbe pre-compiled and merely *registers* the resulting artifact\n(simpler, but the user has to do the build step separately).\n\n## Suggested implementation steps (after Q1–Q5 are resolved)\n\n1. Resolve the open design questions; update this issue with the\n   chosen shape before any code is written.\n2. Add the two built-ins to the language-spec contract\n   (`lang_spec_t` — the runtime exposes them via the spec's\n   built-in table; each language spec wraps them in its native\n   calling convention).\n3. Extend the slot store with the growth primitive Q1 selects\n   (if Q1 picks (a) or (c)).\n4. Add dispatch-layer logic for newly-created boxes — they need to\n   participate in the same push-on-arrival mechanism as static\n   boxes.\n5. Tests under `tests/`: a small map whose first box uses\n   `create_box` + `connect` to build a downstream pipeline, then\n   runs end-to-end and validates outputs.\n6. Update `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` to describe the\n   self-construction contract and the slot-store growth shape.\n7. Update phase-3-progress.md.\n\n## Related issues and documents\n\n- 248 — encapsulated map as box (the function-like abstraction\n  these primitives could be used to construct ad-hoc).\n- 302 — wire value slot store (the structure that needs the growth\n  primitive in Q1).\n- 218 — single output per box (justifies the variadic-on-destinations\n  shape).\n- 217–222 — compile pipeline (relevant to Q5).\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — current threading model these\n  primitives must fit inside.\n",

    "newString":"**The structure: two-level chunked-append index table, no\nstatic ceilings.**\n\nThe slot store keeps a top-level array of \"chunk pointers.\" Each\nchunk is a fixed-size block of slot pointers. Slot bodies\nthemselves are allocated separately and pointed to from chunk\nentries. Three layers of growth, each cheaper than the layer\nabove:\n\n- **Layer 1 — appending a slot inside a chunk** (most common).\n  Atomic-increment the chunk's in-use counter; publish the slot\n  pointer at that index. Lock-free, single-instruction-ish.\n- **Layer 2 — adding a new chunk** (uncommon). Write a new chunk\n  pointer into the top-level array at the next free top-level\n  index; bump the atomic \"chunks in use\" counter. Lock-free.\n- **Layer 3 — growing the top-level array** (rare; logarithmic in\n  total slots across the run). When the top-level array itself\n  fills, use the double-buffer-with-swap pattern: allocate a new\n  top-level array of 2× size, copy existing chunk pointers\n  (pointers only; chunks themselves stay put), atomically swap\n  the top-level array pointer, defer-free the old array via\n  refcount or epoch-based reclamation. Workers caching the old\n  top-level pointer can finish their lookups against it — every\n  chunk and every slot the old array references is still alive.\n\n**No static ceilings anywhere.** Layer 1's chunk capacity is a\ntuning constant (cache-friendly size, e.g. 64), not a limit on\ntotal slots. Layer 2's top-level capacity grows via layer 3.\nLayer 3 has no upper bound. The user pays one extra indirection\non every slot access (top-level → chunk → slot), and a rare\ndouble-buffer swap whose cost amortizes to zero across the run.\n\n**Same machinery serves three callers:** graph load (the first\nbatch of slots), `create_box` (one slot at a time during dispatch),\nand `.map` unzipping for encapsulated maps (a burst of slots when\na sub-map is expanded into the runtime). All three look identical\nto the slot store — append, append, append.\n\nThe allocator-wide-lock-free property is preserved. Only the\nin-use counters and the top-level swap use atomics; everything\non the hot read/write path stays per-slot.\n\n**Removal — refcount, not tombstone.** Issue 315 (compiled\nartifact reference counting) is the safety mechanism. A box's\nrefcount goes to zero only when no other box references it as\nproducer or consumer; any worker about to use the box must hold\na reference that keeps the count positive. Therefore \"refcount\nreached zero\" is a proof that no worker holds a stale pointer.\nSlot indices freed at that moment are safe to reuse.\n\nNo tombstoning required, no generation counters on handles, no\nABA hazard — 315's refcount discipline subsumes all three.\n\n**What this resolution does NOT decide:** the precise API of the\ngrowth primitive on the slot store, the cache-line-aware chunk\nsize choice, and whether ring buffer *cell* growth uses\ndouble-buffer-with-swap under the per-slot lock (the suggested\nshape, since each slot already holds a lock during growth).\nThose are implementation details for the slot store work itself,\nnot the `create_box` / `connect` design."
```

```json
        "input":{
          "old_string":"A map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the\ntop-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to\nopen a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*\non the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a\nsingle box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from input\nports inside the sub-map that have been marked as\nexternally-supplied; its outputs come from the sub-map's\n`write` boxes, packed into a single byte-blob with a leading\nsize index.\n\nEncapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.\nThe parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box\nwith declared input ports, declared output ports, and known\nsemantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across\nparent maps, and packaged once for distribution.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"A map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the\ntop-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to\nopen a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*\non the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a\nsingle box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from `data`\nboxes inside the sub-map that have been marked\n**externally-supplied**; its outputs come from `write` boxes\ninside the sub-map that have been marked **externally-consumed**.\nThe two markings are symmetric: one redirects an input from \"file\non disk\" to \"wire from parent,\" the other redirects an output\nfrom \"file on disk\" to \"wire to parent.\"\n\nEncapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.\nThe parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box\nwith declared input ports, declared output ports, and known\nsemantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across\nparent maps, and packaged once for distribution.\n\n**Encapsulated boxes are the documented exception to issue 218's\n\"single output per box\" rule.** Every other box kind has exactly\none output (with fan-out via multiple wires leaving that one\noutput). An encapsulated map has *N* distinct output ports, one\nper `write` box marked externally-consumed. *N* may be zero (the\nmap is a pure side-effect sink), one (matches the common case),\nor many. The exception exists because an encapsulated map's\noutputs are independent values produced by independent\n`write` boxes — packing them into a single blob (the earlier\ndesign in this issue) would have repurposed file-writing\nmachinery to emit strings into wires, which is the wrong shape:\n`write` boxes should keep their semantics (\"terminate a value\")\nand the destination kind (\"file vs. parent wire\") should be a\nmode toggle, not a substitution.",
```

## [164]

```json
{
  "uuid":"01627538-4832-41de-8ec8-3821b0999e03",
  "type":"assistant",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-23T18:03:42.697Z",
  "parentUuid":"915ace78-85ec-4320-ad0c-8e1ba97ceb86",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "requestId":"req_011CbKzSZR3TNDotD2k8ogdZ",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "name":"Edit",
        "input":{
          "old_string":"## Output collection from `write` boxes\n\nThe sub-map's `write` boxes (issue 229's file-write kind) become\nthe encapsulating box's output ports. Each `write` box's `value`\ninput feeds an output slot of the encapsulating box. The boxes\nkeep their normal disk-write behaviour (they write the file as a\nside effect) AND emit the value upward as the encapsulating\nbox's output.\n\nIf the sub-map has N write boxes, the encapsulating box has one\noutput wire carrying a packed byte-blob with all N values.\n\n### Packed output format\n\n```\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| size[0] | size[1] | ... | size[N-1] | 0       |   ← size index\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| data[0] (size[0] bytes)                       |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| data[1] (size[1] bytes)                       |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| ...                                           |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| data[N-1] (size[N-1] bytes)                   |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n```\n\nEach `size[i]` is a 4-byte unsigned little-endian integer. The\nsize array is **NULL-terminated** with a trailing zero, so a\nreader can walk it without knowing N up front. Data sections\nimmediately follow the size index, packed end-to-end with no\npadding.\n\nTo read field *i*:\n\n```\nsize_array_bytes = (i_count + 1) * 4     // includes terminator\noffset = size_array_bytes + sum(size[0..i-1])\ndata_i = blob[offset .. offset + size[i]]\n```\n\nThis is a self-describing format. The parent map can pull out\nindividual fields with the offset arithmetic, or pass the whole\nblob downstream and let further consumers slice it. A small\nhelper library (probably `libs/encap-output.{lua,c}`) packages\nthe unpack logic so consumers don't have to write the\narithmetic themselves.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"## Marked output ports inside the sub-map\n\nA **write** box inside the sub-map (kind: `write`, issue 229's\nfile-write kind) can be marked as **externally-consumed** via a\nsmall toggle on the box's inspector — the mirror of the\nexternally-supplied toggle on data boxes. Toggling declares:\n\"this write box's value goes to the encapsulating context, not\nto its `path` field.\"\n\nThe toggle is intentionally scoped to `write` boxes — those are\nthe natural exit points for values out of a map. Each\nexternally-consumed write box surfaces as one **distinct output\nport** on the encapsulating box. The port carries that one\nvalue, on its own wire, to whichever downstream box(es) the\nparent wires it to.\n\nThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON, in\nthe same shape as the input-side toggle:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"result_value\",\n    \"kind\": \"write\",\n    \"external\": {\n        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n        \"name\": \"result\",           // for named\n        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n    },\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nThree binding kinds — same vocabulary as the input side:\n\n- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating\n  box's *k*th output port is the externally-consumed write box\n  whose `external.index` is *k*.\n- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index, allowing\n  gaps and reordering.\n- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's\n  output port carries that label.\n\nA write box marked externally-consumed **also** writes to its\n`path` if one is set — the two destinations are independent. The\nwrite box can opt out of the file write (set `path: null`) if it\nexists solely to surface a value to the parent.\n\nEach externally-consumed write box's emitted value becomes an\nindependent output wire on the encapsulating box. The earlier\ndesign in this issue packed all write-box outputs into a single\nbyte-blob with a leading size index; that design is rejected —\nsee the \"Concept\" section for why. No packing, no unpacking\nlibrary; the wire format is the same per-port wire format every\nother box uses.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/248-encapsulated-map-as-box.md"
        },
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01Vn9diAemZ559v1dLhbv81K",
        "type":"tool_use"
      }],
    "usage":{
      "inference_geo":"",
      "cache_read_input_tokens":94071,
      "speed":"standard",
```

```json
    "oldString":"## Quote\n\n> \"the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of\n> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null\n> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index\n> of data. You know that it's i * size_at_index in the size\n> array + the built up total to estimate exactly how far in the\n> array you have to go, so it's really a decent and easy data\n> structure storage place.\" — 2026-05-21",
    "newString":"## Design history\n\nThe original 2026-05-21 design packed all write-box outputs into\na single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, and\nthe encapsulated box had a single output wire carrying that blob:\n\n> \"the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of\n> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null\n> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index\n> of data...\" — 2026-05-21\n\nThat design was reconsidered on 2026-05-23 while specifying the\nself-construction built-ins (issue 319). The reconsideration:\nboxes never \"return\" values to the outside world under the\nexisting model — they push values onto wires that other boxes\nconsume, and `write` boxes specifically terminate values to\nfiles. Repurposing the file-writing destination to emit strings\ninto wires would have been a substitution of one mechanism for\nanother. The symmetric design — mark write boxes\nexternally-consumed, surface each as its own output port —\npreserves the `write` box's semantics (\"terminate a value\") and\ntreats the destination as a mode toggle. Cost: multi-output boxes\nexist for this kind alone; benefit: one mechanism does both jobs\ncleanly."
  },
```

```json
          "old_string":"### Input-port slider\n\nThe inspector for any input port (on read / data / write boxes)\ngrows a small toggle next to the port name:\n\n```\n  ┌─────────────────────────────┐\n  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound\n  │   kind:    named            │\n  │   name:    \"count\"          │\n  └─────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nWhen the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector\n(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.\nWhen off, the port behaves normally (wires-in or literal-value).\n\nA map with no marked inputs encapsulates to a no-input box (just\na source of write-box outputs). A map with no write boxes\nencapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting only —\nunusual but legal).",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"### External-binding toggle (inputs and outputs)\n\nThe inspector for a `data` box's value-input grows a small\ntoggle that marks it externally-supplied; the inspector for a\n`write` box's value-input grows the same toggle that marks it\nexternally-consumed. Both surface in the same visual idiom:\n\n```\n  ┌─────────────────────────────┐\n  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound\n  │   kind:    named            │\n  │   name:    \"count\"          │\n  └─────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nWhen the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector\n(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.\nWhen off, the port behaves normally (wires-in / literal value on\nthe data box; `path` write on the write box).\n\nA map with no marked data boxes encapsulates to a no-input box\n(just a source of values). A map with no externally-consumed\nwrite boxes encapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting\nonly — legal but unusual; useful for \"fire and forget\"\nsub-pipelines).",
```

    "oldString":"### Input-port slider\n\nThe inspector for any input port (on read / data / write boxes)\ngrows a small toggle next to the port name:\n\n```\n  ┌─────────────────────────────┐\n  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound\n  │   kind:    named            │\n  │   name:    \"count\"          │\n  └─────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nWhen the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector\n(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.\nWhen off, the port behaves normally (wires-in or literal-value).\n\nA map with no marked inputs encapsulates to a no-input box (just\na source of write-box outputs). A map with no write boxes\nencapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting only —\nunusual but legal).",
    "newString":"### External-binding toggle (inputs and outputs)\n\nThe inspector for a `data` box's value-input grows a small\ntoggle that marks it externally-supplied; the inspector for a\n`write` box's value-input grows the same toggle that marks it\nexternally-consumed. Both surface in the same visual idiom:\n\n```\n  ┌─────────────────────────────┐\n  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound\n  │   kind:    named            │\n  │   name:    \"count\"          │\n  └─────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nWhen the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector\n(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.\nWhen off, the port behaves normally (wires-in / literal value on\nthe data box; `path` write on the write box).\n\nA map with no marked data boxes encapsulates to a no-input box\n(just a source of values). A map with no externally-consumed\nwrite boxes encapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting\nonly — legal but unusual; useful for \"fire and forget\"\nsub-pipelines)."
  },
