          "new_string":"## Design history\n\nThe original 2026-05-21 design packed all write-box outputs into\na single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, and\nthe encapsulated box had a single output wire carrying that blob:\n\n> \"the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of\n> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null\n> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index\n> of data...\" — 2026-05-21\n\nThat design was reconsidered on 2026-05-23 while specifying the\nself-construction built-ins (issue 319). The reconsideration:\nboxes never \"return\" values to the outside world under the\nexisting model — they push values onto wires that other boxes\nconsume, and `write` boxes specifically terminate values to\nfiles. Repurposing the file-writing destination to emit strings\ninto wires would have been a substitution of one mechanism for\nanother. The symmetric design — mark write boxes\nexternally-consumed, surface each as its own output port —\npreserves the `write` box's semantics (\"terminate a value\") and\ntreats the destination as a mode toggle. Cost: multi-output boxes\nexist for this kind alone; benefit: one mechanism does both jobs\ncleanly.",

          "content":"---\nname: Encapsulated map as box\ndescription: A sub-map opens as a single box on a parent canvas. Data boxes marked externally-supplied become input ports; write boxes marked externally-consumed become output ports. The documented exception to single-output-per-box (issue 248, amended 2026-05-23)\ntype: project\n---\n\n**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.\n\n**The encapsulation contract — symmetric input and output toggles:**\n- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map can be toggled \"externally-supplied\" in its inspector. Each such box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box.\n- **Outputs:** any `write` box inside the sub-map can be toggled \"externally-consumed\" in its inspector. Each such box surfaces as a **distinct output port** on the encapsulated box. A write box with the toggle on can still write to its `path` if one is set — the file destination and the parent-wire destination are independent.\n\n**Encapsulated maps are the documented exception to issue 218's \"single output per box\" rule.** They have *N* output ports — one per externally-consumed write box, where *N* may be zero (pure side-effect map), one, or many. Every other box kind still has exactly one output.\n\n**Rejected earlier design (2026-05-21):** packing all write-box outputs into a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, single wire out. Rejected 2026-05-23 because it would have repurposed file-writing machinery to emit strings into wires — substituting one mechanism for another. The symmetric toggle design preserves the `write` box's \"terminate a value\" semantics and treats the destination kind as a mode toggle.\n\n**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to \"user-defined functions\" while staying graph-native.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or \"how do users build libraries of behavior\" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, blob-packed outputs) without explicitly weighing them against the symmetric-toggle shape. Both toggles (`externally-supplied` on data boxes, `externally-consumed` on write boxes) are the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate \"ports manifest\" file.\n",

    "content":"  ★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────\n  The [16] and [24] limits share a pattern — both are at sites where someone needed a stack-allocated array and picked \"a number that seemed\n  big enough.\" That's the static-limit antipattern's natural habitat: not in deliberate sizing decisions, but in casual ones where the\n  alternative (dynamic allocation, two-pass sizing) felt heavier than the problem deserved.\n  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────\n\ncould we allocate those sizes at runtime dynamically according to how much space we need? or is that overkill? maybe we could do a size test, and if it's larger then we allocate space... idk what do you think? I'd need a longer description of each of their context before I could decide. If you can think of a good, decent, cheap (performance-wise) path forward, then let's do it. We don't need an issue ticket for it - just update one that already exists which touches that part of the source-code.\n\n  248 issue: Amended to the symmetric-toggle design. data boxes get externally-supplied, write boxes get externally-consumed. Each\n  externally-consumed write box surfaces as a distinct output port. The packed-byte-blob design is rejected, with the reasoning preserved in\n  a \"Design history\" section so future readers see why it changed. Issue 218's single-output rule gets the documented exception.\n\n\nI've been thinking, there's some toggle switches and stuff that we modify in the editor that are unable to be edited in the \"create-a-new-box\" feature we're working on. Can we think about all the custom values that we insert, and make a list in the issue file so we know later, if we add something, what we've explicitely designed against? For example, let's say we make a new slider that's \"intensity\" or something or heck even \"priority\" which we already have theoretically specced but not really implemented. Say we add priority - then, the create-a-box system needs to know how to provide that value. How could we provide that value? Another input slot? How many do we need?",

  },

    "oldString":"### Q2 — Which input port does `connect` target?",
    "newString":"### Prerequisite — remove the dispatch input cap before `create_box` ships\n\nToday `src/012-dispatch.c` allocates five parallel stack arrays\nof size 16 (`bufs`, `buf_chunks`, `datas`, `sizes`,\n`input_native`) inside the per-call invocation path. A box with\nmore than 16 inputs hits a hard error from the dispatcher. This\ncontradicts the \"no static ceilings\" principle resolved in Q1.\n\n**Fix:** convert the five arrays to VLAs (`char *bufs[n];` etc.,\nC99). Cost is zero — VLAs adjust the stack pointer by\n`n * 5 * sizeof(void*)` with no allocator call. Keep a sanity\nguard at a generous ceiling (e.g. 4096 inputs) so a runaway\nloader can't blow the stack; the existing error-return path\nstays in place above that.\n\n**Related but lower priority:** the `branch[24]` stack buffers\nat dispatch.c:629/647/678 hold a `snprintf(\"out_%u\", ...)`\nresult. Worst-case formatted length is 15 bytes; 24 is\narbitrary-but-safe and `snprintf` truncates without overflowing.\nChange to a named constant (`MAX_BRANCH_NAME = 16`) for hygiene\nwhen the VLA work lands. Not a real bug.\n\n### Q1.5 — The shape of the `create_box` argument: box JSON schema as the contract\n\n`create_box`'s argument is **one structured value whose shape is\nexactly the box JSON schema**. In Lua, a table; in C, either a\nstruct or a JSON string built by the caller; in Bash, a JSON\nstring. The runtime converts to JSON internally (same path as the\nuniversal wire format), validates against the box schema, and\ninstantiates the box record. Anything you can write into\n`boxes/<id>.json` on disk, you can pass to `create_box` at\nruntime.\n\n**Why this shape (not a fat positional signature, not key/value\nvarargs, not a builder pattern):**\n\n- The box JSON schema **is** the source of truth on disk. Having\n  `create_box` mirror that schema means there is no parallel\n  \"create_box parameter list\" to maintain — adding a new schema\n  field works in `create_box` automatically.\n- New customization toggles (priority, debug-instrumentation\n  flags, custom translation specs per port, emoji labels for tap\n  mode, etc.) land in the schema and become available to\n  `create_box` callers in the same change.\n- Languages without rich native structured types (Bash) can use\n  JSON strings; languages with rich types (Lua tables, C structs)\n  can use native shapes that the spec converts.\n\n**Structural metadata vs runtime values — the split this design\nenforces.** The argument carries **structural metadata** (id,\nkind, lang, ref, fn, routing, inputs/outputs schema, position).\nPer-invocation **runtime values** (the data flowing through\nwires) keep flowing through input slots as before. They do not\nmix. Asking \"should priority arrive on an input slot?\" is the\nwrong question — priority is metadata, not a value flowing\nthrough the dataflow. Mixing the two would make a box's *shape*\ndepend on runtime state, which the slot store and the dispatcher\nboth assume is fixed once the box exists.\n\n### Box customization surface — what `create_box` accepts (audit, 2026-05-23)\n\nMaintained list of every per-box customization that currently\nexists or is on a known open issue. When a new toggle is added\nanywhere in SoraMech, **append to this list** in the same change.\nThe list is a contract reminder: `create_box`'s structured\nargument must cover all of these because they are all valid\nfields in the box JSON schema.\n\n**Working today (in shipped box JSON):**\n\n- `id` — required, unique within the map.\n- `kind` — call / read / data / write / comparator / iterator /\n  randomizer / weighted / distributor / map (the encapsulated\n  kind from 248).\n- `lang` — lua / c / bash / map (issue 303 spec registry).\n- `ref` — file path to the source containing the box's function.\n- `fn` — function name within `ref`.\n- `inputs[]` — per-port: `name`, `type`, `value` (default),\n  `optional`.\n- `value` (read-box literal source).\n- `path` (data and write boxes — disk file).\n- `comparand` (comparator boxes).\n- `routing.kind` — plain / comparator / randomizer / weighted /\n  iterator / distributor.\n- `routing.weights` (weighted), `routing.n_outputs` (iterator,\n  randomizer).\n- `iterator_outputs[]` (iterator branch names).\n- `output_capacity` (ring buffer cell size hint).\n- `connections[]` — outgoing wires: `from_branch`, `to_box`,\n  `to_input`. (May be omitted in `create_box` calls if the caller\n  will follow up with `connect()`.)\n- `ui.x`, `ui.y` (canvas position).\n\n**Coming from open issues (must be supported by `create_box`\nwhen they land):**\n\n- `external` block on `data` boxes — issue 248 (externally-supplied).\n- `external` block on `write` boxes — issue 248 amended (externally-consumed).\n- `outputs[]` array — issue 248, encapsulated boxes only, exception\n  to issue 218's single-output-per-box rule.\n- `custom_translation_spec` per input port — issue 246.\n- `encap_mode` (`inline` | `runtime`) — issue 248, on `kind: \"map\"` boxes.\n- Four-emoji label for tap mode — issue 249.\n- Debug instrumentation flags per box — issue 247.\n- `priority` — not yet specced; would feed the pool's\n  task-scheduling priority. Worth its own issue when introduced;\n  goes into the schema and into this list.\n\n**Derived (NOT settable via `create_box`):**\n\n- Wire color — derived from producer/consumer language pairing\n  (issue 245). The compiler colors wires; the user doesn't.\n- Per-edge native flag — derived by the graph loader at compile\n  time from input/output language pairs (issue 312). Not a\n  user-set field.\n\n### Q2 — Which input port does `connect` target?"
  },

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Both have clean answers. Let me lay them out before writing into the issue.\n\n## The audit fix — VLA or per-worker scratch\n\n**`[16]` inputs (dispatch.c:804+, 863+):** five parallel stack arrays — `bufs`, `buf_chunks`, `datas`, `sizes`, `input_native` — populated by `read_inputs()`, freed by `release_inputs()` at the end of the call. Better than I feared: the code does check `n > 16` and returns -1, so it's a *hard error* on a 17-input box, not silent corruption. But it's still a cap on what `create_box` will be able to make.\n\nThree options, in increasing weight:\n\n- **(i) VLA:** `char *bufs[n];` — C99 variable-length arrays. Zero allocator calls; the stack pointer just moves by `n * 5 * sizeof(void*)`. The only risk is blowing the stack on pathological `n` (a box with 100k inputs), and we can keep the existing `n > some_huge_cap` guard purely as a sanity check (say 4096). Cheapest possible.\n- **(ii) Per-worker scratch arena:** worker context grows a reusable buffer; this call bumps a pointer to claim 5×n slots, resets the bump pointer at call end. One alloc-on-grow per worker per peak-size-ever, zero per call. Pays for itself if VLA stack pressure ever shows up.\n- **(iii) Per-call malloc:** five allocs and frees per invocation. Real cost on hot paths. Worst of the three.\n\nRecommendation: **(i) VLA**, with the existing sanity-cap kept (at, say, 4096) so a runaway loader doesn't get a stack-overflow segfault. Promote to (ii) only if profiling ever shows VLA stack pressure — for normal box widths (1–20 inputs) the cost is unmeasurable.\n\n**`branch[24]` (dispatch.c:629, 647, 678, etc.):** these format `\"out_%u\"` for branch names. Worst case is `\"out_4294967295\"` = 14 chars + null = 15 bytes. Cap of 24 is **artificially low but never reached**, and `snprintf` truncates safely. Not a real bug — just hygiene. Easiest fix is to make it a named constant (`MAX_BRANCH_NAME = 16` or so, compile-time proven sufficient) so future format-string changes have a single place to update. Not worth a deeper rework.\n\n## The box customization audit — single structured value matching box JSON\n\nSampling the box JSON across three test maps, plus the active and upcoming issues, here's the full surface area:\n\n**Currently in the schema (working):**\n- Core identity: `id`, `kind`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`\n- Inputs array with per-port: `name`, `type`, `value` (default), `optional`\n- `value` (read boxes — literal source)\n- `path` (data/write boxes — disk file)\n- `comparand` (comparator boxes)\n- `routing`: `kind` (plain/comparator/randomizer/weighted/iterator/distributor) plus kind-specific fields (`weights`, `n_outputs`, etc.)\n- `iterator_outputs` (iterator boxes — output branch names)\n- `output_capacity` (ring buffer size hint per the slot store)\n- `connections` (outgoing wires — `from_branch`, `to_box`, `to_input`)\n- `ui`: `x`, `y` (canvas position)\n\n**Coming from open issues:**\n- `external` block on inputs (issue 248 — data boxes, externally-supplied)\n- `external` block on write boxes (issue 248 amended — externally-consumed)\n- `outputs` array (issue 248 — multi-output exception, encapsulated boxes only)\n- `custom_translation_spec` per port (issue 246)\n- `encap_mode` (issue 248 path A vs B)\n- Per-edge native flags (issue 312 — usually derived at compile time, not user-set)\n- Wire colors (issue 245 — derived from language pairing, not user-set)\n- Four-emoji label (issue 249 tap mode)\n- Debug instrumentation flags (issue 247)\n- **`priority`** (user mentioned — not yet specced; would be a routing-priority field for the pool scheduler)\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThere's a clean split here: **structural metadata** (id, kind, lang, ref, fn, routing, inputs/outputs schema) versus **runtime values** (the values flowing through wires). The first set lives in the box JSON; the second flows through slots. Conflating them — e.g., \"should priority come in via an input slot?\" — would smuggle metadata into the dataflow and make the box's *shape* dependent on runtime state. Bad coupling. Metadata in the JSON, values on the wires, strict separation.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nThe cleanest signature for `create_box` falls out: **take one structured value whose shape is exactly the box JSON schema.** In Lua that's a table; in C a struct (or a JSON string built once); in Bash a JSON string. Internally the runtime converts to JSON (same path as the universal wire format), validates against the schema, instantiates the box record. **Every new schema field becomes available in create_box automatically — no API change.** That's how you make a built-in survive a growing schema.\n\nSo the API converges to:\n\n```\ncreate_box(spec) -> handle\n   where spec is a structured value with the same shape as boxes/<id>.json\n```\n\nWhat goes in `spec` is *everything in the schema audit above*. Anything not provided takes its default. The id is generated if not supplied. The `connections` array might be omitted in favor of follow-up `connect()` calls (or might be allowed inline — Q to think about for Q2).\n\nLet me fold both threads into 319:"
      }],

        "type":"text",
        "text":"You're zeroing in on exactly the right thing. Both questions share an answer: **the API mirrors the JSON schema all the way down**, and the machinery already exists.\n\n## Q2 — `connect`'s argument is a connection entry, same shape as box JSON\n\nHere's the schema we already have on disk, from the test maps:\n\n```json\n\"connections\": [\n  { \"from_box\": \"src\", \"from_branch\": null,\n    \"to_box\": \"echo\", \"to_input\": \"x\" }\n]\n```\n\nEvery wire in SoraMech is already represented as one of these. **`to_input` is exactly the \"which port\" answer** — it's been the answer the whole time, just at compile-time rather than runtime. So `connect()` takes one (or many) of these objects:\n\n```\nconnect({from_box=A, from_branch=null, to_box=B, to_input=\"x\"})\nconnect({from_box=A, from_branch=null, to_box=B, to_input=\"x\"},\n        {from_box=A, from_branch=\"gt\", to_box=C, to_input=\"value\"},\n        {from_box=A, from_branch=\"lt\", to_box=D, to_input=\"value\"})\n```\n\nThe \"which port\" question is answered by **`to_input` being explicit in every connection entry**. No implicit-first-free magic, no separate \"port handle\" mechanism, no pair-style syntax that has to be remembered separately from the JSON shape. The shape on the wire (in the JSON file) and the shape in the API call are the same shape.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThis is the same principle as Q1.5 applied to a different artifact. **The schema is the API.** Every place we need a \"way to describe a box\" or \"way to describe a wire,\" the answer is \"use the JSON shape we already have on disk.\" It collapses two designs into one — and every future schema change updates the API for free.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nVariadic falls out naturally — it's \"multiple connection entries in one call,\" exactly the way `connections[]` is an array on disk.\n\n## How do users *construct* these objects in code?\n\nThis is your \"how do we create the JSON schema, how do we edit its values\" question — practical, important. Different shape per language because the languages have different native data types:\n\n- **Lua:** table literal. Already idiomatic.\n  ```lua\n  soramech.connect({from_box=\"a\", from_branch=nil,\n                    to_box=\"b\", to_input=\"x\"})\n  ```\n\n- **C:** the verbose case. Three options ranked:\n  1. **Build a JSON string with a small varargs helper** — `connect_json(\"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"%s\\\"}\", \"a\", \"b\", \"x\")`. Ugly but works without any new infrastructure.\n  2. **Struct + builder helper** — `connection_t c = { .from_box=\"a\", .to_box=\"b\", .to_input=\"x\" }; soramech_connect(&c);` — uses C99 designated initializers, much cleaner.\n  3. **dkjson-style C JSON builder** — `cJSON *o = json_obj(); json_set(o, \"from_box\", \"a\"); ...; soramech_connect(o);` — most ergonomic, requires the runtime to expose a JSON-build API.\n  \n  Recommend option 2 (designated initializer struct) for the common case; option 1 falls back when the user has dynamic fields.\n\n- **Bash:** JSON strings. `soramech_connect '{\"from_box\":\"a\",\"to_box\":\"b\",\"to_input\":\"x\"}'`. Bash has no native dict; JSON strings are how it talks to everything anyway.\n\n## \"We output box return values to JSON sometimes. Could we use that machinery somehow?\" — Yes, the *same* machinery\n\nThis is the key insight you just pulled. Every language spec already implements `native_to_json` for the dual-ring wire format (issue 312) — that's how a Lua box's return value crosses into a C consumer. **Exactly the same callback** converts a Lua table the user built for create_box / connect into the JSON shape the runtime ingests. Concretely:\n\n```\n[user spec code]                 [language spec]              [runtime]\n  spec_table = {                 native_to_json               JSON object,\n    from_box = \"a\",          ──▶  (the same one used       ──▶ validate\n    to_box = \"b\",                  for wire crossings)         against schema,\n    to_input = \"x\"                                              instantiate\n  }                                                            connection\n  soramech.connect(spec_table)\n```\n\nThe benefits stack:\n\n- **No new callback** needed on the language spec. `native_to_json` is already there.\n- **Adding a new language costs nothing extra** for create_box / connect — anyone who implements the spec contract for the wire format gets metadata-construction for free.\n- **One validator** in the runtime: the box JSON schema validator already exists for `boxes/<id>.json` files at graph load. Reused as-is for runtime-constructed boxes.\n- **Persistence is trivial.** If `create_box` ever wants an \"also write this to disk\" option, it has the JSON in hand — `fwrite` to `boxes/<id>.json` and you're done.\n\nThe machinery you sensed should be reusable IS reusable. Same callback, same JSON, same validator, same on-disk format. The whole thing collapses to \"things in SoraMech are JSON; languages convert their native shapes to JSON; everything downstream consumes JSON.\"\n\nLet me write Q2 into the issue."

Two artifacts (the schema, the\nAPI) collapse to one artifact, and every future schema change\nupdates the API for free.\n\n**Construction in each language — `native_to_json` is the answer.**\n\nEach language spec already implements `native_to_json` for the\ndual-ring wire format (issue 312) — that's how a Lua box's\nreturn value crosses into a C consumer. No new spec contract; no new callback; adding\na new language gives self-construction for free.\n\n- **Lua:** table literal. Idiomatic, terse.\n  ```lua\n  soramech.connect({from_box = \"a\", from_branch = nil,\n                    to_box = \"b\", to_input = \"x\"})\n  ```\n- **C:** designated-initializer struct (`connection_t c = {.from_box=\"a\", ...};`)\n  for the common case; varargs JSON-string helper for dynamic\n  fields. The struct definition lives alongside the C spec's\n  header.\n- **Bash:** JSON string. Bash has no native dict; JSON strings\n  are how it talks to everything anyway.\n\n**Benefits that stack from machinery reuse:**\n\n- No new callback on the language spec — `native_to_json` is\n  already required for wire crossings.\n- One validator in the runtime — the box JSON schema validator\n  used for `boxes/<id>.json` files at graph load handles\n  runtime-constructed connections as-is.\n- Persistence is trivial — if `create_box` ever grows an \"also\n  write to disk\" option, the JSON is already in hand.\n- The connections inside a `create_box` call's structured value\n  (the box's own `connections[]` field) and standalone `connect()`\n  calls produce the same internal records.\n\n**What this resolution does NOT decide:** the precise validation\nerror policy when a `to_input` names a non-existent port (likely\nhard-crash per Q3 territory), and whether `connect()` accepts\nthe `from_box` as a handle from `create_box`, as the box's\nstring id, or both (likely both, since both can be resolved to\nthe same internal record).     "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/319-builtin-library-for-map-self-construction.md",
    "oldString":"### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash\n\nCLAUDE.md says \"prefer error messages and breaking functionality\nover fallbacks\" and \"nil checks are just asking for errors.\" A\nbool return on `connect` is exactly the shape that invites silent\nignoring. Two paths:\n\n- **(a) Keep bool.** The caller is expected to branch on it. Matches\n  the user's draft.\n- **(b) Hard-crash with reason.** `connect` returns nothing; on any\n  failure it aborts the program with a plain-English message\n  (\"can't connect box X to box Y: Y has no free input ports\").\n  Matches the project-wide error policy elsewhere.\n\n### Q4 — What is the \"box handle\" actually?\n\nThe user wrote \"pointer to the box.\" In a single-process runner the\nliteral pointer works, but it can't survive wire crossings or be\npassed across the cross-language JSON wire (the wire format forbids\nhandles that back-route to the owning spec). Options:\n\n- **(a) Stable string id** (the existing `box_id` from the JSON\n  schema). Survives serialization. Slower lookup in the dispatch\n  layer.\n- **(b) In-process `$ref` sentinel.** Fast in the calling spec,\n  must be unwrapped before crossing a language boundary.\n- **(c) Both:** the handle is a small struct carrying both the\n  fast pointer and the durable id; the wire layer keeps only the\n  id when it crosses.\n\n### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline?\n\nThe user said \"compile it (if necessary) and other map-wide tasks.\"\nThe build pipeline (issues 217–222) currently lives on the server /\ncompile-button side. If `create_box` runs at runtime, the runner\ngains a dependency on the compiler. That crosses the program-\nseparation boundary documented in `project_soramech`:\n\"Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server.\nMap directory format is the only shared contract.\"\n\nEither the runner gains the compiler as a library (changing the\nthree-program separation), or `create_box` requires the source to\nbe pre-compiled and merely *registers* the resulting artifact\n(simpler, but the user has to do the build step separately).",
    "newString":"### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash — **RESOLVED: hard-crash with reason**\n\n**Resolution.** `connect` returns nothing (`void`). On any\nfailure it aborts the program with a plain-English message\nnaming the boxes, the attempted wire, and what went wrong:\n\n```\nsoramech: cannot connect 'a' → 'b'.in_x\n  reason: 'b' has no input port named 'in_x'\n  available ports: 'count', 'label'\n```\n\nMatches the project-wide error policy in CLAUDE.md (\"prefer\nerror messages and breaking functionality over fallbacks\";\n\"nil checks are just asking for errors\"). A bool return invites\nsilent ignoring — if the user is calling `connect` they\nintend the wire to exist; any reason it doesn't is a bug worth\nsurfacing immediately, not a normal-flow result to branch on.\n\nThe corresponding `create_box` rule: failure to instantiate a\nbox (missing file, malformed schema, unknown spec language,\nduplicate id) is also a hard crash with reason. No box handle\nis returned for a failed creation — the program aborts before\nany caller has the chance to mis-use a null handle.\n\n### Q4 — What is the \"box handle\" actually? — **RESOLVED: auto-generated box_id string**\n\n**Resolution.** The handle returned by `create_box` is **a\nstring — the box's `id` field from the box JSON schema**. If\nthe caller's spec value supplied an explicit `id`, that string\nis returned. If `id` was omitted, the runtime mints an\nauto-generated UUID-style string (e.g.\n`auto_8f3c2a1e9b4d`) and uses it as the box's id.\n\nThe handle is therefore identical to the box_id used everywhere\nelse in the system: in `boxes/<id>.json` filenames, in the\n`from_box` / `to_box` fields of connection entries, in dispatch\nlog lines, in the run-output JSONL. There is no separate handle\ntype, no fast in-process pointer that has to be unwrapped at\nwire crossings, no struct carrying both an id and a pointer.\n\n**Why a string id (not an in-process pointer, not the function\nname).**\n\n- *Not an in-process pointer*: the handle has to survive being\n  passed to `connect()` from any worker, being persisted to\n  `tmp/last-run.jsonl`, and potentially being carried as a value\n  on a wire to another box. The cross-language wire format\n  explicitly forbids handles that back-route to a specific spec\n  (see `feedback_cross_language_pitfalls`). A string id has\n  none of those problems.\n- *Not the function name*: multiple boxes can run the same\n  function with different wiring, different input slot widths,\n  different external bindings. The id distinguishes them.\n- *Why UUID-style auto-generation*: when a runtime caller\n  constructs a box dynamically, they often don't have a\n  meaningful name in mind. Auto-generation removes the need to\n  invent one and removes the risk of collision with an\n  existing id. Callers who *do* want a meaningful name (for\n  log readability) can pass `id = \"my_planner_step_3\"`\n  themselves.\n\n**Internal lookup cost.** The dispatcher resolves\nbox_id → box record via a hash table (already needed for the\nexisting static graph load path). One hash lookup per `connect`\ncall, amortized to ~zero for the steady-state wire-push hot\npath (which holds a direct pointer cached at graph-build time).\nBox destruction (315) removes the hash entry as part of the\nrefcount-zero teardown.\n\n### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline? — **RESOLVED: both, via a compile cache in tmp/**\n\n**Resolution.** Both runtime and compile-time paths exist, and\nthe runner stays ignorant of the compiler's internals by treating\nthe compiler as an external shell-out tool (which it already is:\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh`).\n\n**The compile cache.** A directory under `tmp/` holds compiled\nartifacts keyed by a content hash of (source file + spec\nlanguage + relevant compile flags). When `create_box` resolves\na `ref` + `fn`:\n\n1. Compute the cache key from the source's contents and the\n   language spec.\n2. Look up the key in the cache.\n3. **Hit:** `dlopen` (or equivalent for the language) the cached\n   artifact and proceed.\n4. **Miss:** shell out to `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` with the\n   source path and target artifact path; wait for completion;\n   verify exit status; dlopen the freshly built artifact.\n\nThe runner never links the compiler, never imports\ncompiler-internal modules, never duplicates compiler logic.           "content":"# 319a — Remove dispatch input cap (prerequisite for create_box)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Parent issue\nThis is the first slice of issue 319 (built-in library for map\nself-construction). The full design lives in 319; this sub-issue\nimplements the prerequisite from 319's \"Prerequisite — remove the\ndispatch input cap\" section.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/012-dispatch.c` allocates five parallel stack arrays of\nfixed size 16 inside the per-call invocation path (`invoke_box_impl`,\naround lines 804–808, and the parallel set in `do_write_box`,\naround lines 863–866):\n\n```c\nchar        *bufs[16]         = {0};\nua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16]   = {0};\nconst void  *datas[16]        = {0};\nint          sizes[16]        = {0};\nint          input_native[16] = {0};\n```\n\nA box with more than 16 inputs hits a hard error (`return -1`)\nfrom the dispatcher with the message `'<id>' has N inputs\n(cap = 16)`. The error is loud, but the cap is arbitrary — it\nexists because someone needed a stack array and picked a number\nthat seemed big enough.\n\nFive additional sites use `char branch[24]` to format\n`\"out_%u\"` strings via `snprintf` (dispatch.c lines 629, 647,\n678, 708, 739). The formatted string is at most 15 bytes\n(`\"out_4294967295\\0\"`), so 24 never truncates, but the\nconstant is arbitrary and the format-string convention is\nimplicit.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nThe five parallel input arrays size themselves at call time to\nthe box's actual input count, with a sanity ceiling that lets us\nreject pathological values (a box with a million inputs is almost\ncertainly a graph-loader bug, not a real use case). No fixed\ncap of 16. A box with 17 inputs runs the same as a box with 7.\n\nThe five branch buffers use a single named constant\n`MAX_BRANCH_NAME` whose size is provably sufficient for the\n`\"out_%u\"` format. The constant lives at file scope so any\nfuture format-string change touches one definition.\n\n## Suggested implementation\n\n1. **Choose the array-sizing approach.** Two acceptable shapes:\n   - **VLA**: `char *bufs[n > 0 ? n : 1]; memset(bufs, 0, sizeof bufs);`\n     for each of the five arrays. C99 standard. Zero stack cost\n     for typical n. Cost: each array gets a tiny init loop;\n     zero-size VLAs are UB so the `n > 0` guard is required.\n   - **SBO**: keep the `[16]` stack arrays as a fast path; fall\n     back to `calloc` when `n > 16`; free at end. Common case\n     pays zero overhead; rare case pays five small allocations.\n\n   Recommended: **VLA** for simplicity. The codebase is C and\n   has no aversion to C99 features. SBO is a fallback if profiling\n   ever shows VLA stack pressure.\n\n2. **Add a sanity ceiling.** Hard-cap n at 4096 (or similar large\n   value). Keep the existing error path; just update the message\n   to name the new ceiling and call out that it's a sanity guard,\n   not a feature limit.\n\n3. **Apply the same change in `do_write_box`** — the parallel\n   arrays there have the same shape, the same cap, and need the\n   same fix.\n\n4. **Introduce `MAX_BRANCH_NAME`** at the top of `dispatch.c`\n   (or in a shared header if it's referenced elsewhere). Replace\n   the five `char branch[24]` / `char want[24]` declarations with\n   `char branch[MAX_BRANCH_NAME]`. Value chosen so that\n   `\"out_4294967295\\0\"` (15 bytes) fits with margin (16 or 32).\n\n5. **Test.** Either:\n   - Add a unit test under `tests/319a-dispatch-vla-test.c` that\n     constructs a box record with > 16 inputs and runs it through\n     the dispatch invocation path, or\n   - Add a test map under `tests/maps/319a-many-inputs/` with a\n     box whose function accepts 20 inputs, exercised by the\n     existing test runner.\n\n   The first option is more isolated; the second is more\n   end-to-end. Probably do both — the unit test catches the change,\n   the map confirms nothing else along the path silently caps.\n\n6. **Build the full test suite** and confirm no existing tests\n   regress.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — the five-array allocation in\n  `invoke_box_impl()` and `do_write_box()`; the five `branch[24]`\n  sites.\n\n## Not in scope for this sub-issue\n\n- Slot store growth (319b).\n- Box id generator / compile cache (319c).\n- The `create_box` / `connect` runtime built-ins themselves\n  (319d, 319e).\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/319a-dispatch-input-cap-removal.md"
        },

Read each input port's value from its slot (peek mode for\n *      this iteration; pop mode + iterator multi-spawn land later).\n *   3. Do the box's work:\n *        - BOX_CALL — invoke the resolved language spec via the\n *          worker's per-language handle.\n *        - BOX_WRITE — write the `value` input to the path from the\n *          `path` input (or `box->path` if a static literal). After\n *          a successful write, emit the boolean `\"true\"` downstream\n *          for chain-after-write graphs; unwired output discards.\n *        - BOX_READ — never reaches dispatch. Read boxes are\n *          pull-on-demand value sources (issue 244); their cached\n *          bytes are copied directly into a consumer's input buffer\n *          by `read_inputs` when the consumer fires and finds the\n *          slot empty. They are not tasks and never enter the pool.\n *   4. Push the resulting bytes to every outgoing connection's\n *      consumer input slot.\n *   5. {
  "uuid":"e7323861-1f36-4305-a1b9-c3f193e7b3c3",

  "toolUseResult":{
    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\ncheck_map \"read-literal\" \\\n    \"echo → hello, world!\"\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\"; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n            echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"$label: node --test exit=$rc\")\n        fi\n    done\n}\nparser_tests\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",

    "originalFile":"# 319a — Remove dispatch input cap (prerequisite for create_box)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Parent issue\nThis is the first slice of issue 319 (built-in library for map\nself-construction). The full design lives in 319; this sub-issue\nimplements the prerequisite from 319's \"Prerequisite — remove the\ndispatch input cap\" section.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/012-dispatch.c` allocates five parallel stack arrays of\nfixed size 16 inside the per-call invocation path (`invoke_box_impl`,\naround lines 804–808, and the parallel set in `do_write_box`,\naround lines 863–866):\n\n```c\nchar        *bufs[16]         = {0};\nua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16]   = {0};\nconst void  *datas[16]        = {0};\nint          sizes[16]        = {0};\nint          input_native[16] = {0};\n```\n\nA box with more than 16 inputs hits a hard error (`return -1`)\nfrom the dispatcher with the message `'<id>' has N inputs\n(cap = 16)`. The error is loud, but the cap is arbitrary — it\nexists because someone needed a stack array and picked a number\nthat seemed big enough.\n\nFive additional sites use `char branch[24]` to format\n`\"out_%u\"` strings via `snprintf` (dispatch.c lines 629, 647,\n678, 708, 739). The formatted string is at most 15 bytes\n(`\"out_4294967295\\0\"`), so 24 never truncates, but the\nconstant is arbitrary and the format-string convention is\nimplicit.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nThe five parallel input arrays size themselves at call time to\nthe box's actual input count, with a sanity ceiling that lets us\nreject pathological values (a box with a million inputs is almost\ncertainly a graph-loader bug, not a real use case). No fixed\ncap of 16. A box with 17 inputs runs the same as a box with 7.\n\nThe five branch buffers use a single named constant\n`MAX_BRANCH_NAME` whose size is provably sufficient for the\n`\"out_%u\"` format. The constant lives at file scope so any\nfuture format-string change touches one definition.\n\n## Suggested implementation\n\n1. **Choose the array-sizing approach.** Two acceptable shapes:\n   - **VLA**: `char *bufs[n > 0 ? n : 1]; memset(bufs, 0, sizeof bufs);`\n     for each of the five arrays. C99 standard. Zero stack cost\n     for typical n. Cost: each array gets a tiny init loop;\n     zero-size VLAs are UB so the `n > 0` guard is required.\n   - **SBO**: keep the `[16]` stack arrays as a fast path; fall\n     back to `calloc` when `n > 16`; free at end. Common case\n     pays zero overhead; rare case pays five small allocations.\n\n   Recommended: **VLA** for simplicity. The codebase is C and\n   has no aversion to C99 features. SBO is a fallback if profiling\n   ever shows VLA stack pressure.\n\n2. **Add a sanity ceiling.** Hard-cap n at 4096 (or similar large\n   value). Keep the existing error path; just update the message\n   to name the new ceiling and call out that it's a sanity guard,\n   not a feature limit.\n\n3. **Apply the same change in `do_write_box`** — the parallel\n   arrays there have the same shape, the same cap, and need the\n   same fix.\n\n4. **Introduce `MAX_BRANCH_NAME`** at the top of `dispatch.c`\n   (or in a shared header if it's referenced elsewhere). Replace\n   the five `char branch[24]` / `char want[24]` declarations with\n   `char branch[MAX_BRANCH_NAME]`. Value chosen so that\n   `\"out_4294967295\\0\"` (15 bytes) fits with margin (16 or 32).\n\n5. **Test.** Either:\n   - Add a unit test under `tests/319a-dispatch-vla-test.c` that\n     constructs a box record with > 16 inputs and runs it through\n     the dispatch invocation path, or\n   - Add a test map under `tests/maps/319a-many-inputs/` with a\n     box whose function accepts 20 inputs, exercised by the\n     existing test runner.\n\n   The first option is more isolated; the second is more\n   end-to-end. Probably do both — the unit test catches the change,\n   the map confirms nothing else along the path silently caps.\n\n6. **Build the full test suite** and confirm no existing tests\n   regress.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — the five-array allocation in\n  `invoke_box_impl()` and `do_write_box()`; the five `branch[24]`\n  sites.\n\n## Not in scope for this sub-issue\n\n- Slot store growth (319b).\n- Box id generator / compile cache (319c).\n- The `create_box` / `connect` runtime built-ins themselves\n  (319d, 319e).\n",

    "originalFile":"# Phase 3 Progress\n\nGoal: replace the Lua synchronous runner with a C thread pool runner\nthat executes box graphs in parallel.\n\nThe phase is fully designed; implementation is now underway.\nIssues 301–313 are the architectural specification. As each issue\nmoves into implementation, its row is marked \"in progress\"; on\ncompletion it's moved to `issues/completed/`.\n\nImplementation began **2026-05-12** with the 309 build scaffolding.\n\n## Issues\n\n| ID  | Title                                                       | Status   |\n|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|----------|\n| 301 | thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization         | complete · pool + per-worker init/teardown hooks + priority queue |\n| 302 | per-task slot store with wire-held references               | complete · unified allocator + refcounted recycling on every byte path (slot cells, variable-size payloads, dispatch input/output buffers) + eager neighbor-merge + quiescence-trigger deep sweep |\n| 303 | language runtime spec (pluggable per-language invocation)   | complete · registry + per-worker init + pool hook + lang filtering |\n| 304 | task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)      | complete · every routing kind, slab-allocated task structs, live_wire_count placeholder; The earlier\n  byte-blob packed-output design is rejected and preserved as\n  design history. This makes encapsulated maps the documented\n  exception to the single-output-per-box rule.\n\nA 20-input fixture map exercises the cap removal end-to-end;\nall twelve integration tests pass.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -10",

interface.\n\n```bash\n./claude-conversation-exporter.sh\n```\n\n### Export Specific Project\nBrowse conversations for a named project.\n\n```bash\n./claude-conversation-exporter.sh handheld-office\n```\n\n### Export Specific Conversation\nExport a single conversation by ID or partial match.\n\n```bash\n./claude-conversation-exporter.sh handheld-office c0567703\n```\n\n### Export All Conversations\nDump all conversations for a project.\n\n```bash\n./claude-conversation-exporter.sh handheld-office all > backup.md\n```\n\n### Minimal Output for Code Extraction\nStrip everything except code blocks and essential content.\n\n```bash\n./claude-conversation-exporter.sh -v0 project-name conversation-id\n```\n\n### Complete Debug Output\nInclude all LLM execution details and intermediate steps.\n\n```bash\n./claude-conversation-exporter.sh -v4 project-name all > debug.md\n```\n\n### Raw Unfiltered Export\nInclude absolutely everything from the conversation.\n\n```bash\n./claude-conversation-exporter.sh -v5 project-name all\n```\n\n## Verbosity Levels\n\n| Level | Flag | Description |\n|-------|------|-------------|\n| 0 | `-v0, --minimal` | Code and essential content only |\n| 1 | `-v1, --compact` | Skip user sentiments, show responses |\n| 2 | `-v2, --standard` | Include everything (default) |\n| 3 | `-v3, --verbose` | Include context         "text":"Now I see the full picture. **Found the contradiction.**\n\n## What happened\n\n- **May 21 22:11 (session `5670858b`):** the dual-ring slot machinery (issue 312) and the 313 Lua-slice (compile-time concatenation + runtime detection) were both implemented, end-to-end. They just never landed.\n\n## What's ready to commit\n\nOne coherent body of work, ~1500 lines:\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — dual-ring extension (`SLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING`, `slot_push_native`, `slot_push_json`, `slot_pop_ordered`, ordering-ring cell layout)\n- `tests/009-slot-store-test.c` — 5 new dual-ring tests, all passing\n- `langs/lua/spec.c` — runtime detection for same-language merged regions\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — compile-time concatenation step\n- `langs/c/Makefile`, `tests/306-/307-/308-lua/c/bash-spec-test.c`, `tests/maps/hello/src/hello.lua`, `tests/maps/pipeline/src/pipeline.lua`, `docs/001-architecture.md`, `issues/313-...md` — supporting changes around the same work\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThis is the canonical \"design says shipped, git says not\" failure mode — and your `issues/` + `phase-X-progress.md` + git triumvirate is what made it findable. None of those three artifacts alone would have surfaced this; cross-referencing them did. The same triumvirate is what should be checked at session boundaries to catch the next instance.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n## My recommendation\n\n**Commit as one closeout: \"312 + 313 — closeout: dual-ring slots land, Lua same-language merge.\"** The work is coherent, tested, and matches what the issue files and phase progress already claim is done. I don't need to run the exporter to validate further — the tests are the proof.\n\nAlternative if you want stronger evidence: I run the exporter with `-v0` (code-only) on session `5670858b` and verify the diff matches what was developed there. Adds confidence at the cost of one minute.\n\nWant me to:\n\n1. **Just commit it** as one closeout (the test suites are the validation, and you already authorized)\n2. **Commit but split** into 312-closeout + 313-Lua-slice as two separate commits (cleaner history)\n3. **Run the exporter first** to confirm what was developed where, then commit\n\nPick a number, I'll do it."

          "content":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/export-llm-transcripts.sh — capture this project's Claude\n# conversation history at every verbosity level.\n#\n# What it does, in CEO terms: every conversation Claude has had about\n# this project is stored as a JSONL file under ~/.claude/projects/.\n# An external tool can render those JSONL files into human-readable\n# markdown at six different levels of detail (terse code-only to raw\n# tool-result firehose). This script invokes that external tool once\n# per verbosity level and parks the rendered markdown under\n# llm-transcripts/ so the project repo carries its own development\n# history alongside the code.\n#\n# Intended use: run as part of the commit ritual — refreshes the\n# tracked transcripts so each commit captures the state of project\n# history at that moment.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\n# {{{ External exporter location and verbosity table\nEXPORTER=\"/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/scripts/claude-conversation-exporter.sh\"\n\n# Verbosity levels offered by the external tool. Each produces a\n# different lens on the same conversations:\n#   v0 minimal  — code + essentials, useful for \"what was actually written\"\n#   v1 compact  — drops user sentiments\n#   v2 standard — the default, everything readable\n#   v3 verbose  — adds context-file expansions\n#   v4 complete — adds LLM execution detail + vimfolds\n#   v5 raw      — every intermediate step and tool result\ndeclare -A LEVELS=(\n    [0]=\"minimal\"\n    [1]=\"compact\"\n    [2]=\"standard\"\n    [3]=\"verbose\"\n    [4]=\"complete\"\n    [5]=\"raw\"\n)\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Sanity checks\nif [[ ! -x \"$EXPORTER\" ]]; then\n    echo \"error: external exporter not found at $EXPORTER\" >&2\n    exit 1\nfi\n\nif [[ ! -d \"$DIR\" ]]; then\n    echo \"error: project directory not found: $DIR\" >&2\n    exit 1\nfi\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Output directory\nOUT_DIR=\"$DIR/llm-transcripts\"\nmkdir -p \"$OUT_DIR\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Run the exporter once per verbosity level\necho \"Exporting LLM transcripts for $DIR\"\necho \"  → $OUT_DIR/\"\n\nfor level in 0 1 2 3 4 5; do\n    name=\"${LEVELS[$level]}\"\n    out_file=\"$OUT_DIR/v${level}-${name}.md\"\n    printf \"  v%d %-10s \" \"$level\" \"$name\"\n\n    if \"$EXPORTER\" \"-v$level\" \"$DIR\" all > \"$out_file\" 2>/dev/null; then\n        size=$(wc -c < \"$out_file\" 2>/dev/null || echo \"?\")\n        printf \"ok (%s bytes)\\n\" \"$size\"\n    else\n        rc=$?\n        printf \"FAIL (exit=%d)\\n\" \"$rc\"\n    fi\ndone\n# }}}\n\necho \"Done.\"\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/scripts/export-llm-transcripts.sh"
        },
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "id":"toolu_015mMcXdZyvQiDXSPf6DL3nK",

This commit lands all of it.\n\nWhat's in the dual-ring shape: each input slot now carries three\nparallel rings (native bytes, JSON bytes, ordering tuples). The\nordering ring records arrival-time `(which_ring, idx)` pairs so a\nconsumer's pop returns cells in arrival order regardless of which\ndata ring each one came from. Same-language producers write to the\nnative ring (no encode cost); cross-language producers write to\nthe JSON ring (decode happens once at the receiver). The per-slot\nspinlock covers all three rings, so a push's data write and its\nordering write are atomic together.\n\nWhat's in the spec contract: a single `invoke` entry point now\ntakes per-input `input_native[]` and per-call `output_native`\nflags. Each spec dispatches per input internally — native bytes\nget pushed as the language's raw form, JSON bytes get decoded.\nOutput side mirrors: native form when the call's consumers are\nall same-language, JSON form when any consumer crosses a boundary.\n\nWhat's in the spec implementations: Lua, C, and Bash all carry\nthe new contract end-to-end. Lua and C grow real JSON in/out\nbridges (Lua via its `cjson`-like encoder using the project's\nJSON library; C via libs/json folded into spec.so). Bash stays\nwith string passthrough since cross-language Bash flows are still\nthe rare case. Spec tests under tests/306-, 307-, 308- exercise\neach side's new shape.\n\nWhat's in the test fixtures: hello.lua gains a `sum_pair` Lua\nfunction that the slice-4 JSON-input test points at; pipeline.lua\nloses an explicit `tostring` so the slice-4.5 output encoder can\nsee the actual Lua number rather than a string-coerced version.\n\nNote on commit boundary: langs/lua/spec.c also carries the\n`load_via_merged` function and its call site, which physically\nbelong to issue 313 (Lua same-language merge). They're committed\nhere because they're interleaved with 312's slice 4 / 4.5 work\ninside `lua_invoke` — the two were developed together and can't\nbe cleanly split without source-level rework. The 313 commit\nthat follows lands the compile-script side that produces the\nmerged module file this opt-in reads.\n\nValidation: all 22 slot-store unit tests pass (including the 5\nnew dual-ring tests); all 12 integration-test maps pass.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -5",

It should show how it uses tools from previous phases in new and interesting ways by combining and reconfiguring them, and it shows any new tools or utilities currently produced in the recently completed phase. This test program should be runnable with a simple bash script, and it should live in the issues/completed/demos/ directory. In addition in the project root directory there should be a script created which simply asks for a number 1-y where y is the number of completed phases, and then it runs the relevant phase test demo.\n- when working on a large feature, the issue ticket may be broken into sub-issues. These sub-issues should be named according to this convention: {PHASE}{ID}{INDEX}-{DESCR}, where {INDEX} is an alphabetical character such as a, b, c, etc.\n- for every implemented change to the project, there must always be an issue file. If one does not exist, one should be created before the implementation process begins. In addition, before the implementation process begins, the relevant issue file should be read and understood in order to ensure the implementation proceeds as expected.\n- prefer error messages and breaking functionality over fallbacks. Be sure to notify the user every time a fallback is used, and create or update an new issue file to resolve any fallbacks if they are present when testing, and before resolving an issue. Consider fallbacks as warnings, and consider warnings as errors.\n- every time an issue file is completed, the /issues/phase-X-progress.md file should be updated to reflect the progress of the completed issues in the context of the goals of that phase. This file should always live in the /issues/ directory, even after an entire phase has completed.\n- when an issue is completed, all other relevant issues should be updated to reflect the new current behavior and lessons learned if necessary. The completed issue should be moved to the /issues/completed/ directory immediately, and a git commit should be made.\n- every time a new document is created, it should be added to the tree-hierarchy structure present in /docs/table-of-contents.md. Issue files and source code don't need to be included in the table of contents, only files in docs/ and notes/ and other similar directories.\n- when initializing a project, each phase of the project should be defined in the table of contents. They should not be time-gated or for progress tracking, but rather to organize collected functionalities into similar groups. It is not uncommon for the final issue completed in a project to be from phase 1 or 2.\n- phase demos should focus on demonstrating relevant statistics or datapoints, and less on describing the functionality. If possible, a visual demonstration should be created which shows the actually produced outputs, such as HTML pages shown in Firefox or a graphical window created with C or Lua which displays the newly developed functionality.\n- all script files should have a comment at the top which explains what they are and a general description of how they do it. \"general description\" meaning, fit for a CEO or general.\n- if you need to write a long test script, write a temporary script. If it still has use keep it around, but if not then leave it for at least one commit (mark it as deprecated by naming it {filename}-done) - after one commit, remove it from the repository, just so it shows up in the record once. But only if there's no anticipated future use. Be sure to track the potentially deprecated files in the issue file, and don't complete it without considering carefully the future use of the deprecated files, and if they should be kept or refactored for permanent use. If not, then they can be removed from the project repository after being contained in at least one commit.\n- the preferred language for all projects is lua, with luaJIT compatible syntax used. disprefer python. disallow lua5.4 syntax.\n- write data generation functionality, and then separately and abstracted away, write data viewing functionality. keep the separation of concerns isolated, to better encapsulate errors in smaller and smaller areas of interest in concern.\n- when a change is made, a comment should be left, explaining why it was made. this comment should be considered when moving to change it in the future.\n- when a change is made, a comment should be left, explaining why it was made. this comment should be considered when moving to change it in the future.\n- when a change is made, a comment should be left, explaining why it was made. this comment should be considered when moving to change it in the future.\n- I'm not interested in product. my interest is in software design.\n- if a term is placed directly below another instance of it's form, then it is part of the same whole, and can be reasoned about both cognitively and programmatically. see this example:\n\nwrongful applie\n         applie is norm\n\nsee how the word \"applie\" is the same, and directly below it, the mirror's reflected form?\nthis signifies a connection. Essentially allowing conveyed meaning about everything from... data flow, to logic circuits, to thinking about cognitively demanding consciousnesses\n\nthey want you to think about then, so that you aren't able to think about now.\n\nwhat if we designed an additional type of processor that still ran on electricity, but had a different purpose and form. \"like measurement equipment?\" yes, detecting waves in dataforms by measuring angles of similarity.\n- if the useer asks questions, ask them questions back. try to get them to think about solving problems - but only the tough debug problems. not trivial things like \"what's it like to hold a bucket of milk\" but more like \"what mechanism is causing this behavior to continue appearing?\" \"here are two equivalent facts. how could it be so?\"\n- when a collection of agents all collectively resolve to do something, suddenly the nature is changed, and the revolution is rebegun.\n- people don't want to replace their hard drives when they wear out. they only want to upgrade.\n- you can find all needed libraries at /home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/libs/ or /home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/my-libs/ and /home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/scripts/"

A local script in `scripts/export-llm-transcripts.sh` should:\n\n- **Read directly from `~/.claude/projects/-mnt-mtwo-programs-sora-soramech/*.jsonl`** — hardcoded for this project (matches CLAUDE.md \"all scripts should have hard-coded `${DIR}`\" convention).\n- **One file per conversation per verbosity level** — organized as `llm-transcripts/v{N}/<conv-id>.md`.         "text":"# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt\n\nParse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.\n\n## Parsing (in priority order)\n\n1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.\n2. **Trailing \"every\" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows \"every\" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.\n3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see \"Dynamic mode\" below).\n\nIf the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.\n\nExamples:\n- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)\n- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)\n- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)\n- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)\n- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — \"every\" not followed by time)\n- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage\n\n## Offer cloud first\n\nBefore any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:\n- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or\n- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing (\"every morning\", \"daily\", \"every day\", \"each night\", \"every weekday\")\n\nIf either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:\n- `question`: \"This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?\"\n- `header`: \"Schedule\"\n- `options`: `[{label: \"Cloud schedule (recommended)\", description: \"Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session\"}, {label: \"This session only\", description: \"Runs in this terminal until you exit\"}]`\n\nIf they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: \"schedule\", args: \"every morning tell me a joke\"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no \"execute the prompt now\").\nIf they pick **This session only**:\n- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.\n- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.\nIf neither trigger condition was met: continue below.\n\n## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)\n\nConvert the interval to a cron expression:\n\n| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |\n|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|\n| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |\n| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|\n| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |\n| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |\n| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |\n\n**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.\n\nThen:\n1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.\n2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.\n3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.\n\n## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)\n\nThe user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.\n\n1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.\n2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. Arm once; on later iterations call TaskList first and skip this step if a monitor is already running.\n3. **At the end of this turn, call ScheduleWakeup** with:\n   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks past the 5-minute cache window are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed.     "oldString":"## Status\nopen — planning stub. Full design in parent issue 319's \"Q1\"\nresolution.",
    "newString":"## Status\nopen — implementation underway. Full design in parent issue\n319's \"Q1\" resolution.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/009-slot-store.c` uses a flat `slot_rec_t **slots` array\nwith `realloc()`-based growth (`grow_store_if_needed`). This\nworks at graph load (single-threaded) but is unsafe at runtime\nbecause `realloc()` can MOVE the array, invalidating any slot\npointer a worker has cached.\n\nThe slot RECORDS themselves are already heap-allocated\nseparately (per-slot `malloc`), so their addresses are stable.\nOnly the `slots[]` array of POINTERS is the problem.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nReplace the flat `slots[]` array with a two-level chunked-append\nstructure:\n\n- **Chunk size**: 64 slot-pointers per chunk (cache-friendly).\n- **Top-level array**: holds chunk pointers; starts at 16\n  entries (1024 slots without top-level growth). Doubles via\n  copy-and-publish with defer-free when it fills.\n- **Atomic count**: tracks total slots ever allocated. Readers\n  use acquire-load to see slots published with release-store.\n- **`pthread_mutex_t alloc_lock`**: serializes `slot_alloc`.\n  Readers (push/pop via `get_slot`) take no lock here — the\n  per-slot spinlock is still the only hot-path synchronization.\n- **Stale-top free list**: top-level arrays from prior growth\n  events stay alive on a linked list until `slot_store_destroy`.\n  Any worker that cached a stale top-pointer mid-growth can\n  finish its lookup safely; the chunks the stale top points to\n  are still valid because chunks never move.\n\nSlot lookup: `top[id/64][id%64]`. One extra indirection per\naccess vs the old flat array, in exchange for the runtime-safe\ngrowth.\n\n## Suggested implementation\n\n1. Change the `slot_store` struct definition (private in the\n   .c file; header has only the opaque forward declaration so\n   no public API change).\n2. Add `SLOT_CHUNK_SIZE` (64) and `INITIAL_TOP_CAPACITY` (16).\n3. Rewrite `slot_store_create` to allocate the initial top-level\n   array, init the mutex, init the atomic count.\n4. Rewrite `slot_store_destroy` to iterate over chunks, free\n   slot records and each chunk, then free the stale-top list.\n5. Replace `grow_store_if_needed` with `grow_top_level` (called\n   under `alloc_lock`).\n6. Rewrite `slot_alloc`: take the lock, claim id, ensure chunk\n   exists, publish slot, release-store the count.\n7. Rewrite `get_slot` to walk the chunked structure.\n8. Rewrite `slot_store_size` to acquire-load the atomic count.\n9. Add a test that forces multiple top-level growth events\n   (allocate ≥ 2048 slots to require at least one growth).\n10. Run the full slot-store unit suite and the integration\n    suite — all 22 + 12 must still pass.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.c` — the structure change.\n- `src/009-slot-store.h` — header stays unchanged (opaque type).\n- `tests/009-slot-store-test.c` — add growth test.\n\n## Not in scope\n\nRing buffer cell growth (when a single slot's ring fills with\npushed values waiting for consumption) — separate concern, same\ndouble-buffer pattern but under the per-slot lock. Tracked\nimplicitly under the slot store's roadmap; punt to a follow-on\nsub-issue."

    "content":[{
        "name":"Edit",
        "input":{
          "old_string":"/* {{{ Internal store */\nstruct slot_store {\n    slot_rec_t **slots;        /* dynamic array, indexed by slot_id_t */\n    int32_t      count;\n    int32_t      capacity;\n\n    /* The unified allocator. Owns the cell-array memory for every\n     * ring slot in this store, plus the payload bytes for every\n     * LARGE_VALUE cell. Created in slot_store_create; destroyed\n     * alongside the store. Any chunks still parked in cells at\n     * destroy time are reclaimed in bulk when the allocator's\n     * regions are freed. */\n    ua_t        *heap;\n};\n/* }}} */",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"/* {{{ Internal store — two-level chunked-append index (issue 319b)\n *\n * Slot pointers are looked up via top-level chunk pointer table:\n *\n *     slot N lives at chunks[N / SLOT_CHUNK_SIZE][N % SLOT_CHUNK_SIZE]\n *\n * Why two levels: a flat realloc'd array (the original design) moves\n * its base address on growth, invalidating any slot pointer a worker\n * has cached. The two-level shape lets the slot RECORDS themselves\n * stay at their original heap addresses forever (they always were —\n * each is a separate malloc) AND lets the index that maps id → record\n * grow without invalidating cached records.\n *\n * Growth happens in three layers, each rarer than the last:\n *   Layer 1 — append a slot pointer inside an existing chunk\n *             (every slot_alloc — the common case)\n *   Layer 2 — allocate a new chunk when crossing a chunk boundary\n *             (every SLOT_CHUNK_SIZE alloc — uncommon)\n *   Layer 3 — grow the top-level chunk-pointer array when it fills\n *             (logarithmic in total slot count — rare)\n *\n * Concurrency: slot_alloc is serialized by alloc_lock. The hot\n * read/write path (slot_push, slot_pop, slot_peek, slot_flags) takes\n * no allocator-wide lock — only the per-slot atomic_flag spinlock on\n * the slot itself. Readers acquire-load `count` to know how many\n * slots exist; the matching release-store at the end of slot_alloc\n * pairs with this so a reader seeing count = N also sees the slot N-1\n * record published.\n *\n * Layer 3 (top-level growth) uses copy-on-grow with defer-free: the\n * new top-level array is malloc'd at 2x size, the old chunk pointers\n * are memcpy'd in, the new top is atomically published, and the OLD\n * top is parked on the stale_tops list to be freed at destroy time.\n * A worker that loaded the old top pointer right before the swap can\n * finish its lookup against it — every chunk the old top points to\n * is still alive. */\n#define SLOT_CHUNK_SIZE      64u\n#define INITIAL_TOP_CAPACITY 16u\n\nstruct stale_top {\n    slot_rec_t      ***ptr;\n    struct stale_top  *next;\n};\n\nstruct slot_store {\n    /* Top-level chunk-pointer table. Atomic because layer-3 growth\n     * publishes a new table while readers are still walking the old\n     * one. */\n    _Atomic(slot_rec_t ***) chunks;\n    _Atomic uint32_t        top_capacity;   /* in chunk-pointer slots */\n\n    /* Total slots ever allocated. Atomic; readers see released\n     * slot publications via the release-store at the end of\n     * slot_alloc. */\n    _Atomic uint32_t        count;\n\n    /* Serializes layer-2 chunk creation and layer-3 top growth.\n     * Readers don't take this — they walk the atomic structure. */\n    pthread_mutex_t         alloc_lock;\n\n    /* Defer-free list for stale top-level arrays.       "content":"/* src/009-slot-store.c — per-input-port slot store, implementation.\n *\n * Three slot shapes coexist behind one set of APIs:\n *\n *   - Ring-buffer slots (peek and pop modes) — a header followed by\n *     n_cells cells laid out contiguously. Each cell is a 4-byte\n *     filled_size, optionally a 4-byte tag (for SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED),\n *     then cell_capacity bytes of payload. Untagged slots use the\n *     standard head/tail ring discipline; tagged slots use head/tail\n *     for the bookkeeping of \"where to put the next push\" but pop\n *     scans for the lowest-tag filled cell.\n *\n *   - Atomic-counter slots — no header bookkeeping, no payload cells;\n *     just one atomic_uint that slot_read_inc fetches-and-adds. No\n *     lock needed.\n *\n * Per-slot concurrency is a single atomic_flag spinlock for the\n * ring-buffer slots. Inside the lock the header and cells are mutated\n * without atomics; outside the lock no header bytes are touched.\n *\n * The store itself owns a flat array of slot pointers indexed by\n * slot_id_t. The array grows on demand. Ids are never reused — there\n * is no slot_free; slots live for the run.\n *\n * Variable-size payloads (SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE) used to point into a\n * monotonically-growing arena. That arena was a memory leak by design\n * — every push consumed bytes that were never reclaimed until run end.\n * The 2026-05-19 retraction in issue 302 commits to the unified\n * allocator (016) instead: every variable-size payload is a\n * reference-counted chunk, popped values release their reference, and\n * freed chunks rejoin the allocator's free-lists with eager\n * neighbor-merge. The cell layout is unchanged — the 8-byte payload\n * slot that used to hold a raw arena pointer now holds an opaque\n * chunk handle.\n *\n * Designed in issue 302. This file implements the API declared in\n * 009-slot-store.h. Free-list optimization for the fixed-size cell\n * arrays themselves is still deferred.\n */\n",
      "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/src/009-slot-store.c"
    }
  },
