          "command":"git commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\n319d — closeout: maps build more of themselves at runtime\n\nThe headline feature for 319 lands. A running Lua box can now mint\na new box and wire to it from inside its own function body:\n\n  local id = soramech.create_box{\n    kind = \"call\", lang = \"lua\",\n    ref = \"src/echo.lua\", fn = \"echo\",\n    inputs = {{name = \"x\", type = \"string\"}}\n  }\n  soramech.connect{from_box = \"self\", to_box = id, to_input = \"x\"}\n\nWhen the box's function returns, the dispatcher walks the producer's\nconnections — now including the freshly-added wire — and pushes the\nreturn value into the newly-created box's input slot. The spawn\ncheck fires, the new box runs, its output is captured. End-to-end.\n\nWhat had to grow under the hood. The graph's box index was a flat\nrealloc'd array of box_t structs; that's now a pointer-array of\nindividually-malloc'd box records (so each box's address stays\nstable across pointer-array growth), with copy-and-publish under\na mutex when the index itself needs to grow. The per-box connection\nlist got the same treatment via atomic copy-and-publish, with old\narrays parked on a stale-list and freed at graph teardown. Both\nchanges are invisible above the graph_box / graph_n_boxes accessor\nboundary, so dispatch and the event log didn't have to learn about\nthe shape change.\n\nThe dispatch context's per-box bookkeeping arrays (spawn guards,\noutput-capture buffers) are sized at init time and aren't yet\ngrowable. Slice 1 oversizes them by a generous headroom (4096\nruntime-created boxes) instead of plumbing growable arrays end\nto end. The headroom is documented in the issue file as a known\nlimit; raising it or making the arrays properly growable is a\nfollow-on.\n\nPlumbing for spec → runtime API. The runtime targets (graph, slot\nstore, spec registry) live in a thread-local that dispatch_action\nsets before each spec invoke and clears after. The Lua builtin\nwrappers read the TLS to find them — no change to the spec invoke\nsignature was needed. The runner is linked with -rdynamic so the\ndlopen'd spec.so plugins can call back into the runner's runtime_*\nsymbols at load time.\n\nSlice 1 restrictions, documented in the issue: Lua only (C and\nBash bindings come in 319e), kind=call only, plain routing only,\nand the connect call assumes the from_box is the currently-firing\nspec (the common case is safe under the existing single-spawn CAS;\nthe general concurrent case is deferred).\n\nValidation: 13 integration tests pass, including a new fixture\nwhere the trigger box uses create_box + connect to spawn a\ndownstream echo_dyn box that runs and produces output. The\nslot store's 23 unit tests still pass.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -5",

        "text":"319d landed at **`db3fe67`**.\n\n## Recap\n\nIssue 319's headline feature — **runtime self-construction** — is now working end-to-end:\n\n| Sub-issue | Status | What ships |\n|-----------|--------|-----------|\n| 319a | ✓ | Dispatch holds boxes of any width |\n| 319b | ✓ | Slot store grows without moving slots |\n| 319c | ✓ | Box ids minted thread-safely |\n| **319d** | **✓ (slice 1)** | **Lua boxes can `create_box` + `connect` mid-run** |\n| 319e | next | C + Bash bindings + non-call kinds + docs |\n\nThe fixture proves the full path:\n\n```\ntrigger.lua calls soramech.create_box → gets \"auto_00000000\"\n            calls soramech.connect    → wires trigger → auto_00000000\n            returns \"trigger-fired:auto_00000000:hello-from-trigger\"\n            (dispatcher pushes through the new connection)\nauto_00000000 (newly created box) runs\n              returns \"echo_dyn-received:trigger-fired:auto_00000000:hello-from-trigger\"\n```\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nYou were right — I was scaring myself into diminution. The actual changes turned out smaller than I feared because every layer was already shaped right: the dispatch went through `graph_box()` accessors (so changing storage was invisible), the spec contract already had the `box_t *` parameter (so no signature change), and the per-slot lock pattern from 319b was directly reusable for connections. The \"compromise\" I almost made would have foregone the whole headline feature for the sake of avoiding work that turned out to be largely mechanical. **Believing it would work made it tractable.**\n\nThe documented limits in this slice (Lua only, call only, plain routing, 4096-box headroom, single-firing-box assumption for connect) are the right kind of \"ship and audit\" — each is a clear seam for a follow-on, not load-bearing for the feature itself.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nWant to do 319e next, or pause here?"

    "type":"message",
    "stop_reason":"end_turn",
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"You're right and I made a wrong call. Let me think through it properly.\n\n## What I did\n\n`runtime_create_box` and `runtime_connect` are language-agnostic C functions in `src/018-runtime-builtins.c` — those are fine. But to make them *callable from user code*, I exposed them as **Lua functions** (`soramech.create_box`, `soramech.connect`) registered in `langs/lua/spec.c`. The plan for 319e was to repeat the same wrapping in `langs/c/spec.c` and `langs/bash/spec.c`.\n\nThat repetition-per-language is the smell you're spotting. Read boxes and write boxes don't get re-implemented per language — they're **box kinds** in the JSON schema, handled by the runtime itself (`do_write_box` in dispatch.c), and user code interacts with them by wiring data in and out.\n\n## What I should have done\n\nMake `create_box` and `connect` **new box kinds**, alongside `read` / `write` / `call` / `comparator` / `iterator`:\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"spawn_step\", \"kind\": \"create_box\",\n  \"inputs\": [ { \"name\": \"spec\", \"type\": \"json\" } ],\n  \"connections\": [ ... wire the resulting id somewhere ... ] }\n\n{ \"id\": \"wire_it\",   \"kind\": \"connect\",\n  \"inputs\": [ { \"name\": \"from_box\", \"type\": \"string\" },\n              { \"name\": \"to_box\",   \"type\": \"string\" },\n              { \"name\": \"to_input\", \"type\": \"string\" } ] }\n```\n\nThen a Lua box (or C box, or Bash box) wanting to spawn a downstream pipeline just:\n1. Outputs a JSON spec on its wire\n2. The spec flows into a `create_box` kind box\n3. The `create_box` box outputs the new id\n4. The id flows wherever it's needed (probably into a `connect` box)\n\n**Same machinery for every language. Zero per-language bindings.** Matches the rest of SoraMech's \"the language spec writes data, the runtime moves data, special box kinds do special things\" model.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nWhy I drifted: when I asked \"how does user code invoke this?\" my brain went to \"expose a callback the spec wraps\" because that's the standard FFI pattern in C/Lua/etc. But SoraMech's primary FFI is **wires**, not function calls. The right question was \"what does this look like as a box?\" — same way `read` is the FFI for \"read file\" and `write` is the FFI for \"write file.\" `create_box` should be the FFI for \"create box.\" I skipped a step.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n## Tradeoff to flag\n\nThere's one thing the box-kind model handles differently from the in-spec-callback model: **getting the new box's id back to the creator synchronously**. With Lua bindings, the planner calls `create_box(spec)` and gets the id on the next line. With box-kinds, the planner outputs a spec, fires once, and the id arrives back via a wire later (potentially in the next iteration).\n\nFor most use cases this is fine — the dataflow shape is natural and async anyway. For some patterns it's awkward, e.g. \"create N boxes in a loop and remember all their ids.\" But those patterns can still be expressed via iterator-style boxes or via batching the spec into an array, so I don't think it's load-bearing.\n\n## What to do about 319d\n\nThree options:\n\n1. **Revert the Lua binding bits of 319d, add `create_box` and `connect` as box kinds in a new sub-issue 319d.2.** Cleanest history. The runtime API + graph mutation infrastructure (the bulk of 319d) stays valuable; only the Lua wrapper layer comes out.\n2. **Leave 319d as-is and add box kinds in 319e (instead of C/Bash bindings).** Keeps the Lua bindings around as a \"fast path\" alongside the box-kind path. Two parallel mechanisms; clutter risk.\n3. **Amend 319d via a follow-up commit that removes the Lua bindings and adds box kinds.** Same end result as (1) but with the messier history of \"added then removed.\"\n\nI'd lean (1). The runtime mutation infrastructure I built (graph_add_box, box_add_connection, slot store growth, dispatch headroom, runtime-builtins.c) is all reusable for the box-kind implementation; only `langs/lua/spec.c`'s `soramech_*` functions and the TLS plumbing become unnecessary.\n\nWant me to do (1)? And does the tradeoff about sync-vs-async id-back-to-creator matter enough to add a \"fast path\" for it, or is async always fine?"
      }],
    "role":"assistant",
    "model":"claude-opus-4-7",

}

      "content":"#!/bin/bash\n# langs/bash/bash-server.sh — persistent bash subprocess, one per\n# worker thread, that talks to the C spec over a Unix-domain\n# socketpair connected to stdin/stdout.\n#\n# Designed in issue 308. Replaces the fork+exec-per-call model\n# with a long-lived process: process startup happens once at\n# pool init, every box invocation reuses the same bash state\n# (and the sourced module cache).\n#\n# Protocol — line-oriented, all values UTF-8:\n#\n#   Request:\n#     <n_args>\\n            (or \"QUIT\" to terminate)\n#     <file_path>\\n\n#     <fn_name>\\n\n#     <arg1>\\n              (n_args of these)\n#     <arg2>\\n\n#     ...\n#\n#   Response:\n#     <exit_status>\\n        (0 on success)\n#     <output_length>\\n      (decimal byte count, no newline at end of payload)\n#     <output_bytes>         (output_length bytes, NOT followed by \\n)\n#\n# Limitations of this iteration:\n#   - Arguments cannot contain literal newlines (line-oriented protocol).\n#   - Output is read as bytes — newlines inside the payload are fine,\n#     but trailing newlines from bash builtins like `echo` are part\n#     of the output. Box functions use `printf '%s' \"$x\"` to avoid them.\n#\n# Caching: each box file is sourced on first use and remembered in\n# the `sourced` associative array; subsequent invocations skip the\n# `source` and reuse the loaded functions. Per-worker, no locking.\n\nset -u\n\ndeclare -A sourced\n\nwhile IFS= read -r n_args; do\n    [[ \"$n_args\" == \"QUIT\" ]] && break\n\n    IFS= read -r file_path\n    IFS= read -r fn_name\n\n    args=()\n    for ((i = 0; i < n_args; i++)); do\n        IFS= read -r a\n        args+=(\"$a\")\n    done\n\n    if [[ ! -f \"$file_path\" ]]; then\n        printf '127\\n0\\n'\n        continue\n    fi\n\n    if [[ -z \"${sourced[$file_path]:-}\" ]]; then\n        # shellcheck disable=SC1090\n        if ! source \"$file_path\" 2>/dev/null; then\n            printf '126\\n0\\n'\n            continue\n        fi\n        sourced[$file_path]=1\n    fi\n\n    # Capture function output and exit status. The function name\n    # itself failing (not a callable) surfaces as exit 127.\n    if ! declare -F \"$fn_name\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf '127\\n0\\n'\n        continue\n    fi\n\n    out=$(\"$fn_name\" \"${args[@]}\" 2>/dev/null)\n    status=$?\n    n=${#out}\n    printf '%d\\n%d\\n' \"$status\" \"$n\"\n    printf '%s' \"$out\"\ndone\n",
      "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/langs/bash/bash-server.sh"
    }

    "content":"/* langs/c/soramech.h — runtime self-construction API for C boxes.\n *\n * User C box code that wants to spawn a new box at runtime or\n * connect wires between boxes can `#include \"soramech.h\"` and call\n * these functions. The symbols are resolved at dlopen time —\n * soramech-pool is linked with -rdynamic so the dlopen'd box.so\n * binaries find the runner's runtime_* implementations.\n *\n * The C bindings are thin pass-throughs to the runtime API in\n * src/018-runtime-builtins.h; they exist so user code doesn't need\n * to know the project's internal layout. Designed in issue 319;\n * landed in issue 319e (C slice of the bindings).\n *\n * Argument shape: both functions take JSON text matching the on-disk\n * box JSON schema. For `create_box`, pass an object shaped like an\n * entry in `boxes/<id>.json`. For `connect`, pass an object shaped\n * like an entry in `connections[]`.\n *\n * Failure handling: both return -1 on any error with `*err` set to\n * a malloc'd diagnostic string (caller frees). Error semantics\n * follow the project-wide rule: callers should treat -1 as a hard\n * fault, not a normal-flow result.\n */\n#ifndef SORAMECH_LANG_C_SORAMECH_H\n#define SORAMECH_LANG_C_SORAMECH_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n/* Minimum buffer size for create_box's out_id parameter. Holds\n * \"auto_\" + 8 hex chars + null. */\n#define SORAMECH_BOX_ID_BUF_SIZE 14u\n\n/* Mint a new box from the JSON spec text. Returns 0 on success\n * and fills `out_id` with the new box's id; -1 on failure with\n * `*err` set. */\nint soramech_create_box(const char *spec_json, int spec_len,\n                        char *out_id, size_t out_id_size,\n                        char **err);\n\n/* Append a wire from one box's output to another box's input port.\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on failure with `*err` set. */\nint soramech_connect(const char *conn_json, int conn_len,\n                     char **err);\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_LANG_C_SORAMECH_H */\n",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/langs/c/soramech.h",

For `create_box`, pass an object shaped like an\n * entry in `boxes/<id>.json`. For `connect`, pass an object shaped\n * like an entry in `connections[]`.\n *\n * Failure handling: both return -1 on any error with `*err` set to\n * a malloc'd diagnostic string (caller frees). Holds\n * \"auto_\" + 8 hex chars + null. */\n#define SORAMECH_BOX_ID_BUF_SIZE 14u\n\n/* Forward declarations of the runner-side implementations. The\n * actual definitions live in src/018-runtime-builtins.c and are\n * exported to dlopen'd plugins via -rdynamic. */\nint runtime_create_box(const char *spec_json, int spec_len,\n                       char *out_id, size_t out_id_size,\n                       char **err);\nint runtime_connect(const char *conn_json, int conn_len,\n                    char **err);\n\n/* User-friendly aliases. */\n#define soramech_create_box runtime_create_box\n#define soramech_connect    runtime_connect\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_LANG_C_SORAMECH_H */\n",

      "content":"# langs/c/Makefile — build the C language spec.\n#\n# Produces spec.so, a small .so the pool runner dlopens at startup.\n# Links against -ldl only; the C spec's runtime work is dlopen +\n# dlsym, no third-party runtime needed.\n#\n# Invokable standalone (`make -C langs/c`) or from the top-level\n# Makefile via `make specs`.\n\n# {{{ Resolve project root\nDIR ?= $(abspath $(dir $(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST)))/../..)\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Toolchain & flags\nCC ?= gcc\n\nCFLAGS  = -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -I$(DIR)/langs -I$(DIR)/libs/json -I$(DIR)/src\nLDFLAGS = -ldl\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Build rules\n# spec.c folds libs/json/json.c directly into spec.so for the\n# JSON-input acceptance path (issue 307 slice unblocking 312's\n# deferred Lua output side). Same pattern the Lua spec uses for\n# its own JSON bridges.\n.PHONY: all clean\n\nall: spec.so\n\nspec.so: spec.c $(DIR)/langs/lang-spec.h $(DIR)/libs/json/json.c $(DIR)/libs/json/json.h\n\t@$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ spec.c $(DIR)/libs/json/json.c $(LDFLAGS)\n\nclean:\n\t@rm -f spec.so\n# }}}\n",

    }

          "content":"/* tests/maps/319e-c-create/src/trigger.c — C box that spawns a\n * downstream Lua box at runtime, mirroring the 319d Lua fixture\n * but driven from a C box function instead. Proves the C bindings\n * for runtime self-construction (issue 319e) work end-to-end.\n *\n * The trigger box receives one input (\"input\"), uses\n * soramech_create_box to mint a new Lua box, uses soramech_connect\n * to wire its own output to the new box's \"x\" input, and returns\n * a marker string. The runtime then pushes the marker through the\n * freshly-added connection and the dynamically-created Lua box\n * fires.\n */\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n#include \"soramech.h\"\n\n/* {{{ trigger */\nint trigger(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n            void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    if (n < 1) return -1;\n\n    /* Build the spec for a new Lua box. The shape mirrors what\n     * would be on disk at boxes/<id>.json. */\n    const char *spec =\n        \"{\"\n          \"\\\"kind\\\":\\\"call\\\",\"\n          \"\\\"lang\\\":\\\"lua\\\",\"\n          \"\\\"ref\\\":\\\"src/echo_dyn.lua\\\",\"\n          \"\\\"fn\\\":\\\"echo\\\",\"\n          \"\\\"inputs\\\":[\"\n            \"{\\\"name\\\":\\\"x\\\",\\\"type\\\":\\\"string\\\"}\"\n          \"]\"\n        \"}\";\n\n    char  new_id[SORAMECH_BOX_ID_BUF_SIZE];\n    char *err = NULL;\n    if (soramech_create_box(spec, (int)strlen(spec),\n                            new_id, sizeof new_id, &err) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"trigger.c: create_box failed: %s\\n\",\n                err ? err : \"(no message)\");\n        free(err);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Build the connection entry: wire trigger.output → new.x */\n    char conn[256];\n    int  n_conn = snprintf(conn, sizeof conn,\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"trigger\\\",\"\n         \"\\\"from_branch\\\":null,\"\n         \"\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\"\n         \"\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\", new_id);\n    if (n_conn < 0 || n_conn >= (int)sizeof conn) return -1;\n\n    if (soramech_connect(conn, n_conn, &err) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"trigger.c: connect failed: %s\\n\",\n                err ? err : \"(no message)\");\n        free(err);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Output a marker so the test runner can verify both that\n     * trigger ran AND what the new id was. */\n    int marker_n = snprintf((char *)out_buf, (size_t)out_capacity,\n                            \"c-trigger-fired:%s:%.*s\",\n                            new_id, sizes[0], (const char *)inputs[0]);\n    if (marker_n < 0 || marker_n >= out_capacity) return -1;\n    *out_size = marker_n;\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/tests/maps/319e-c-create/src/trigger.c"
        },

C-to-C is the simplest end-to-end shape: the worker thread\n * already has the C spec's per-worker state initialised, so the\n * new box has somewhere to run. (Cross-language runtime-create\n * needs spec auto-init for languages not in the static graph —\n * documented limit, follow-on slice.) */\n\n#include <string.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n\n/* {{{ echo */\nint echo(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n         void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    if (n < 1) return -1;\n    const char *prefix = \"c-echo-received:\";\n    int prefix_len = (int)strlen(prefix);\n    int total = prefix_len + sizes[0];\n    if (total > out_capacity) return -1;\n    memcpy((char *)out_buf,              prefix,    (size_t)prefix_len);\n    memcpy((char *)out_buf + prefix_len, inputs[0], (size_t)sizes[0]);\n    *out_size = total;\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

    "originalFile":"/* tests/maps/319e-c-create/src/trigger.c — C box that spawns a\n * downstream Lua box at runtime, mirroring the 319d Lua fixture\n * but driven from a C box function instead. Proves the C bindings\n * for runtime self-construction (issue 319e) work end-to-end.\n *\n * The trigger box receives one input (\"input\"), uses\n * soramech_create_box to mint a new Lua box, uses soramech_connect\n * to wire its own output to the new box's \"x\" input, and returns\n * a marker string. The runtime then pushes the marker through the\n * freshly-added connection and the dynamically-created Lua box\n * fires.\n */\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n#include \"soramech.h\"\n\n/* {{{ trigger */\nint trigger(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n            void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    if (n < 1) return -1;\n\n    /* Build the spec for a new Lua box. The shape mirrors what\n     * would be on disk at boxes/<id>.json. */\n    const char *spec =\n        \"{\"\n          \"\\\"kind\\\":\\\"call\\\",\"\n          \"\\\"lang\\\":\\\"lua\\\",\"\n          \"\\\"ref\\\":\\\"src/echo_dyn.lua\\\",\"\n          \"\\\"fn\\\":\\\"echo\\\",\"\n          \"\\\"inputs\\\":[\"\n            \"{\\\"name\\\":\\\"x\\\",\\\"type\\\":\\\"string\\\"}\"\n          \"]\"\n        \"}\";\n\n    char  new_id[SORAMECH_BOX_ID_BUF_SIZE];\n    char *err = NULL;\n    if (soramech_create_box(spec, (int)strlen(spec),\n                            new_id, sizeof new_id, &err) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"trigger.c: create_box failed: %s\\n\",\n                err ? err : \"(no message)\");\n        free(err);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Build the connection entry: wire trigger.output → new.x */\n    char conn[256];\n    int  n_conn = snprintf(conn, sizeof conn,\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"trigger\\\",\"\n         \"\\\"from_branch\\\":null,\"\n         \"\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\"\n         \"\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\", new_id);\n    if (n_conn < 0 || n_conn >= (int)sizeof conn) return -1;\n\n    if (soramech_connect(conn, n_conn, &err) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"trigger.c: connect failed: %s\\n\",\n                err ? err : \"(no message)\");\n        free(err);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Output a marker so the test runner can verify both that\n     * trigger ran AND what the new id was. */\n    int marker_n = snprintf((char *)out_buf, (size_t)out_capacity,\n                            \"c-trigger-fired:%s:%.*s\",\n                            new_id, sizes[0], (const char *)inputs[0]);\n    if (marker_n < 0 || marker_n >= out_capacity) return -1;\n    *out_size = marker_n;\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

    "oldString":"    /* Required: lang. Slice 1 — only \"lua\" is supported. */\n    json_node_t *lang_n = json_object_get(root, \"lang\");\n    if (!lang_n || json_kind(lang_n) != JSON_STRING ||\n        strcmp(json_string_value(lang_n), \"lua\") != 0) {\n        json_arena_destroy(arena);\n        return set_err(err_out, \"create_box: only lang='lua' is supported \"\n                                \"in this slice (issue 319d)\");\n    }\n    int spec_idx = find_spec_idx(specs, \"lua\");\n    if (spec_idx < 0) {\n        json_arena_destroy(arena);\n        return set_err(err_out, \"create_box: lua spec not registered\");\n    }",
    "newString":"    /* Required: lang. Issue 319e extends supported langs to any\n     * spec that's already registered AND whose per-worker state\n     * has been initialised on the current worker. The \"already\n     * initialised\" constraint surfaces as a runtime error when\n     * the new box gets dispatched (worker handle NULL); the\n     * compile pipeline's spec filter is what decides which langs\n     * a worker init's, and that filter runs at graph load.\n     * Workaround: include at least one static box of each lang\n     * you intend to create_box at runtime. Lifting this is a\n     * follow-on (on-demand spec init). */\n    json_node_t *lang_n = json_object_get(root, \"lang\");\n    if (!lang_n || json_kind(lang_n) != JSON_STRING) {\n        json_arena_destroy(arena);\n        return set_err(err_out, \"create_box: 'lang' string required\");\n    }\n    const char *lang = json_string_value(lang_n);\n    int spec_idx = find_spec_idx(specs, lang);\n    if (spec_idx < 0) {\n        json_arena_destroy(arena);\n        return set_err(err_out, \"create_box: lang='%s' not registered \"\n                                \"in the spec registry\", lang);\n    }"

```json
{
  "uuid":"855b5a15-3114-46b7-b94e-3a685103f266",
  "type":"user",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-24T00:32:52.082Z",
  "parentUuid":"434610c8-cc65-40db-97b4-25f7a1e29134",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\ncheck_map \"read-literal\" \\\n    \"echo → hello, world!\"\n\ncheck_map \"319a-many-inputs\" \\\n    \"combine → count=20 sum=210\"\n\ncheck_map \"319d-runtime-create\" \\\n    \"trigger → trigger-fired:auto_\" \\\n    \"auto_\" \\\n    \"echo_dyn-received:trigger-fired:auto_\"\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\";           "old_string":"## Relevant files",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"## Runtime self-construction (issue 319)\n\nUser box code can spawn new boxes and wire them into the live graph\nmid-run. Two primitives, exposed as language-native function calls\nthat thin-wrap a single underlying C runtime API:\n\n- **`create_box(spec)`** — takes a structured value matching the\n  on-disk box JSON schema (a Lua table, a JSON string, etc.).\n  Returns the new box's id. The runtime parses the spec, allocates\n  a box record + one slot per input port (slot store growth — 319b),\n  and appends to the graph's box index (graph 319d).\n\n- **`connect(connection)`** — takes a structured value matching one\n  entry in `connections[]` on disk (`{from_box, from_branch,\n  to_box, to_input}`). Appends a wire to the producer's atomic\n  connections array via copy-and-publish; the dispatcher walks the\n  new array on the producer's next push.\n\n**Plumbing.** Specs reach the active graph and slot store via a\nthread-local that `dispatch_action` sets immediately before each\nspec invoke and clears immediately after. The runner is linked\nwith `-rdynamic` so dlopen'd spec plugins can call back into the\nrunner's `runtime_*` symbols at load time.\n\n**Three growable structures back the feature**:\n\n- Slot store: two-level chunked-append index for slot pointers\n  (319b). Slot records and chunks never move; only the top-level\n  index can grow, via copy-and-publish + defer-free.\n- Graph box index: pointer-array of individually-allocated box\n  records, grown under a graph-level mutex via the same pattern.\n- Per-box connection lists: atomic copy-and-publish under the\n  graph mutex; old arrays stay alive on a stale-list until\n  graph teardown.\n\nIn all three cases the hot read path is lock-free; mutation\ntakes a mutex on the rare path. The pattern is the same recipe\napplied at three layers.\n\n**Documented limits, slice 1**:\n\n- The dispatch context's per-box arrays (spawn guards, output\n  capture) are sized at init with a 4096-box headroom for runtime\n  additions. Beyond the cap, spawns silently fail. Growable arrays\n  are a follow-on.\n- A worker can only dispatch boxes whose language spec was\n  initialised on that worker. Specs are initialised at pool start\n  based on the static graph's language set; a `create_box` call\n  introducing a new language fails at dispatch time with \"worker\n  handle NULL.\" Workaround: include one static box of every\n  language you intend to runtime-create.\n- The connect primitive is race-safe when called from the spec\n  of the currently-firing producer (the single-spawn CAS guard\n  prevents concurrent reads of that box's connections array).\n  Calling `connect` to add a wire FROM a different, potentially-\n  firing box is not guaranteed race-safe.\n- Bash spec doesn't yet expose the bindings — the bash server's\n  line protocol needs extension. Follow-on slice.\n\n## Relevant files",

        },

Bash bindings need the bash","+  server line protocol extended with new request types — deferred","+  to a follow-on slice.","+- The primitives are exposed as per-language function callbacks","+  rather than as box kinds (`kind: \"create_box\"`, `kind: \"connect\"`).","+  The box-kind shape would be more in line with the rest of","+  SoraMech's data-flow philosophy; the per-language shape is","+  documented as a slice-1 expedient pending a refactor.","+","+---","+"," ## Relevant files"," "," - `src/004-executor.lua` — `run_task` boundary, ready-queue"],

    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md",
    "oldString":"Same-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.\n\n---\n\n## Relevant files",
    "newString":"Same-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.\n\n---\n\n## Runtime self-construction (issue 319)\n\nUser box code can spawn new boxes and wire them into the live graph\nmid-run. Two primitives, exposed as language-native function calls\nthat thin-wrap a single underlying C runtime API:\n\n- **`create_box(spec)`** — takes a structured value matching the\n  on-disk box JSON schema (a Lua table, a JSON string, etc.).\n  Returns the new box's id. The runtime parses the spec, allocates\n  a box record + one slot per input port (slot store growth — 319b),\n  and appends to the graph's box index (graph 319d).\n\n- **`connect(connection)`** — takes a structured value matching one\n  entry in `connections[]` on disk (`{from_box, from_branch,\n  to_box, to_input}`). Appends a wire to the producer's atomic\n  connections array via copy-and-publish; the dispatcher walks the\n  new array on the producer's next push.\n\n**Plumbing.** Specs reach the active graph and slot store via a\nthread-local that `dispatch_action` sets immediately before each\nspec invoke and clears immediately after. The runner is linked\nwith `-rdynamic` so dlopen'd spec plugins can call back into the\nrunner's `runtime_*` symbols at load time.\n\n**Three growable structures back the feature**:\n\n- Slot store: two-level chunked-append index for slot pointers\n  (319b). Slot records and chunks never move; only the top-level\n  index can grow, via copy-and-publish + defer-free.\n- Graph box index: pointer-array of individually-allocated box\n  records, grown under a graph-level mutex via the same pattern.\n- Per-box connection lists: atomic copy-and-publish under the\n  graph mutex; old arrays stay alive on a stale-list until\n  graph teardown.\n\nIn all three cases the hot read path is lock-free; mutation takes\na mutex on the rare path. The pattern is the same recipe applied\nat three layers.\n\n**Documented limits in slice 1 (issues 319d / 319e)**:\n\n- The dispatch context's per-box arrays (spawn guards, output\n  capture) are sized at init with a 4096-box headroom for runtime\n  additions. Beyond the cap, spawns silently fail. Growable arrays\n  are a follow-on.\n- A worker can only dispatch boxes whose language spec was\n  initialised on that worker. Specs are initialised at pool start\n  based on the static graph's language set; a `create_box` call\n  introducing a new language fails at dispatch time with \"worker\n  handle NULL.\" Workaround: include one static box of every\n  language you intend to runtime-create.\n- The connect primitive is race-safe when called from the spec\n  of the currently-firing producer (the single-spawn CAS guard\n  prevents concurrent reads of that box's connections array).\n  Calling `connect` to add a wire FROM a different, potentially-\n  firing box is not guaranteed race-safe.\n- Lua and C bindings ship in 319e. Bash bindings need the bash\n  server line protocol extended with new request types — deferred\n  to a follow-on slice.\n- The primitives are exposed as per-language function callbacks\n  rather than as box kinds (`kind: \"create_box\"`, `kind: \"connect\"`).\n  The box-kind shape would be more in line with the rest of\n  SoraMech's data-flow philosophy; the per-language shape is\n  documented as a slice-1 expedient pending a refactor.\n\n---\n\n## Relevant files"
  },

        "input":{
          "content":"# 319e — C bindings, end-to-end test, docs (Bash deferred)\n\n## Status\ncomplete (slice 1 — C). Bash bindings deferred to a follow-on.\n\n## Parent issue\nSub-issue of 319. Extends 319d's runtime self-construction\nprimitives from Lua-only to also include C, with an end-to-end\ntest fixture and the docs update for `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n## What lands\n\n- `langs/c/soramech.h` — header user C box code includes to get\n  declarations for `soramech_create_box` and `soramech_connect`.\n  The names are `#define`'d aliases for the runner's `runtime_*`\n  symbols (already exported via `-rdynamic` from 319d).\n- `langs/c/Makefile` — adds `-DSORAMECH_LANGS_C_INCLUDE=...` so the\n  C spec knows the path to embed in box-compile `-I` flags.\n- `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `-I<langs/c>` to every box compile so user\n  source can `#include \"soramech.h\"`.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.c` — removes the slice-1 \"lang must be\n  lua\" restriction. Any language registered in the spec registry is\n  now acceptable. Each language's per-worker initialisation still\n  has to have happened on the dispatching worker, which surfaces\n  the \"worker handle NULL\" error if the static graph didn't include\n  that language. Workaround documented; auto-init follow-on.\n- `tests/maps/319e-c-create/` — end-to-end fixture. A C box uses\n  `soramech_create_box` to spawn a downstream C box at runtime,\n  uses `soramech_connect` to wire its output to the new box's\n  input, returns a marker. The dispatcher pushes through the new\n  connection, the dynamically-created C box fires and produces\n  output. Verified end-to-end.\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — new \"Runtime self-construction\"\n  section documents the contract, the three-layer growable\n  machinery, and every slice-1 limit.\n\n## What's deferred\n\n- **Bash bindings.** The bash spec uses a persistent subprocess\n  speaking a line-oriented request/response protocol over a Unix\n  socketpair (issue 308). Exposing `create_box` / `connect` to\n  user bash scripts requires either extending that protocol with\n  new request types and threading them back to the C runtime, or\n  giving user bash a side-channel to talk to the runner. Neither\n  fits cleanly in this slice; deferred to a future sub-issue.\n- **Auto-initialisation of specs for runtime-introduced languages.**\n  Currently a worker only initialises specs for languages used by\n  the static graph. A `create_box` call introducing a new language\n  fails at dispatch time. Fix is to have specs auto-init on first\n  use; not in this slice.\n- **The architectural redesign.** Per parent-issue discussion, the\n  correct shape is `create_box` and `connect` as box KINDS (like\n  `read` / `write`), not as per-language callbacks. The current\n  per-language design is the slice-1 expedient. Refactor planned\n  but explicitly out of scope here.\n\n## Validation\n\n- 14 integration tests pass, including the new `319e-c-create`\n  fixture and the existing `319d-runtime-create` from the Lua\n  side.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/c/soramech.h` (new)\n- `langs/c/Makefile`\n- `langs/c/spec.c`\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.c`\n- `tests/maps/319e-c-create/`\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh`\n",

    "content":"# 319e — C bindings, end-to-end test, docs (Bash deferred)\n\n## Status\ncomplete (slice 1 — C). Bash bindings deferred to a follow-on.\n\n## Parent issue\nSub-issue of 319. Extends 319d's runtime self-construction\nprimitives from Lua-only to also include C, with an end-to-end\ntest fixture and the docs update for `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n## What lands\n\n- `langs/c/soramech.h` — header user C box code includes to get\n  declarations for `soramech_create_box` and `soramech_connect`.\n  The names are `#define`'d aliases for the runner's `runtime_*`\n  symbols (already exported via `-rdynamic` from 319d).\n- `langs/c/Makefile` — adds `-DSORAMECH_LANGS_C_INCLUDE=...` so the\n  C spec knows the path to embed in box-compile `-I` flags.\n- `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `-I<langs/c>` to every box compile so user\n  source can `#include \"soramech.h\"`.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.c` — removes the slice-1 \"lang must be\n  lua\" restriction. Any language registered in the spec registry is\n  now acceptable. Each language's per-worker initialisation still\n  has to have happened on the dispatching worker, which surfaces\n  the \"worker handle NULL\" error if the static graph didn't include\n  that language. Workaround documented; auto-init follow-on.\n- `tests/maps/319e-c-create/` — end-to-end fixture. A C box uses\n  `soramech_create_box` to spawn a downstream C box at runtime,\n  uses `soramech_connect` to wire its output to the new box's\n  input, returns a marker. The dispatcher pushes through the new\n  connection, the dynamically-created C box fires and produces\n  output. Verified end-to-end.\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — new \"Runtime self-construction\"\n  section documents the contract, the three-layer growable\n  machinery, and every slice-1 limit.\n\n## What's deferred\n\n- **Bash bindings.** The bash spec uses a persistent subprocess\n  speaking a line-oriented request/response protocol over a Unix\n  socketpair (issue 308). Exposing `create_box` / `connect` to\n  user bash scripts requires either extending that protocol with\n  new request types and threading them back to the C runtime, or\n  giving user bash a side-channel to talk to the runner. Neither\n  fits cleanly in this slice; deferred to a future sub-issue.\n- **Auto-initialisation of specs for runtime-introduced languages.**\n  Currently a worker only initialises specs for languages used by\n  the static graph. A `create_box` call introducing a new language\n  fails at dispatch time. Fix is to have specs auto-init on first\n  use; not in this slice.\n- **The architectural redesign.** Per parent-issue discussion, the\n  correct shape is `create_box` and `connect` as box KINDS (like\n  `read` / `write`), not as per-language callbacks. The current\n  per-language design is the slice-1 expedient. Refactor planned\n  but explicitly out of scope here.\n\n## Validation\n\n- 14 integration tests pass, including the new `319e-c-create`\n  fixture and the existing `319d-runtime-create` from the Lua\n  side.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/c/soramech.h` (new)\n- `langs/c/Makefile`\n- `langs/c/spec.c`\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.c`\n- `tests/maps/319e-c-create/`\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh`\n",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/319e-c-and-bash-bindings-and-end-to-end.md",
    "userModified":false
  },

Captured and asserted by the test\nrunner. 14 integration tests now pass.\n\nBash deferred. The bash spec talks to user scripts over a\nline-oriented request/response protocol on a Unix socketpair;\nexposing create_box / connect to user bash needs the protocol\nextended with new request types that thread back to the C\nruntime. That work doesn't fit in this slice — documented as\na follow-on.\n\nThe docs gain a Runtime Self-Construction section in\ndocs/004-ipc-and-threading.md describing the contract, the\nthree layers of growable structure (slot store, graph box\nindex, per-box connection lists), and every documented limit\n(4096-box headroom, worker-spec-init constraint, single-spawn\nconnect race shape, Bash gap, and the per-language-callback\nshape that should eventually be replaced with create_box /\nconnect as box kinds).\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -5",

Follow-on sub-issue.\n- **Per-language-callback shape** — should be `create_box`/`connect` as box KINDS for data-flow consistency. Refactor planned per your design feedback.\n- **Auto-init of specs for runtime-introduced languages** — currently a worker can only dispatch boxes whose language was in the static graph.\n- **4096-box runtime headroom** — dispatch context's per-box arrays should be growable, not just oversized.\n- **Concurrent-safe `connect` for non-firing producers** — current race safety relies on the single-spawn CAS guard for the producer.\n- **Transcript exporter** — wrong project lookup, no incremental mode. Needs a local replacement.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nYou were right to push through. The \"bad design\" of per-language bindings turned out to cost only ~5 lines in `langs/c/soramech.h` to add a second language, because the runner-side `runtime_*` functions are already language-agnostic — the per-language layer is the thinnest possible wrapper. The refactor to box-kinds is now a localized change: delete the wrapper layer in each `langs/*/spec.c`, add two new box kinds in `dispatch.c`. The cost of \"fix it later\" was bounded the whole time; my earlier worry about per-language work was misplaced.\n\nThe headline feature — *a running graph can build more of itself* — is in users' hands.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`"

Wire color\nencodes routing kind, not language pairing. Two wires leaving the\nsame producer — one to a Lua consumer, one to a C consumer — look\nidentical.\n\nThe runtime treats those wires very differently: the same-language\nhop carries native bytes, the cross-language hop carries JSON\n(issue 312). The editor gives the box author no visual signal that\nthe JSON translation step exists. It's invisible until someone\nreads the dispatch code.\n\n## Concept\n\nWires are colored by **language pairing across the edge**, with a\nthird color for wires whose destination port has a user-written\ncustom translation (issue 246):\n\n- **Forest green** (`#228b22` or similar) — cross-language wire.\n  Producer and consumer are different languages; the runtime\n  translates via JSON at the wire. A reminder that this hop costs\n  encode + decode.\n- **Dark gray** (`#666` or similar; \"forest-gray\" is the verbal\n  cue) — same-language wire. Producer and consumer share a\n  language; native bytes pass without translation.\n- **Bright goldenrod cheddar** (`#e8a317` or similar — calibrate\n  on canvas) — the destination input port has a custom\n  translation shim attached. This signal overrides the green/gray\n  classification because user-written code is the more interesting\n  thing to surface: it tells the box author \"this wire's value\n  passes through my own decode logic before invoke sees it.\"\n- **Existing branch colors** (`lt` / `eq` / `gt` / iterator\n  branches) remain — they encode routing semantics, which is\n  orthogonal to language classification and custom shims.\n\nWhen a wire is both branch-colored AND language-classified, the\ntwo signals compose. One workable composition: branch color drives\nthe wire's stroke, language classification drives a small marker\n(a colored dot at the midpoint, or a dashed-vs-solid line style).\nThe implementation picks the form; the rule is that both signals\nare visible on the same wire.\n\n## How the editor computes the classification\n\nFor each connection `{from_box, to_box, to_input, ...}`:\n\n1. Look up the destination input port on `to_box` (the port named\n   `to_input`). If that port has a `custom_translation` field set\n   (issue 246), the wire is **goldenrod**, regardless of language\n   pairing. Skip the rest.\n2. Look up `from_box`'s box JSON; read its `lang` field.\n3. Look up `to_box`'s box JSON; read its `lang` field.\n4. If either box is a `read` / `write` / `data` kind (no `lang`\n   field), treat the wire as cross-language — those boxes deal in\n   language-agnostic bytes and any consumer's spec reads them\n   through its JSON bridge.\n5. Otherwise: same-language iff `from_box.lang === to_box.lang`.\n\nThe editor already has every box's JSON in memory (state populated\nby the HTTP backend). The classification is one comparison per\nconnection at draw time — no separate index needed.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — wire rendering. Add a `wire_classification(from_box, to_box)` helper returning\n   `\"native\"` or `\"json\"`, in `assets/js/006-wires.js` or wherever\n   it composes with the rest of the draw loop.\n2. Update the color-picking branch in `006-wires.js` to use the\n   classification when `from_branch` is null. Pick the two\n   concrete hex values for forest-green and forest-gray.\n3. For branch wires (`from_branch` set), pick a composition: keep\n   the branch color as the stroke, add a midpoint dot in the\n   classification color. Or pick the dashed-vs-solid route. The\n   issue's only requirement is both signals visible.\n4. Add a legend somewhere unobtrusive — bottom-left corner of the\n   canvas, behind the existing zoom indicator — so the color\n   meaning isn't tribal knowledge.\n5. Verify on `maps/driver-test` (multi-language map) and on a\n   single-language map (everything one color).\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Exact hex values for forest-green and forest-gray. Pick something\n  that reads well against the dark canvas background and doesn't\n  collide with the branch palette.\n- Branch + classification composition: stroke vs. dot vs. dash.\n  Whichever is more legible.\n- Whether `read` / `write` / `data` boxes should also visually\n  carry a \"language-agnostic\" badge somewhere on the box itself,\n  so users can see at a glance which boxes will trigger JSON\n  translation when wired to typed call boxes.           "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"  const BRANCH_COLOR = { lt: '#ff8c42', eq: '#4a9eff', gt: '#4caf7d' };\n\n  // {{{ Language-pairing classification (issue 245)\n  // Three categories, with the visible palette tuned for the dark canvas:\n  //\n  //   native  — producer and consumer share a language; native bytes\n  //             pass without translation. Dim slate-blue, the original\n  //             default. (Was the only color in the old palette.)\n  //   json    — cross-language wire; the runtime JSON-encodes at the\n  //             producer and decodes at the consumer. Forest green so\n  //             box authors can see the encode/decode cost at a glance.\n  //   custom  — the destination input port has a user-written\n  //             translation shim (issue 246). Goldenrod-cheddar; this\n  //             signal dominates the others because user code is the\n  //             more interesting thing to surface.\n  //\n  // For branch wires the branch color drives the stroke and the\n  // classification drives a small mid-wire dot; for plain wires the\n  // classification IS the stroke color.\n  const CLASS_COLOR = {\n    native: '#4a6080',   // dim slate-blue, the historical default\n    json:   '#228b22',   // forest green\n    custom: '#e8a317',   // bright goldenrod cheddar\n  };\n\n  // The box kinds that don't carry a `lang` (read / write / data deal\n  // in language-agnostic bytes — any consumer reads them through its\n  // JSON bridge, so wires to/from them are cross-language by default).\n  const LANG_AGNOSTIC_KINDS = new Set(['read', 'write', 'data']);\n\n  // {{{ classify_wire\n  // Returns one of \"native\", \"json\", \"custom\" for the given connection.\n  // Defensive against missing boxes and missing fields — the editor's\n  // box cache may be out of sync mid-edit.\n  function classify_wire(c) {\n    const from = Boxes.boxes[c.from_box];\n    const to   = Boxes.boxes[c.to_box];\n    if (!from || !to) return 'native';\n\n    // Custom translation shim on the destination port dominates.\n    // Issue 246's field; tolerate it being absent until that lands.\n    const port = (to.inputs || []).find(p => p && p.name === c.to_input);\n    if (port && port.custom_translation) return 'custom';\n\n    // Language-agnostic box kinds force the cross-language path.\n    if (LANG_AGNOSTIC_KINDS.has(from.kind) ||\n        LANG_AGNOSTIC_KINDS.has(to.kind))   return 'json';\n\n    // Both are typed call boxes — compare langs.\n    if (from.lang && to.lang && from.lang === to.lang) return 'native';\n    return 'json';\n  }\n  // }}}\n  // }}}",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/assets/js/006-wires.js"
        },

(BRANCH_COLOR[c.from_branch] || '#4a6080') : '#4a6080';\n\n        const is_selected = _selected_wire &&\n          _selected_wire.from_box    === c.from_box &&\n          _selected_wire.from_branch === c.from_branch &&\n          _selected_wire.to_box      === c.to_box &&\n          _selected_wire.to_input    === c.to_input;\n\n        // self-loop wires need control points that route around the\n        // box body; everything else uses the default straight-out controls\n        const self_box = (c.from_box === c.to_box) ? box : null;\n        const { cx0, cy0, cx1, cy1 } = endpoint_controls(src, dst, self_box);\n        draw_bezier_cp(ctx, src.x, src.y, cx0, cy0, cx1, cy1, dst.x, dst.y,\n                       color, is_selected);\n      }\n    }\n  }\n  // }}}",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"        // Two orthogonal signals on each wire (issue 245):\n        //  - branch color (routing kind: lt / eq / gt etc.)\n        //  - language-pairing classification (native / json / custom)\n        // Plain wires (no branch) use the classification as their stroke;\n        // branch wires keep the branch color as stroke and surface the\n        // classification via a small midpoint dot below.\n        const klass = classify_wire(c);\n        const class_color = CLASS_COLOR[klass];\n        const color = c.from_branch\n          ? (BRANCH_COLOR[c.from_branch] || class_color)\n          : class_color;\n\n        const is_selected = _selected_wire &&\n          _selected_wire.from_box    === c.from_box &&\n          _selected_wire.from_branch === c.from_branch &&\n          _selected_wire.to_box      === c.to_box &&\n          _selected_wire.to_input    === c.to_input;\n\n        // self-loop wires need control points that route around the\n        // box body; everything else uses the default straight-out controls\n        const self_box = (c.from_box === c.to_box) ? box : null;\n        const { cx0, cy0, cx1, cy1 } = endpoint_controls(src, dst, self_box);\n        draw_bezier_cp(ctx, src.x, src.y, cx0, cy0, cx1, cy1, dst.x, dst.y,\n                       color, is_selected);\n\n        // If the wire's stroke color was the branch color (so the\n        // classification was hidden), surface the classification as a\n        // small dot at the midpoint of the bezier. Skip for plain\n        // wires — their stroke already conveys the classification.\n        if (c.from_branch) {\n          const mid = bezier_point(0.5, src.x, src.y, cx0, cy0, cx1, cy1, dst.x, dst.y);\n          ctx.fillStyle = class_color;\n          ctx.beginPath();\n          ctx.arc(mid.x, mid.y, 4, 0, Math.PI * 2);\n          ctx.fill();\n        }\n      }\n    }\n  }\n  // }}}\n\n  // {{{ draw_legend\n  // Small bottom-left swatch indexing the language-pairing palette.\n  // Drawn in screen space (not world space) so panning / zooming\n  // doesn't move it. Sits where the user can glance for translation.\n  function draw_legend(ctx) {\n    const w = 168, h = 64;\n    const x = 12, y = ctx.canvas.height - h - 12;\n    ctx.save();\n    // Reset any world transform so we draw in screen-space pixels.\n    ctx.setTransform(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0);\n    ctx.fillStyle = 'rgba(20, 24, 32, 0.78)';\n    ctx.fillRect(x, y, w, h);\n    ctx.strokeStyle = 'rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.10)';\n    ctx.strokeRect(x + 0.5, y + 0.5, w - 1, h - 1);\n\n    ctx.font = '11px monospace';\n    ctx.textBaseline = 'middle';\n    const rows = [\n      ['native  (same lang)',     CLASS_COLOR.native],\n      ['json    (cross-lang)',    CLASS_COLOR.json],\n      ['custom  (user shim)',     CLASS_COLOR.custom],\n    ];\n    rows.forEach(([label, col], i) => {\n      const cy = y + 14 + i * 16;\n      ctx.fillStyle = col;\n      ctx.fillRect(x + 10, cy - 5, 18, 10);\n      ctx.fillStyle = '#cfd2d8';\n      ctx.fillText(label, x + 36, cy);\n    });\n    ctx.restore();\n  }\n  // }}}",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/assets/js/006-wires.js"
        },

          "old_string":"# 245 — Wire color by cross-language classification\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nEvery wire on the canvas is drawn the same dim slate-blue (`#4a6080`)\nwhen its `from_branch` is null, or one of the comparator branch\ncolors (orange / blue / green) when it's a branch wire. Wire color\nencodes routing kind, not language pairing. Two wires leaving the\nsame producer — one to a Lua consumer, one to a C consumer — look\nidentical.\n\nThe runtime treats those wires very differently: the same-language\nhop carries native bytes, the cross-language hop carries JSON\n(issue 312). The editor gives the box author no visual signal that\nthe JSON translation step exists. It's invisible until someone\nreads the dispatch code.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"# 245 — Wire color by cross-language classification\n\n## Status\ncomplete (code-only — visual verification is on the user)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nWires are coloured by **language pairing across the edge**, with\ncustom-translation shims overriding the language signal. Three\nclassifications drive the palette:\n\n- **`native`** — producer and consumer share a language. Slate-blue\n  (`#4a6080`), the historical default.\n- **`json`** — cross-language wire. Forest green (`#228b22`). The\n  runtime JSON-encodes at the producer and decodes at the consumer;\n  the colour is a standing reminder of that cost.\n- **`custom`** — destination input port has a user-written\n  translation shim attached (issue 246's `custom_translation` field;\n  defensive support — works whether 246 has landed or not).\n  Goldenrod (`#e8a317`); dominates the language signal because user\n  code is the more interesting thing to surface.\n\nExisting branch wires (`lt` / `eq` / `gt` etc.) compose with the\nclassification: branch colour drives the stroke, classification\ndrives a small 4 px dot at the bezier midpoint. Both signals are\nvisible on the same wire.\n\nA bottom-left screen-space legend keeps the colour vocabulary\nvisible without panning or zooming away from it.",

Wire color\nencodes routing kind, not language pairing. Two wires leaving the\nsame producer — one to a Lua consumer, one to a C consumer — look\nidentical.\n\nThe runtime treats those wires very differently: the same-language\nhop carries native bytes, the cross-language hop carries JSON\n(issue 312). The editor gives the box author no visual signal that\nthe JSON translation step exists. It's invisible until someone\nreads the dispatch code.\n\n## Concept\n\nWires are colored by **language pairing across the edge**, with a\nthird color for wires whose destination port has a user-written\ncustom translation (issue 246):\n\n- **Forest green** (`#228b22` or similar) — cross-language wire.\n  Producer and consumer are different languages; the runtime\n  translates via JSON at the wire. A reminder that this hop costs\n  encode + decode.\n- **Dark gray** (`#666` or similar; \"forest-gray\" is the verbal\n  cue) — same-language wire. Producer and consumer share a\n  language; native bytes pass without translation.\n- **Bright goldenrod cheddar** (`#e8a317` or similar — calibrate\n  on canvas) — the destination input port has a custom\n  translation shim attached. This signal overrides the green/gray\n  classification because user-written code is the more interesting\n  thing to surface: it tells the box author \"this wire's value\n  passes through my own decode logic before invoke sees it.\"\n- **Existing branch colors** (`lt` / `eq` / `gt` / iterator\n  branches) remain — they encode routing semantics, which is\n  orthogonal to language classification and custom shims.\n\nWhen a wire is both branch-colored AND language-classified, the\ntwo signals compose. One workable composition: branch color drives\nthe wire's stroke, language classification drives a small marker\n(a colored dot at the midpoint, or a dashed-vs-solid line style).\nThe implementation picks the form; the rule is that both signals\nare visible on the same wire.\n\n## How the editor computes the classification\n\nFor each connection `{from_box, to_box, to_input, ...}`:\n\n1. Look up the destination input port on `to_box` (the port named\n   `to_input`). If that port has a `custom_translation` field set\n   (issue 246), the wire is **goldenrod**, regardless of language\n   pairing. Skip the rest.\n2. Look up `from_box`'s box JSON; read its `lang` field.\n3. Look up `to_box`'s box JSON; read its `lang` field.\n4. If either box is a `read` / `write` / `data` kind (no `lang`\n   field), treat the wire as cross-language — those boxes deal in\n   language-agnostic bytes and any consumer's spec reads them\n   through its JSON bridge.\n5. Otherwise: same-language iff `from_box.lang === to_box.lang`.\n\nThe editor already has every box's JSON in memory (state populated\nby the HTTP backend). The classification is one comparison per\nconnection at draw time — no separate index needed.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — wire rendering. Line 121–122 is the\n  current color-picking site. Add the language classification\n  there.\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, source of the `lang` field\n  for each box.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Add a `wire_classification(from_box, to_box)` helper returning\n   `\"native\"` or `\"json\"`, in `assets/js/006-wires.js` or wherever\n   it composes with the rest of the draw loop.\n2. Update the color-picking branch in `006-wires.js` to use the\n   classification when `from_branch` is null. Pick the two\n   concrete hex values for forest-green and forest-gray.\n3. For branch wires (`from_branch` set), pick a composition: keep\n   the branch color as the stroke, add a midpoint dot in the\n   classification color. Or pick the dashed-vs-solid route. The\n   issue's only requirement is both signals visible.\n4. Add a legend somewhere unobtrusive — bottom-left corner of the\n   canvas, behind the existing zoom indicator — so the color\n   meaning isn't tribal knowledge.\n5. Verify on `maps/driver-test` (multi-language map) and on a\n   single-language map (everything one color).\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Exact hex values for forest-green and forest-gray. Pick something\n  that reads well against the dark canvas background and doesn't\n  collide with the branch palette.\n- Branch + classification composition: stroke vs. dot vs. dash.\n  Whichever is more legible.\n- Whether `read` / `write` / `data` boxes should also visually\n  carry a \"language-agnostic\" badge somewhere on the box itself,\n  so users can see at a glance which boxes will trigger JSON\n  translation when wired to typed call boxes.     "stdout":"# 246 — Custom translation specs per input port\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nThe default language specs (issues 306 / 307 / 308) handle most\ndata flow via the dual-ring shape in issue 312: producer's spec\nserializes native or JSON per the per-edge bit; consumer's spec\ndispatches per input flag and decodes accordingly. The default\ncontract is sufficient for primitives, strings, arrays, and\nobjects — the cases JSON's structure covers cleanly and the cases\nnative pass-through covers cleanly.\n\nA custom translation spec lets the user intervene at a specific\ninput port for **any reason** — not just cross-language\nambiguity. Two motivating cases:\n\n**Cross-language ambiguity.** Some translations cannot be\ninferred by the spec because the language constructs don't have\nuniversal mappings:\n\n- A C++ class with both data fields and method functions arrives\n  at a C box. C has no notion of methods; whether to expose them\n  as function pointers, drop them, or restructure into a tagged\n  union is a development-time decision the user has to make.\n- A `void *` arrives carrying a libcurl handle the receiving\n  language's spec has no general way to interpret.\n- A union type whose discriminator lives in a separate input\n  port — the spec doesn't know which port is the tag.\n\n**Same-language transformation the user wants.** Even when no\nlanguage boundary is crossed, the default native pass-through\nmay not be what the user wants on a particular port:\n\n- A C box emits a float; a downstream C box wants it truncated\n  and rounded up before consumption. The default native pass\n  copies the bytes verbatim and downstream code sees the wrong\n  precision. A custom shim on the destination port applies\n  truncate-then-round before invoke sees the value. No language\n  ambiguity — just user-specific semantics at that wire.\n- A consumer wants units normalized on one port but not on a\n  sibling port (degrees → radians on the angle input, leave the\n  magnitude input alone).\n- A consumer wants to clamp or range-check a value before its\n  function sees it.\n\nIn both cases the principle is the same: **the user has knowledge\nabout how this specific port should interpret its input, and the\ndefault spec doesn't.** A per-port shim is where that knowledge\ngets written down.\n\n**A custom translation spec is a per-input-port shim** the user\nwrites to handle these cases. It runs at the start of the\nconsumer box's task, replaces the default decode (or pass-through)\nfor that one port, and otherwise leaves the dispatch path\nunchanged.\n\n### Why per-port, not per-box\n\n> \"the custom spec should be defined on a per-slot basis. Each\n> slot should (ideally) only need to handle one particular type\n> of information. That's why we have separate arguments at all,\n> instead of just using void pointers for everything.\" —\n> 2026-05-21\n\nPer-port matches the principled reason input ports exist in the\nfirst place: each port carries one kind of value, and the user\ndeclares the kind. If a box has three input ports — two of them\nordinary strings and one of them a C++ class instance — only the\nclass-instance port needs custom translation. The two string ports\nkeep the default decode. A per-box shim would force the user to\nwrite decode code for every port even when only one is weird.\n\n### Why no output-side custom translation\n\nA producer's spec always knows how to serialize every one of its\nown language's values losslessly — Lua's spec knows every Lua type,\nC's spec knows every typed struct field. Writing depends only on\nthe sending language, which has full reflective access to its own\ntype system. The Lua spec's `encode_value` is expected to grow\nsentinel primitives (`$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque`) for the\nvalues JSON can't represent structurally; that's a spec-author\nresponsibility, not a user-shim responsibility.\n\nReading is the asymmetric direction. The receiver doesn't know\nwhat the sender meant by an opaque pointer or a sentinel-tagged\nvalue — that interpretation is the user's call. Hence the custom\nshim lives on the input side only.\n\n## Lifecycle (editor)\n\nThe box inspector's input-port rows each grow a small affordance\nfor managing the port's custom translation:\n\n- **New** — creates a translation file in\n  `maps/<name>/translations/<box_id>__<port_name>.<lang_ext>`\n  and sets the port's `custom_translation` field in the box JSON\n  to that path. The file is initialized to a copy of what the\n  default spec would do for that port's declared type — the user\n  can run it without edits and behaviour is identical to no\n  custom shim. Edits add or replace the decode logic.\n- **View** — opens the translation file in the editor's read-only\n  source view (same affordance as \"view source\" on the box's main\n  function). The user-facing message is \"this is what gets baked\n  into the map at compile time.\"\n- **Delete** — clears the port's `custom_translation` field. The\n  translation file itself stays on disk. Box-delete (the whole\n  box) with any custom translations attached prompts: \"this box\n  has N custom translation specs; the files stay on disk for\n  re-use, but the box's references will go.\" Confirm or cancel.\n\nThe \"file stays on disk if you delete the box\" rule means custom\ntranslations are identifiable by path, not by box. The user can\nattach the same file to a different box's port later, or delete\nthe file explicitly through a file-browser pane.\n\n## Lifecycle (runtime)\n\nThe dispatch's input-read step gains a per-port branch:\n\n```\nfor each input port i:\n    (which_ring, idx) = ring_order_pop(slot)\n    raw_bytes         = ring_at(...)\n    if box->inputs[i].custom_translation:\n        translated[i] = custom_translation[i](raw_bytes, which_ring)\n        input_native[i] = NATIVE   # custom shim output is always native\n    else:\n        translated[i] = raw_bytes\n        input_native[i] = (which_ring == NATIVE)\n```\n\nWhen the port has a custom shim, the shim does the decode and the\nspec's `invoke` sees native bytes (with `input_native[i] = NATIVE`).\nWhen the port has no custom shim, the default decode runs inside\nthe spec's invoke as today.\n\nThree consequences fall out from running on the consumer's worker:\n\n- A custom shim that does something slow or surprising holds the\n  consumer's worker, not the producer's. The producer is free as\n  soon as it's done writing raw bytes to the ring.\n- Each consumer eats its own translation cost; mixed fan-in\n  consumers translate cell-by-cell as they pop.\n- The custom shim is in the same language as the box's main\n  function, so it has full access to that language's runtime\n  (Lua tables, C structs, etc.) without crossing another\n  language boundary first.\n\n## Where it sits relative to the dual-ring (issue 312)\n\nThe dual-ring routing still applies. The producer chooses a ring\nper `output_edge_native[j]` as today. The consumer's per-port\ncustom shim sees the raw bytes plus the `which_ring` tag — so it\ncan distinguish \"these bytes are my own language's native format\"\nfrom \"these bytes are JSON from a cross-language producer\" and act\naccordingly.\n\nIn the easy cases (same-language same-shape), no custom shim is\nneeded; the default native pass-through still works. The custom\nshim earns its keep on the cells where the default\n`json_to_native` would error or produce something useless — that's\nwhere the user-written code takes over.\n\n## File layout\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n    boxes/\n        <box_id>.json                ← per-input port may reference translations/\n    translations/\n        <box_id>__<port_name>.<lang_ext>     ← per-port shim\n    src/\n        <box_id>.<lang_ext>                  ← box's main function\n```\n\nThe box JSON's `inputs` array grows an optional per-port field:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"consume_class\",\n    \"lang\": \"c\",\n    \"ref\": \"consume.c\",\n    \"fn\": \"consume\",\n    \"inputs\": [\n        { \"name\": \"instance\", \"type\": \"bytes\",\n          \"custom_translation\": \"translations/consume_class__instance.c\" },\n        { \"name\": \"weight\",   \"type\": \"int\" }\n    ],\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nIf a port omits `custom_translation`, the default-spec decode runs\nfor that port as today. The `translations/` directory may contain\nshims with no attached port (orphaned, kept on disk by the\ndelete-doesn't-delete-file rule).\n\n## Custom translation function signature\n\nPer-port shims take one input's raw bytes and the `which_ring`\nflag, return one translated value in the consumer's native form.\nWorking draft for C:\n\n```c\nint sm_translate(const void *input_raw, int input_size,\n                 int input_native,\n                 void *output_native, int output_capacity,\n                 int *output_size);\n```\n\nLua's shape is analogous but in Lua-native terms — the function\ntakes a Lua string (the raw bytes) and a boolean (the native\nflag), returns the translated Lua value.\n\nOne signature per port keeps each shim's surface area exactly\nmatched to the port's job. A shim that needs to consult other\nports has a problem this design doesn't try to solve (per-port\nisolation is the principled choice); the user can fall back to\nplain decode-then-validate inside the box's main function for\ncross-port logic.\n\n## Default content of a freshly-created shim\n\nThe \"New\" button writes a file containing a literal copy of what\nthe default spec would do for that port's declared type. For C,\nthat's the small generated wrapper that parses `input_raw` per\nthe port's declared type and writes the result. For Lua, it's a\nfew lines that decode via the existing JSON / native helpers\nbased on `input_native`.\n\nThe user can run the shim without edits and behaviour matches the\nno-shim default. Edits typically replace one branch (the\nspecific weird case) and leave the rest alone. The \"starts as\ndefault, edits in place\" shape matches the project's preference\nfor upgrade paths over from-scratch authoring.\n\n## Compile pipeline (issue 309)\n\nThe compile pipeline already walks every box's `ref` to copy\nsource into `compiled/src/`. The same walk inspects each input\nport's `custom_translation` field and copies referenced files\ninto `compiled/translations/`. For C, each translation file\ncompiles to a `.so` alongside the box's main function. For Lua,\nfiles load into the worker's `lua_State` like any other Lua\nsource.\n\nWhen issue 313 (same-language source merge) lands, translation\nfiles get concatenated into the per-language bundle the same way\nbox main functions do — a translation file is just another\nfunction in the merged module.\n\n## Why this is the right escape hatch\n\nThe default spec contract is \"JSON is the universal interop, each\nspec handles its own native form, sentinels carry the in-process\nexotic cases on the producer side.\" That's enough for the\noverwhelming majority of data flow. The cases where it fails are\nexactly the cases where the user has knowledge the system can't\never infer — what a `void *` points to, how a serialized object\nis structured, which port is a discriminator for which other port.\n\nPushing those back to the user via a per-port shim is honest\nabout where the knowledge has to come from. It also lets the\ndefault spec contract stay narrow and predictable — the spec\nauthors don't have to chase every possible ambiguous receive-side\ntype with new special cases.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state; per-input\n  `custom_translation` field read/write.\n- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI (New / View / Delete buttons\n  on each input-port row).\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend for translation file\n  CRUD (path validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`).\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — load each input port's\n  `custom_translation` onto `box_t->inputs[i]`.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — input-read branch on\n  `box->inputs[i].custom_translation`.\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — package translation files into\n  the compiled map (issue 309).\n- `issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md` —\n  goldenrod-cheddar wires for ports with custom translations.\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — dual-ring shape\n  the translation slots into.\n- `issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md` —\n  custom translations get merged alongside box source.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add the optional per-input\n   `custom_translation` field. Graph loader reads it; absence\n   means default path for that port.\n2. **HTTP backend**: CRUD routes for translation files. Path\n   validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`.\n3. **Editor inspector**: New / View / Delete affordances on each\n   input-port row. \"New\" generates the file with\n   default-spec-equivalent contents parameterized on the port's\n   declared type. The 245 wire-coloring change activates\n   automatically once the field exists.\n4. **Box-delete confirmation**: detect any ports with attached\n   translations; prompt before deletion; preserve the files on\n   disk regardless.\n5. **Dispatch**: input-read per-port branch on\n   `custom_translation`; route bytes through the shim instead of\n   the default decode for that port.\n6. **Compile pipeline**: walk each input port's\n   `custom_translation`; package files into\n   `compiled/translations/` and the per-language source bundle.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Shared translations across multiple ports.** Two ports on\n  different boxes that need the same shim can both reference the\n  same file path — the system supports it implicitly. The\n  editor's \"New\" button always creates a fresh file with the\n  default naming so users don't accidentally share by default.\n  Library imports inside translation files (for shared helpers\n  inside a shim) are out of scope here — the user can do that via\n  the language's normal import mechanism.\n- **Compile-time validation.** Should the compile button check\n  that every `custom_translation` path exists and parses? Easy\n  add to the existing compile validation; do once translations\n  exist as a feature.\n- **Shim author seeing cross-port context.** Per-port isolation\n  means a shim only sees its own input. A union whose\n  discriminator is in another port has to validate inside the\n  box's main function rather than in the shim. If a real\n  cross-port case shows up, the workaround is a follow-on\n  ticket — not a reason to abandon per-port isolation.",
