          "command":"git commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\n246 — closeout: per-port custom translation shims, end-to-end\n\nA user can now attach a small per-port translation file to any\ninput port on a Lua or C call box. The file runs at the start of\nthe consumer's task and replaces the default decode for THAT\nport — other ports keep the default path. It earns its keep on\ninputs where the default JSON-or-native pass-through doesn't\nknow what the user means: a void* carrying a specific handle, a\nunion whose tag is on a sibling port, a number the consumer\nwants clamped, units the user wants normalised on one port but\nnot another.\n\nThe runtime shape. The graph loader reads an optional\n`custom_translation` field per input port. The language-spec\ninterface grows a `translate` callback that takes the raw bytes\nand a \"was this native\" flag and writes native bytes the spec's\ninvoke then sees. Lua's translate loads the file once per worker\n(caching the returned function in the Lua registry) and calls\nit. C's translate lazy-compiles + dlopens the shim .c, dlsyms\n`sm_translate`, and calls it. Dispatch walks the inputs after\nread_inputs; ports with a shim route through, ports without\nproceed as before.\n\nThe editor side. Inspector input-port rows on call boxes grow\nthree states: `+xlate` to create a default shim file matching\nthe box's language (identity pass-through, user edits in place),\n`xlate` to open the shim in the source-view window, and `×` to\nclear the box's reference (file stays on disk per the issue's\ndelete rule). The source-view detects translations/ paths and\nroutes to a new translation-file endpoint. The HTTP backend\ngrows list / get / put / delete routes for files under\nmaps/<name>/translations/. The wire-color module from 245\nalready paints shim-port wires in goldenrod because it\nchecks port.custom_translation — no change there.\n\nThe compile pipeline copies translations/ into the compiled\nartifact. The runtime self-construction path (319d's\ncreate_box) reads custom_translation from spec JSON, so\ndynamically-created boxes can carry shims too.\n\nTwo end-to-end fixtures verify the path. A C box with an\nuppercase shim emits `seen:HELLO-FROM-SEED` from input\n`hello-from-seed`. A Lua box with a reverse+prepend shim emits\n`seen:REV-fedcba` from input `abcdef`. 16 integration tests\nnow pass.\n\nDeferred per the issue file: Bash spec's translate callback\n(needs the bash server line protocol extended back to the C\nruntime, same shape as the 319e Bash deferral); compile-time\nvalidation that every referenced translation file exists; type-\naware default-content generators; the box-delete-confirmation\nflow.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -5",
          "description":"Commit 246"
        },

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"246 landed at `981b2b8`.\n\n## What shipped\n\n| Layer | Change |\n|-------|--------|\n| Schema | `input_decl_t.custom_translation` (optional path) |\n| Graph loader | parses the field |\n| Spec interface | new `translate` callback in `lang_spec_t` |\n| Lua spec | `lua_translate` — loads file once per worker, caches via Lua registry, calls `(raw, raw_native)` |\n| C spec | `c_translate` — lazy-compile + dlsym `sm_translate` |\n| Bash spec | translate left NULL (deferred — needs protocol extension) |\n| Dispatch | per-port branch routes through shim, replaces data/size, sets `input_native=1` |\n| Runtime self-construction | `runtime_create_box` accepts `custom_translation` in spec JSON |\n| HTTP backend | 4 routes: list/get/put/delete translation files |\n| Editor API | `list/get/put/delete_translation` |\n| Editor inspector | per-port `+xlate` / `xlate` / `×` buttons |\n| Source view | routes `translations/` paths to the new endpoint |\n| Compile pipeline | copies `translations/` into compiled artifact |\n| Tests | C shim fixture + Lua shim fixture, both passing |\n\n**16 integration tests pass.** Both end-to-end shim fixtures (C uppercase shim, Lua reverse+prepend shim) demonstrate the runtime → spec → translate → invoke chain working.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThe 245 wire-color change from earlier was forward-compatible — it already painted goldenrod when `port.custom_translation` was set, even though no path yet wrote that field. Today the field gets written and the color comes alive automatically. That's the value of building visual signals around fields rather than around events: when the field appears, the signal turns on for free.\n\nThe Bash deferral pattern is becoming the project's recognizable shape — same shape as 319e. The bash spec gets a follow-on slice once the line-protocol extension lands; everything else ships now. That's a tidy seam.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nWhat's next? The remaining untracked issues are **247** (debug build + per-box stats lens), **249** (tap input mode with radial ports), **318** (sentinel primitives in JSON), and the deferred work pile from 319/246 (Bash bindings, exporter rewrite, box-kind refactor for create_box/connect)."
      }],

See the\nAmendment section below; the original FFI-based reconstruction\ntext in the body is retained for context but is no longer the\ntarget.\n\n## Amendment (2026-05-22) — function pointers via wrapper binaries, not FFI\n\nThe original design had the consumer's spec reconstruct a\n`$function_pointer` by FFI-casting the raw process-local\naddress (LuaJIT's `ffi.cast`, ctypes, etc.). Specs that used\nto publish \"I can reconstruct `$function_pointer` via FFI\" in\ntheir capability declaration now publish \"I can emit a\nforeign-call wrapper\" instead — same capability slot, different\nmeaning.\n\n### Why agnostic wins here\n\nLuaJIT FFI is fast and would have been the easy path for\nLua↔C. But locking SoraMech's wire format to LuaJIT's ABI\nexpectations would (a) tie the project to one specific Lua\nimplementation, (b) leave Bash with no `$function_pointer`\nreconstruction at all, (c) require every future language we\nadd to either ship an FFI binding or be a second-class\ncitizen, and (d) make windows / non-POSIX targets harder than\nthey need to be. Subprocess-and-socket is slower per call than\nFFI but it works everywhere, for every language, today, and\non every OS that speaks sockets. The cost is real but bounded;\nthe agnosticism is structural and worth more.\n\n## Concept\n\nJSON's structure covers six kinds of value cleanly — object,\narray, number, string, bool, null — and the cross-language ring\nin the dual-ring slot (issue 312) carries JSON for any wire that\ncrosses a language boundary. The structural cases that don't fit\nthose six kinds — Lua closures, libcurl handles, C++ class\ninstances, file handles, function pointers, large byte buffers\nwhere serialization would be expensive — need somewhere to live\nin the JSON ring without forcing the wire format to grow new\ntop-level shapes.\n\n**Sentinel primitives** are JSON object shapes with reserved key\nnames that mean \"this isn't a structural value, it's a reference\nto something the consumer must reconstruct using language-specific\nmachinery.\"\n\nThree kinds, each solving a different structural gap:\n\n```json\n{\"$ref\":              {\"ptr\": \"0x...\",  \"len\": 1048576,\n                       \"type\": \"bytes\"}}\n{\"$function_pointer\": {\"addr\": \"0x...\", \"signature\": \"int(void*,void*)\"}}\n{\"$lang_opaque\":      {\"lang\": \"lua\",   \"tag\": 12345,\n                       \"shape\": \"coroutine\"}}\n```\n\nSentinels are **emitted by the producer's spec** when its language\nhas a value JSON can't represent structurally. They are\n**reconstructed by the consumer's spec** using whatever runtime\nmachinery that language provides (LuaJIT FFI, ctypes for Python,\ndirect cast for C, etc.). Wires whose consumer cannot reconstruct\na sentinel kind **fail at compile time** — the editor catches the\nmismatch when the user wires a function-pointer output into a\nBash input.\n\n## Why these three, not more\n\nThe three sentinels carve up the structural gap by ownership:\n\n- **`$ref`** — bytes in a shared heap. The producer wrote the\n  bytes to the large-value heap (issue 302 / `src/015-large-value-heap.c`)\n  and emits a pointer-and-length reference. The bytes are\n  immutable for the wire's lifetime; refcount tracks consumers.\n  Solves: \"I have a megabyte to share; copying it through the\n  slot would be wasteful.\"\n- **`$function_pointer`** — a callable, identified by a raw\n  address and a signature interpretable in C-function-pointer\n  syntax. The address is process-local. The signature is the\n  contract between producer and consumer. Solves: \"I have a\n  function I want my consumer to be able to call directly.\"\n- **`$lang_opaque`** — a language-private value. The spec author writes the emit logic; it's not generic.\n\n### Lua\n\n`encode_value` in `langs/lua/spec.c:188` currently hard-errors on\nfunction / userdata / thread / lightuserdata. Decision is per-call,\n  driven by size threshold or output annotation.\n\n### C\n\nThe C spec's generated wrapper (issue 307) knows the box's\ndeclared output type. The wrapper emits the right sentinel\nshape based on the type:\n\n- A declared `function_pointer` return — `$function_pointer`\n  with the type's signature.\n- A declared `bytes` return whose size exceeds the inline\n  threshold — `$ref` with the bytes written to the heap.\n- A declared opaque struct — `$lang_opaque` if the struct's\n  shape is C-only.\n\n### Bash\n\nBash has no native values besides strings; sentinels don't apply\non the emit side. A Bash producer always emits structural JSON\nstrings.\n\n## Consumer protocol\n\nEach spec's `json_to_native` walks the JSON tree and, when it\nsees a sentinel key, reconstructs the value using its language's\nmachinery. The reconstruction is the spec author's responsibility.\n\n### Lua\n\n**Superseded by the Amendment (2026-05-22)** for the\n`$function_pointer` case — the FFI-cast reconstruction below\nis no longer the target; instead, the consumer's spec emits a\nforeign-call wrapper that round-trips through a compiled binary\nor a long-lived subprocess. `$ref` and `$lang_opaque`\nreconstruction below remains current.\n\n```c\n// inside lua_json_to_native, on seeing {\"$function_pointer\": {...}}:\nconst char *sig = json_string_value(obj, \"signature\");\nuintptr_t   addr = json_int_value(obj, \"addr\");\nlua_getglobal(L, \"ffi\");\nlua_getfield(L, -1, \"cast\");\nlua_pushstring(L, sig);                 // \"int (*)(void*, void*)\"\nlua_pushinteger(L, (lua_Integer)addr);\nlua_call(L, 2, 1);\n// stack top: an FFI callable Lua can invoke as compare_fn(a, b)\n```\n\n`$ref` reconstruction in Lua copies the bytes (`lua_pushlstring(ptr, len)`)\nsince Lua's value model needs values in Lua's heap. The\nproducer's refcount handles the lifetime.\n\n`$lang_opaque` with `lang: \"lua\"` resolves the tag through the\nworker's per-worker registry; with `lang != \"lua\"` it's a wire\ncompile error.\n\n### C\n\nDirect casts. `$function_pointer` becomes a typed function\npointer the wrapper can invoke. `$ref` is a `(void*, size_t)`\npair the wrapper hands to the user's function. `$lang_opaque`\nwith `lang: \"c\"` is a typed-struct pointer; other langs fail.\n\n### Bash\n\nBash cannot reconstruct any sentinel except possibly `$ref`\n(by reading the bytes from the file the marshaller staged at the\nprocess boundary). `$function_pointer` and `$lang_opaque` fail\nunless the producer chose the cross-process escape hatch (see\nbelow).\n\n## Compile-time validation\n\nThe compile step walks every wire and checks:\n\n- If the producer's declared output type can emit sentinel kind\n  K (per the producer language's spec capability), then\n- The consumer's language must be able to reconstruct sentinel\n  kind K (per the consumer language's spec capability).\n- If not, **the compile fails** with the specific wire and the\n  specific sentinel kind named.\n\nThis is editor-time feedback. The\ndefault-is-FFI / escape-hatch-is-binary framing below is no\nlonger accurate; both cases now use a compiled binary, optionally\nbacked by a long-lived subprocess + socket. Two options when a\nfunction pointer's wire targets such a consumer:\n\n1. **Fail at compile time** (the default). Clear, honest.\n2. **Producer-side compiled binary** (opt-in). When the C spec\n   detects that a function-pointer output is wired to a\n   cross-process consumer, it compiles the function into a\n   standalone executable in `compiled/cross-process/<box>__<port>.bin`.\n   The sentinel becomes:\n\n   ```json\n   {\"$function_pointer\": {\"binary\": \"compiled/cross-process/...\",\n                          \"signature\": \"int(int,int)\"}}\n   ```\n\n   Bash invokes the binary with `$(./bin args...)` per call. Cost:\n   process spawn per invocation (1-10 ms). The escape hatch is\n   opt-in per box output — the user explicitly chooses the cost\n   in the inspector.\n\nThe default behaviour is option 1 because hiding the spawn cost\nwould mislead the user about runtime behaviour. The user picks\ntheir language; the cost follows from the choice. Option 2 is\nthe escape hatch for cases where the user genuinely needs\nC-from-Bash and accepts the cost.\n\n## Relationship to custom translation specs (issue 246)\n\nSentinels are the **spec author's tool** for representing\nnon-structural values. Custom translations are the **user's\ntool** for interpreting them (or any other value) when the\ndefault reconstruction isn't what they want.\n\nThe escalation path:\n\n1. Default spec encode / decode handles JSON-structural values\n   transparently.\n2. When the producer's value can't be encoded structurally, the\n   spec author's emit logic produces the right sentinel.\n3. When the consumer's spec can reconstruct the sentinel\n   generically (FFI cast, ctypes, direct pointer), the default\n   reconstruction runs.\n4. When the user wants a different interpretation than the\n   default (treat a function pointer as a method on a class\n   instance, dereference a `$ref` and parse its bytes as a\n   custom format, etc.), they attach a per-port custom\n   translation that overrides the default reconstruction.\n\nSo sentinels and custom translations are layered: sentinels\nprovide the *bytes that arrive at the wire* for non-structural\nvalues; custom translations decide *what to do with those bytes*\nwhen the default isn't enough.\n\n## Where in the dispatch this lives\n\nSentinels live inside the JSON ring of the dual-ring slot. The\nslot store (issue 312) doesn't know about them — it just carries\nbytes. The producer's `native_to_json` emits them when writing\nto the JSON ring; the consumer's `json_to_native` recognizes\nand reconstructs them when reading from the JSON ring.\n\nInside the native ring, sentinels don't appear — native values\nare encoded in the language's own binary form, which can\nrepresent its own callables / opaque values directly without\nneeding a JSON-side hack.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — bridges (`native_to_json`,\n  `json_to_native`) are where sentinel handling lives per spec.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c:188` (`encode_value`) — emit-side extension\n  point. Currently hard-errors on function / userdata / thread;\n  this issue replaces those errors with sentinel emission.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c:370` (`decode_node`) — reconstruct-side\n  extension point. The map compiler walks what it can — declared\n   inputs and statically reachable references — and fails the\n   compile with a clear error if the function pointer's\n   closure can't be enumerated. Honest failure mode.\n\n### New spec responsibility: foreign-call wrappers\n\nThis adds one responsibility to `lang_spec_t`. Each spec\nprovides a function that emits a wrapper in its own language\ngiven a foreign-call protocol descriptor:\n\n```c\nint (*emit_foreign_call_wrapper)(void *handle,\n                                 const char *binary_path,\n                                 const char *socket_path_or_null,\n                                 const char *signature,\n                                 const char *out_wrapper_src_path);\n```\n\n- For Lua: writes a `.lua` file containing a function that\n  opens the socket (or popen's the binary) and round-trips\n  arguments / response.\n- For C: writes a `.c` file with the same logic, compiled\n  alongside the rest of the C-side merged module.\n- For Bash: writes a function definition that wraps a\n  `socat`-or-`nc`-or-`./bin` call.\n\nThe wrapper-recipe is the *only* per-language code the\nforeign-call story needs. The binaries themselves are produced\nby the producing spec's existing `compile` function. The\nprotocol on the wire is a single shared definition — not\nper-language — so the consuming spec doesn't need to know what\nlanguage wrote the binary.\n\n### What this leaves of the original sentinel design\n\nThe two other sentinels survive unchanged:\n\n- **`$ref`** — pointer + length into the large-value heap; same\n  in-process semantics as before, same cross-process inlining\n  at the UDS marshaller.\n- **`$lang_opaque`** — still a \"this language's private value,\n  consumer either understands or fails compile\" sentinel; the\n  fail-compile path stays the default.\n\n`$function_pointer`'s wire shape stays the same JSON-object\nform; only the reconstruction recipe changes. Specs that used\nto publish \"I can reconstruct `$function_pointer` via FFI\" in\ntheir capability declaration now publish \"I can emit a\nforeign-call wrapper\" instead — same capability slot, different\nmeaning.\n\n### Why agnostic wins here\n\nLuaJIT FFI is fast and would have been the easy path for\nLua↔C. But locking SoraMech's wire format to LuaJIT's ABI\nexpectations would (a) tie the project to one specific Lua\nimplementation, (b) leave Bash with no `$function_pointer`\nreconstruction at all, (c) require every future language we\nadd to either ship an FFI binding or be a second-class\ncitizen, and (d) make windows / non-POSIX targets harder than\nthey need to be. Subprocess-and-socket is slower per call than\nFFI but it works everywhere, for every language, today, and\non every OS that speaks sockets. The cost is real but bounded;\nthe agnosticism is structural and worth more.\n\n## Concept\n\nJSON's structure covers six kinds of value cleanly — object,\narray, number, string, bool, null — and the cross-language ring\nin the dual-ring slot (issue 312) carries JSON for any wire that\ncrosses a language boundary. The structural cases that don't fit\nthose six kinds — Lua closures, libcurl handles, C++ class\ninstances, file handles, function pointers, large byte buffers\nwhere serialization would be expensive — need somewhere to live\nin the JSON ring without forcing the wire format to grow new\ntop-level shapes.\n\n**Sentinel primitives** are JSON object shapes with reserved key\nnames that mean \"this isn't a structural value, it's a reference\nto something the consumer must reconstruct using language-specific\nmachinery.\"\n\nThree kinds, each solving a different structural gap:\n\n```json\n{\"$ref\":              {\"ptr\": \"0x...\",  \"len\": 1048576,\n                       \"type\": \"bytes\"}}\n{\"$function_pointer\": {\"addr\": \"0x...\", \"signature\": \"int(void*,void*)\"}}\n{\"$lang_opaque\":      {\"lang\": \"lua\",   \"tag\": 12345,\n                       \"shape\": \"coroutine\"}}\n```\n\nSentinels are **emitted by the producer's spec** when its language\nhas a value JSON can't represent structurally. They are\n**reconstructed by the consumer's spec** using whatever runtime\nmachinery that language provides (LuaJIT FFI, ctypes for Python,\ndirect cast for C, etc.). Wires whose consumer cannot reconstruct\na sentinel kind **fail at compile time** — the editor catches the\nmismatch when the user wires a function-pointer output into a\nBash input.\n\n## Why these three, not more\n\nThe three sentinels carve up the structural gap by ownership:\n\n- **`$ref`** — bytes in a shared heap. The producer wrote the\n  bytes to the large-value heap (issue 302 / `src/015-large-value-heap.c`)\n  and emits a pointer-and-length reference. The bytes are\n  immutable for the wire's lifetime; refcount tracks consumers.\n  Solves: \"I have a megabyte to share; copying it through the\n  slot would be wasteful.\"\n- **`$function_pointer`** — a callable, identified by a raw\n  address and a signature interpretable in C-function-pointer\n  syntax. The address is process-local. The signature is the\n  contract between producer and consumer. Solves: \"I have a\n  function I want my consumer to be able to call directly.\"\n- **`$lang_opaque`** — a language-private value. The producer\n  tags it with the language name and a worker-private reference\n  the producer's spec can resolve back. Solves: \"I have a value\n  with no general structural representation; only my own\n  language knows what it is.\"\n\nAnything that doesn't fit one of the three either (a) has a\nJSON-structural representation and shouldn't be a sentinel, or\n(b) is genuinely unrepresentable and the wire is wrong, not the\nformat.\n\n## Producer protocol\n\nEach language spec's `native_to_json` walks its native values and\nemits the appropriate sentinel when it encounters a non-structural\nvalue. The spec author writes the emit logic; it's not generic.\n\n### Lua\n\n`encode_value` in `langs/lua/spec.c:188` currently hard-errors on\nfunction / userdata / thread / lightuserdata. The extension:\n\n- **Function** (`LUA_TFUNCTION`) — if the function is a C function\n  registered with FFI, emit `$function_pointer` with its FFI\n  signature; if it's a Lua function, emit `$lang_opaque` with\n  `lang: \"lua\"` and a tag the spec can use to resolve the\n  function back later (a registry index, for example).\n- **Userdata** with an FFI ctype — emit `$function_pointer` if\n  the type is a function pointer; `$ref` if the type is a sized\n  buffer; `$lang_opaque` otherwise.\n- **Coroutine** (`LUA_TTHREAD`) — `$lang_opaque` with\n  `shape: \"coroutine\"`.\n- **Large strings or tables** — at the spec's discretion, the\n  producer may write the value to the large-value heap and emit\n  `$ref` instead of inlining the bytes. Decision is per-call,\n  driven by size threshold or output annotation.\n\n### C\n\nThe C spec's generated wrapper (issue 307) knows the box's\ndeclared output type. The wrapper emits the right sentinel\nshape based on the type:\n\n- A declared `function_pointer` return — `$function_pointer`\n  with the type's signature.\n- A declared `bytes` return whose size exceeds the inline\n  threshold — `$ref` with the bytes written to the heap.\n- A declared opaque struct — `$lang_opaque` if the struct's\n  shape is C-only.\n\n### Bash\n\nBash has no native values besides strings; sentinels don't apply\non the emit side. A Bash producer always emits structural JSON\nstrings.\n\n## Consumer protocol\n\nEach spec's `json_to_native` walks the JSON tree and, when it\nsees a sentinel key, reconstructs the value using its language's\nmachinery. The reconstruction is the spec author's responsibility.\n\n### Lua\n\n**Superseded by the Amendment (2026-05-22)** for the\n`$function_pointer` case — the FFI-cast reconstruction below\nis no longer the target; instead, the consumer's spec emits a\nforeign-call wrapper that round-trips through a compiled binary\nor a long-lived subprocess. `$ref` and `$lang_opaque`\nreconstruction below remains current.\n\n```c\n// inside lua_json_to_native, on seeing {\"$function_pointer\": {...}}:\nconst char *sig = json_string_value(obj, \"signature\");\nuintptr_t   addr = json_int_value(obj, \"addr\");\nlua_getglobal(L, \"ffi\");\nlua_getfield(L, -1, \"cast\");\nlua_pushstring(L, sig);                 // \"int (*)(void*, void*)\"\nlua_pushinteger(L, (lua_Integer)addr);\nlua_call(L, 2, 1);\n// stack top: an FFI callable Lua can invoke as compare_fn(a, b)\n```\n\n`$ref` reconstruction in Lua copies the bytes (`lua_pushlstring(ptr, len)`)\nsince Lua's value model needs values in Lua's heap. The\nproducer's refcount handles the lifetime.\n\n`$lang_opaque` with `lang: \"lua\"` resolves the tag through the\nworker's per-worker registry; with `lang != \"lua\"` it's a wire\ncompile error.\n\n### C\n\nDirect casts. `$function_pointer` becomes a typed function\npointer the wrapper can invoke. `$ref` is a `(void*, size_t)`\npair the wrapper hands to the user's function. `$lang_opaque`\nwith `lang: \"c\"` is a typed-struct pointer; other langs fail.\n\n### Bash\n\nBash cannot reconstruct any sentinel except possibly `$ref`\n(by reading the bytes from the file the marshaller staged at the\nprocess boundary). `$function_pointer` and `$lang_opaque` fail\nunless the producer chose the cross-process escape hatch (see\nbelow).\n\n## Compile-time validation\n\nThe compile step walks every wire and checks:\n\n- If the producer's declared output type can emit sentinel kind\n  K (per the producer language's spec capability), then\n- The consumer's language must be able to reconstruct sentinel\n  kind K (per the consumer language's spec capability).\n- If not, **the compile fails** with the specific wire and the\n  specific sentinel kind named.\n\nThis is editor-time feedback. The user fixes the wire\n(reroute it, change the consumer's language, attach a custom\ntranslation per issue 246) before the program ever runs.\n\nThe per-spec capability is a static fact each spec declares.\nAdding a new language K declares K's emit set and reconstruct\nset; the compile validator consults the declaration.\n\n## Cross-process escape hatch for `$function_pointer`\n\n**Superseded by the Amendment (2026-05-22)** — what this section\ndescribed as an opt-in escape hatch is now the *only* path. The\ndefault-is-FFI / escape-hatch-is-binary framing below is no\nlonger accurate; both cases now use a compiled binary, optionally\nbacked by a long-lived subprocess + socket. Keeping the text for\ncontext.\n\nBash (and any other process-isolated language) can't dereference\nan in-process function-pointer address. Two options when a\nfunction pointer's wire targets such a consumer:\n\n1. **Fail at compile time** (the default). Clear, honest.\n2. **Producer-side compiled binary** (opt-in). When the C spec\n   detects that a function-pointer output is wired to a\n   cross-process consumer, it compiles the function into a\n   standalone executable in `compiled/cross-process/<box>__<port>.bin`.\n   The sentinel becomes:\n\n   ```json\n   {\"$function_pointer\": {\"binary\": \"compiled/cross-process/...\",\n                          \"signature\": \"int(int,int)\"}}\n   ```\n\n   Bash invokes the binary with `$(./bin args...)` per call. Cost:\n   process spawn per invocation (1-10 ms). The escape hatch is\n   opt-in per box output — the user explicitly chooses the cost\n   in the inspector.\n\nThe default behaviour is option 1 because hiding the spawn cost\nwould mislead the user about runtime behaviour. The user picks\ntheir language; the cost follows from the choice. Option 2 is\nthe escape hatch for cases where the user genuinely needs\nC-from-Bash and accepts the cost.\n\n## Relationship to custom translation specs (issue 246)\n\nSentinels are the **spec author's tool** for representing\nnon-structural values. Custom translations are the **user's\ntool** for interpreting them (or any other value) when the\ndefault reconstruction isn't what they want.\n\nThe escalation path:\n\n1. Default spec encode / decode handles JSON-structural values\n   transparently.\n2. When the producer's value can't be encoded structurally, the\n   spec author's emit logic produces the right sentinel.\n3. When the consumer's spec can reconstruct the sentinel\n   generically (FFI cast, ctypes, direct pointer), the default\n   reconstruction runs.\n4. When the user wants a different interpretation than the\n   default (treat a function pointer as a method on a class\n   instance, dereference a `$ref` and parse its bytes as a\n   custom format, etc.), they attach a per-port custom\n   translation that overrides the default reconstruction.\n\nSo sentinels and custom translations are layered: sentinels\nprovide the *bytes that arrive at the wire* for non-structural\nvalues; custom translations decide *what to do with those bytes*\nwhen the default isn't enough.\n\n## Where in the dispatch this lives\n\nSentinels live inside the JSON ring of the dual-ring slot. The\nslot store (issue 312) doesn't know about them — it just carries\nbytes. The producer's `native_to_json` emits them when writing\nto the JSON ring; the consumer's `json_to_native` recognizes\nand reconstructs them when reading from the JSON ring.\n\nInside the native ring, sentinels don't appear — native values\nare encoded in the language's own binary form, which can\nrepresent its own callables / opaque values directly without\nneeding a JSON-side hack.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — bridges (`native_to_json`,\n  `json_to_native`) are where sentinel handling lives per spec.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c:188` (`encode_value`) — emit-side extension\n  point. Currently hard-errors on function / userdata / thread;\n  this issue replaces those errors with sentinel emission.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c:370` (`decode_node`) — reconstruct-side\n  extension point. Add sentinel recognition before generic\n  object handling.\n- `langs/c/spec.c` — C spec's `native_to_json` / `json_to_native`\n  (currently NULL); both grow when this issue lands.\n- `langs/bash/spec.c` — Bash spec; only `$ref` is reconstructable.\n- `src/015-large-value-heap.c` — `$ref` storage.\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — compile-time wire validation\n  walks producer/consumer sentinel capabilities.\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — dual-ring shape;\n  sentinels ride inside its JSON ring.\n- `issues/246-custom-translation-specs-per-port.md` — user-side\n  override layered on top of sentinel reconstruction.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — wire format section; gains a brief\n  sentinel reference.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Define the canonical JSON shapes**. Three sentinel kinds,\n   exact key names, value-object schemas. Document in\n   `docs/001-architecture.md`.\n2. **Lua emit**: replace the hard-errors in `encode_value` with\n   sentinel emission per the producer protocol above. Start with\n   `$function_pointer` for FFI callables and `$lang_opaque` for\n   Lua functions / coroutines.\n3. **Lua reconstruct**: extend `decode_node` to recognize the\n   three sentinels and reconstruct them.\n4. **Per-spec capability declarations**. Each spec declares its\n   emit set (sentinel kinds it can produce) and reconstruct set\n   (sentinel kinds it can consume). Lives next to the\n   `lang_spec_t` declaration.\n5. **C spec sentinels**. Emit via the generated wrapper based on\n   declared output types; reconstruct via direct cast.\n6. **Bash spec sentinels**. Only `$ref` on the reconstruct side\n   (read bytes from the marshaller's staged file).\n7. **Compile-time validation**. Walk every wire; check the\n   producer's emit set against the consumer's reconstruct set;\n   fail with a clear message on mismatch.\n8. **Cross-process escape hatch for `$function_pointer`**.\n   Opt-in flag in the box output declaration; the C spec emits a\n   standalone binary instead of (or alongside) the in-process\n   address.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **`$ref` lifetime across iterator-fed slots**. A producer's\n  output is referenced by an N-cell ring of consumer slots; each\n  cell holds the `$ref`, each pop decrements. Already supported\n  by the large-value heap's refcount, but worth verifying the\n  test coverage when sentinels land.\n- **Sentinel inside sentinel.** A `$ref` whose bytes are\n  themselves JSON containing a `$function_pointer` is legal but\n  weird. Document the recursive case; probably falls out of the\n  walker for free.\n- **Versioning the sentinel format**. The reserved key names\n  (`$ref`, `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque`) and the\n  value-object schemas are part of the compile-time contract.\n  Changing them is breaking. Worth a one-line stability note\n  somewhere.\n- **Cross-process `$ref` semantics**. In-process `$ref` is a raw\n  pointer + length. Cross-process (Bash via UDS), the marshaller\n  stages the bytes at the socket boundary. Decide whether the\n  Bash-side `$ref` reconstruction reads from a file path or\n  inlines the bytes in the request. The latter is simpler; the\n  former scales to bigger values.\n- **`bytes` returns on the C spec currently passthrough raw bytes\n  into the JSON ring.** The C spec's typed-output-JSON path\n  (issue 307 item 2) wraps strings in JSON quotes and passes\n  ints / doubles / bools through as valid JSON fragments — but for\n  a declared `bytes` return it writes the raw payload verbatim,\n  which is *not* valid JSON in the general case (non-UTF-8 bytes\n  break parsers; embedded quotes / backslashes mangle the wire).\n  The proper resolution belongs here, not in 307: small `bytes`\n  outputs should be base64-wrapped into a JSON string (or its own\n  sentinel kind), and large `bytes` outputs should follow the\n  `$ref` path already described for the heap. Until that lands,\n  cross-language `bytes` wires from C producers are an honest\n  hazard — flag in the compile-time validator if possible, or at\n  minimum document the gap so users don't wire a `bytes`\n  C-output into a Lua / Bash consumer expecting clean JSON."
      }],
    "role":"user"
  },

Today: hard error. */\n622\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: cannot JSON-encode value of type %s\\n\",\n623\t                lua_typename(L, t));\n624\t        return -1;\n625\t    }\n626\t}\n627\t/* }}} */\n628\t\n629\t/* {{{ lua_native_to_json() — top-of-stack Lua value → JSON bytes */"
      }],

    "content":"/* src/020-sentinels.c — sentinel primitives implementation.\n *\n * Three sentinel kinds, three responsibilities each (detect, emit,\n * for two of them also reconstruct via the per-spec json_to_native\n * path). This file is the spec-independent machinery; per-spec\n * emission and reconstruction lives in each language's spec.c.\n *\n * Slice-1 scope (issue 318): $lang_opaque and $ref are end-to-end\n * for intra-language and in-process cases respectively;\n * $function_pointer is parsed and rejected pending the amendment's\n * wrapper-binary subsystem.\n */\n#include \"020-sentinels.h\"\n#include \"json.h\"\n\n#include <pthread.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* {{{ sentinel_detect()\n *\n * Single-key match against the three reserved key names. We accept\n * any value type for the sentinel's payload — checking the inner\n * shape is the reconstructor's job, not the detector's. */\nsentinel_kind_t sentinel_detect(const struct json_node *node)\n{\n    if (!node) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    json_node_t *n = (json_node_t *)node;\n    if (json_kind(n) != JSON_OBJECT) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    if (json_object_size(n) != 1) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    const char *key = json_object_key(n, 0);\n    if (!key) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    if (strcmp(key, \"$ref\") == 0)              return SENTINEL_REF;\n    if (strcmp(key, \"$lang_opaque\") == 0)      return SENTINEL_LANG_OPAQUE;\n    if (strcmp(key, \"$function_pointer\") == 0) return SENTINEL_FUNCTION_POINTER;\n    return SENTINEL_NONE;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Emission writers */\nvoid sentinel_write_ref(json_writer_t *w, uintptr_t chunk_ptr, int len)\n{\n    /* The pointer is rendered as hex inside a JSON string so it\n     * survives JSON-string-canonicalisation regardless of platform\n     * pointer width. Decoders parse via strtoull. */\n    char ptr_buf[32];\n    snprintf(ptr_buf, sizeof ptr_buf, \"0x%lx\", (unsigned long)chunk_ptr);\n    json_writer_object(w);\n      json_writer_key(w, \"$ref\");\n      json_writer_object(w);\n        json_writer_key   (w, \"chunk_ptr\"); json_writer_string(w, ptr_buf);\n        json_writer_key   (w, \"len\");       json_writer_int   (w, len);\n      json_writer_end(w);\n    json_writer_end(w);\n}\n\nvoid sentinel_write_lang_opaque(json_writer_t *w,\n                                const char *lang, uint64_t tag,\n                                const char *shape)\n{\n    json_writer_object(w);\n      json_writer_key(w, \"$lang_opaque\");\n      json_writer_object(w);\n        json_writer_key (w, \"lang\"); json_writer_string(w, lang ? lang : \"\");\n        json_writer_key (w, \"tag\");  json_writer_int   (w, (long long)tag);\n        if (shape && *shape) {\n            json_writer_key(w, \"shape\"); json_writer_string(w, shape);\n        }\n      json_writer_end(w);\n    json_writer_end(w);\n}\n\nvoid sentinel_write_function_pointer_stub(json_writer_t *w,\n                                          const char *signature)\n{\n    /* Per the amendment: the wrapper-binary subsystem hasn't landed,\n     * so this writer emits a self-describing stub that the\n     * consumer's json_to_native is expected to reject with a clear\n     * \"not yet implemented\" message. Keeping the shape stable lets\n     * future wrapper-binary work migrate fixture data without\n     * rewriting the producer side. */\n    json_writer_object(w);\n      json_writer_key(w, \"$function_pointer\");\n      json_writer_object(w);\n        json_writer_key(w, \"signature\");\n        json_writer_string(w, signature ? signature : \"void(void)\");\n        json_writer_key(w, \"status\");\n        json_writer_string(w, \"wrapper-binary system not yet implemented\");\n      json_writer_end(w);\n    json_writer_end(w);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ $ref bytes store\n *\n * Process-wide hash-less append-only table. We don't need fast\n * lookup; producers and consumers reference chunks by raw pointer,\n * which IS the lookup key. Keeping a table at all lets us\n * (a) own the lifetime explicitly and (b) bulk-free at run end\n * via sentinel_ref_store_clear so memory doesn't leak across\n * fresh invocations of the runner in long-lived tests.\n *\n * Concurrency: single mutex guards both append and clear. The\n * lookup path returns a stable pointer (the chunks themselves\n * never move) so reads outside the mutex are safe. */\ntypedef struct ref_entry {\n    void  *bytes;\n    int    len;\n} ref_entry_t;\n\nstatic ref_entry_t  *ref_table;\nstatic int           ref_count;\nstatic int           ref_capacity;\nstatic pthread_mutex_t ref_mu = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;\n\nuintptr_t sentinel_ref_alloc(const void *bytes, int len)\n{\n    if (len < 0) return 0;\n    void *copy = malloc((size_t)len);\n    if (!copy && len > 0) return 0;\n    if (len > 0) memcpy(copy, bytes, (size_t)len);\n\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&ref_mu);\n    if (ref_count == ref_capacity) {\n        int new_cap = ref_capacity == 0 ? 16 : ref_capacity * 2;\n        ref_entry_t *grown = realloc(ref_table,\n                                     (size_t)new_cap * sizeof *ref_table);\n        if (!grown) { pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu); free(copy); return 0; }\n        ref_table    = grown;\n        ref_capacity = new_cap;\n    }\n    ref_table[ref_count].bytes = copy;\n    ref_table[ref_count].len   = len;\n    ref_count++;\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n    return (uintptr_t)copy;\n}\n\nconst void *sentinel_ref_lookup(uintptr_t chunk_ptr, int *out_len)\n{\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&ref_mu);\n    for (int i = 0; i < ref_count; i++) {\n        if ((uintptr_t)ref_table[i].bytes == chunk_ptr) {\n            if (out_len) *out_len = ref_table[i].len;\n            pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n            return ref_table[i].bytes;\n        }\n    }\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n    if (out_len) *out_len = 0;\n    return NULL;\n}\n\nvoid sentinel_ref_store_clear(void)\n{\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&ref_mu);\n    for (int i = 0; i < ref_count; i++) free(ref_table[i].bytes);\n    free(ref_table);\n    ref_table    = NULL;\n    ref_count    = 0;\n    ref_capacity = 0;\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Capability validation */\nunsigned int sentinel_validate(unsigned int producer_mask,\n                               unsigned int consumer_mask)\n{\n    unsigned int gap = producer_mask & ~consumer_mask;\n    if (gap == 0) return 0;\n    /* Return the lowest-numbered offending bit so callers can name\n     * one specific kind in their diagnostic. */\n    for (unsigned int b = 1; b != 0; b <<= 1) {\n        if (gap & b) return b;\n    }\n    return gap;   /* unreachable in practice */\n}\n\nconst char *sentinel_kind_name(sentinel_kind_t k)\n{\n    switch (k) {\n        case SENTINEL_NONE:             return \"(none)\";\n        case SENTINEL_REF:              return \"$ref\";\n        case SENTINEL_LANG_OPAQUE:      return \"$lang_opaque\";\n        case SENTINEL_FUNCTION_POINTER: return \"$function_pointer\";\n        default:                        return \"(unknown)\";\n    }\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

          "content":"/* src/020-sentinels.c — sentinel primitives implementation.\n *\n * Three sentinel kinds, three responsibilities each (detect, emit,\n * for two of them also reconstruct via the per-spec json_to_native\n * path). This file is the spec-independent machinery; per-spec\n * emission and reconstruction lives in each language's spec.c.\n *\n * Slice-1 scope (issue 318): $lang_opaque and $ref are end-to-end\n * for intra-language and in-process cases respectively;\n * $function_pointer is parsed and rejected pending the amendment's\n * wrapper-binary subsystem.\n */\n#include \"020-sentinels.h\"\n#include \"json.h\"\n\n#include <pthread.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* {{{ sentinel_detect()\n *\n * Single-key match against the three reserved key names. We accept\n * any value type for the sentinel's payload — checking the inner\n * shape is the reconstructor's job, not the detector's. */\nsentinel_kind_t sentinel_detect(const struct json_node *node)\n{\n    if (!node) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    json_node_t *n = (json_node_t *)node;\n    if (json_kind(n) != JSON_OBJECT) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    if (json_object_size(n) != 1) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    const char *key = json_object_key(n, 0);\n    if (!key) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    if (strcmp(key, \"$ref\") == 0)              return SENTINEL_REF;\n    if (strcmp(key, \"$lang_opaque\") == 0)      return SENTINEL_LANG_OPAQUE;\n    if (strcmp(key, \"$function_pointer\") == 0) return SENTINEL_FUNCTION_POINTER;\n    return SENTINEL_NONE;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Emission writers */\nvoid sentinel_write_ref(json_writer_t *w, uintptr_t chunk_ptr, int len)\n{\n    /* The pointer is rendered as hex inside a JSON string so it\n     * survives JSON-string-canonicalisation regardless of platform\n     * pointer width. Decoders parse via strtoull. */\n    char ptr_buf[32];\n    snprintf(ptr_buf, sizeof ptr_buf, \"0x%lx\", (unsigned long)chunk_ptr);\n    json_writer_object(w);\n      json_writer_key(w, \"$ref\");\n      json_writer_object(w);\n        json_writer_key   (w, \"chunk_ptr\"); json_writer_string(w, ptr_buf);\n        json_writer_key   (w, \"len\");       json_writer_int   (w, len);\n      json_writer_end(w);\n    json_writer_end(w);\n}\n\nvoid sentinel_write_lang_opaque(json_writer_t *w,\n                                const char *lang, uint64_t tag,\n                                const char *shape)\n{\n    json_writer_object(w);\n      json_writer_key(w, \"$lang_opaque\");\n      json_writer_object(w);\n        json_writer_key (w, \"lang\"); json_writer_string(w, lang ? lang : \"\");\n        json_writer_key (w, \"tag\");  json_writer_int   (w, (long long)tag);\n        if (shape && *shape) {\n            json_writer_key(w, \"shape\"); json_writer_string(w, shape);\n        }\n      json_writer_end(w);\n    json_writer_end(w);\n}\n\nvoid sentinel_write_function_pointer_stub(json_writer_t *w,\n                                          const char *signature)\n{\n    /* Per the amendment: the wrapper-binary subsystem hasn't landed,\n     * so this writer emits a self-describing stub that the\n     * consumer's json_to_native is expected to reject with a clear\n     * \"not yet implemented\" message. Keeping the shape stable lets\n     * future wrapper-binary work migrate fixture data without\n     * rewriting the producer side. */\n    json_writer_object(w);\n      json_writer_key(w, \"$function_pointer\");\n      json_writer_object(w);\n        json_writer_key(w, \"signature\");\n        json_writer_string(w, signature ? signature : \"void(void)\");\n        json_writer_key(w, \"status\");\n        json_writer_string(w, \"wrapper-binary system not yet implemented\");\n      json_writer_end(w);\n    json_writer_end(w);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ $ref bytes store\n *\n * Process-wide hash-less append-only table. We don't need fast\n * lookup; producers and consumers reference chunks by raw pointer,\n * which IS the lookup key. Keeping a table at all lets us\n * (a) own the lifetime explicitly and (b) bulk-free at run end\n * via sentinel_ref_store_clear so memory doesn't leak across\n * fresh invocations of the runner in long-lived tests.\n *\n * Concurrency: single mutex guards both append and clear. The\n * lookup path returns a stable pointer (the chunks themselves\n * never move) so reads outside the mutex are safe. */\ntypedef struct ref_entry {\n    void  *bytes;\n    int    len;\n} ref_entry_t;\n\nstatic ref_entry_t  *ref_table;\nstatic int           ref_count;\nstatic int           ref_capacity;\nstatic pthread_mutex_t ref_mu = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;\n\nuintptr_t sentinel_ref_alloc(const void *bytes, int len)\n{\n    if (len < 0) return 0;\n    void *copy = malloc((size_t)len);\n    if (!copy && len > 0) return 0;\n    if (len > 0) memcpy(copy, bytes, (size_t)len);\n\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&ref_mu);\n    if (ref_count == ref_capacity) {\n        int new_cap = ref_capacity == 0 ? 16 : ref_capacity * 2;\n        ref_entry_t *grown = realloc(ref_table,\n                                     (size_t)new_cap * sizeof *ref_table);\n        if (!grown) { pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu); free(copy); return 0; }\n        ref_table    = grown;\n        ref_capacity = new_cap;\n    }\n    ref_table[ref_count].bytes = copy;\n    ref_table[ref_count].len   = len;\n    ref_count++;\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n    return (uintptr_t)copy;\n}\n\nconst void *sentinel_ref_lookup(uintptr_t chunk_ptr, int *out_len)\n{\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&ref_mu);\n    for (int i = 0; i < ref_count; i++) {\n        if ((uintptr_t)ref_table[i].bytes == chunk_ptr) {\n            if (out_len) *out_len = ref_table[i].len;\n            pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n            return ref_table[i].bytes;\n        }\n    }\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n    if (out_len) *out_len = 0;\n    return NULL;\n}\n\nvoid sentinel_ref_store_clear(void)\n{\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&ref_mu);\n    for (int i = 0; i < ref_count; i++) free(ref_table[i].bytes);\n    free(ref_table);\n    ref_table    = NULL;\n    ref_count    = 0;\n    ref_capacity = 0;\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Capability validation */\nunsigned int sentinel_validate(unsigned int producer_mask,\n                               unsigned int consumer_mask)\n{\n    unsigned int gap = producer_mask & ~consumer_mask;\n    if (gap == 0) return 0;\n    /* Return the lowest-numbered offending bit so callers can name\n     * one specific kind in their diagnostic. */\n    for (unsigned int b = 1; b != 0; b <<= 1) {\n        if (gap & b) return b;\n    }\n    return gap;   /* unreachable in practice */\n}\n\nconst char *sentinel_kind_name(sentinel_kind_t k)\n{\n    switch (k) {\n        case SENTINEL_NONE:             return \"(none)\";\n        case SENTINEL_REF:              return \"$ref\";\n        case SENTINEL_LANG_OPAQUE:      return \"$lang_opaque\";\n        case SENTINEL_FUNCTION_POINTER: return \"$function_pointer\";\n        default:                        return \"(unknown)\";\n    }\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

    "originalFile":"/* langs/lang-spec.h — public interface for SoraMech language specs.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: the C contract that every language\n * spec (Lua, C, Bash, anything user-added) implements. The pool\n * runner discovers specs by dlopen()ing langs/<name>/spec.so at\n * startup and reading the exported soramech_lang_spec symbol.\n *\n * Designed in issue 303. This is intentional.\n *\n * Issue 312 adds per-input / per-output format flags to `invoke`\n * (so a spec can decode each cell as native or JSON based on the\n * per-edge classification the loader assigned) and a pair of\n * bridges, `native_to_json` / `json_to_native`, used by the\n * dispatch's push path at language boundaries and by data boxes\n * (issue 317) that author values in their language's native\n * idioms. For `json_to_native`:\n * the bridge pushes the reconstructed value onto the same store.\n * `src` / `dst` carry only the JSON side. */\ntypedef int (*lang_bridge_fn)(void *handle,\n                              const void *src, int src_size,\n                              void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lang_spec_t */\ntypedef struct lang_spec {\n    const char *name;       /* \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ... */\n    const char *file_ext;   /* \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"        */\n\n    /* init: once per worker thread at pool startup. Frees the handle\n     * and any per-worker resources (e.g. lua_State, dlopen caches,\n     * persistent socket connections). */\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    /* compile: optional. Called once per source file at map-load\n     * (or at editor compile-button time). For languages that don't\n     * compile (Lua, Bash), leave this NULL.     "originalFile":"/* src/020-sentinels.h — cross-language JSON sentinel primitives.\n *\n * Three reserved JSON object shapes for values JSON can't represent\n * structurally (issue 318):\n *\n *   {\"$ref\":              {\"chunk_ptr\": \"0x...\", \"len\": N}}\n *   {\"$function_pointer\": {...}}    -- amendment: wrapper-binary path\n *   {\"$lang_opaque\":      {\"lang\": \"lua\", \"tag\": N, \"shape\": \"...\"}}\n *\n * The producer's spec emits the appropriate sentinel when its\n * encode walker hits a value JSON can't carry.     "originalFile":"/* src/020-sentinels.c — sentinel primitives implementation.\n *\n * Three sentinel kinds, three responsibilities each (detect, emit,\n * for two of them also reconstruct via the per-spec json_to_native\n * path). This file is the spec-independent machinery; per-spec\n * emission and reconstruction lives in each language's spec.c.\n *\n * Slice-1 scope (issue 318): $lang_opaque and $ref are end-to-end\n * for intra-language and in-process cases respectively;\n * $function_pointer is parsed and rejected pending the amendment's\n * wrapper-binary subsystem.\n */\n#include \"020-sentinels.h\"\n#include \"json.h\"\n\n#include <pthread.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* {{{ sentinel_detect()\n *\n * Single-key match against the three reserved key names. We accept\n * any value type for the sentinel's payload — checking the inner\n * shape is the reconstructor's job, not the detector's. */\nsentinel_kind_t sentinel_detect(const struct json_node *node)\n{\n    if (!node) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    json_node_t *n = (json_node_t *)node;\n    if (json_kind(n) != JSON_OBJECT) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    if (json_object_size(n) != 1) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    const char *key = json_object_key(n, 0);\n    if (!key) return SENTINEL_NONE;\n    if (strcmp(key, \"$ref\") == 0)              return SENTINEL_REF;\n    if (strcmp(key, \"$lang_opaque\") == 0)      return SENTINEL_LANG_OPAQUE;\n    if (strcmp(key, \"$function_pointer\") == 0) return SENTINEL_FUNCTION_POINTER;\n    return SENTINEL_NONE;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Emission writers */\nvoid sentinel_write_ref(json_writer_t *w, uintptr_t chunk_ptr, int len)\n{\n    /* The pointer is rendered as hex inside a JSON string so it\n     * survives JSON-string-canonicalisation regardless of platform\n     * pointer width. Decoders parse via strtoull. */\n    char ptr_buf[32];\n    snprintf(ptr_buf, sizeof ptr_buf, \"0x%lx\", (unsigned long)chunk_ptr);\n    json_writer_object(w);\n      json_writer_key(w, \"$ref\");\n      json_writer_object(w);\n        json_writer_key   (w, \"chunk_ptr\"); json_writer_string(w, ptr_buf);\n        json_writer_key   (w, \"len\");       json_writer_int   (w, len);\n      json_writer_end(w);\n    json_writer_end(w);\n}\n\nvoid sentinel_write_lang_opaque(json_writer_t *w,\n                                const char *lang, uint64_t tag,\n                                const char *shape)\n{\n    json_writer_object(w);\n      json_writer_key(w, \"$lang_opaque\");\n      json_writer_object(w);\n        json_writer_key (w, \"lang\"); json_writer_string(w, lang ? lang : \"\");\n        json_writer_key (w, \"tag\");  json_writer_int   (w, (long long)tag);\n        if (shape && *shape) {\n            json_writer_key(w, \"shape\"); json_writer_string(w, shape);\n        }\n      json_writer_end(w);\n    json_writer_end(w);\n}\n\nvoid sentinel_write_function_pointer_stub(json_writer_t *w,\n                                          const char *signature)\n{\n    /* Per the amendment: the wrapper-binary subsystem hasn't landed,\n     * so this writer emits a self-describing stub that the\n     * consumer's json_to_native is expected to reject with a clear\n     * \"not yet implemented\" message. Keeping the shape stable lets\n     * future wrapper-binary work migrate fixture data without\n     * rewriting the producer side. */\n    json_writer_object(w);\n      json_writer_key(w, \"$function_pointer\");\n      json_writer_object(w);\n        json_writer_key(w, \"signature\");\n        json_writer_string(w, signature ? signature : \"void(void)\");\n        json_writer_key(w, \"status\");\n        json_writer_string(w, \"wrapper-binary system not yet implemented\");\n      json_writer_end(w);\n    json_writer_end(w);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ $ref bytes store\n *\n * Process-wide hash-less append-only table. We don't need fast\n * lookup; producers and consumers reference chunks by raw pointer,\n * which IS the lookup key. Keeping a table at all lets us\n * (a) own the lifetime explicitly and (b) bulk-free at run end\n * via sentinel_ref_store_clear so memory doesn't leak across\n * fresh invocations of the runner in long-lived tests.\n *\n * Concurrency: single mutex guards both append and clear. The\n * lookup path returns a stable pointer (the chunks themselves\n * never move) so reads outside the mutex are safe. */\ntypedef struct ref_entry {\n    void  *bytes;\n    int    len;\n} ref_entry_t;\n\nstatic ref_entry_t  *ref_table;\nstatic int           ref_count;\nstatic int           ref_capacity;\nstatic pthread_mutex_t ref_mu = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;\n\nuintptr_t sentinel_ref_alloc(const void *bytes, int len)\n{\n    if (len < 0) return 0;\n    void *copy = malloc((size_t)len);\n    if (!copy && len > 0) return 0;\n    if (len > 0) memcpy(copy, bytes, (size_t)len);\n\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&ref_mu);\n    if (ref_count == ref_capacity) {\n        int new_cap = ref_capacity == 0 ? 16 : ref_capacity * 2;\n        ref_entry_t *grown = realloc(ref_table,\n                                     (size_t)new_cap * sizeof *ref_table);\n        if (!grown) { pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu); free(copy); return 0; }\n        ref_table    = grown;\n        ref_capacity = new_cap;\n    }\n    ref_table[ref_count].bytes = copy;\n    ref_table[ref_count].len   = len;\n    ref_count++;\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n    return (uintptr_t)copy;\n}\n\nconst void *sentinel_ref_lookup(uintptr_t chunk_ptr, int *out_len)\n{\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&ref_mu);\n    for (int i = 0; i < ref_count; i++) {\n        if ((uintptr_t)ref_table[i].bytes == chunk_ptr) {\n            if (out_len) *out_len = ref_table[i].len;\n            pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n            return ref_table[i].bytes;\n        }\n    }\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&ref_mu);\n    if (out_len) *out_len = 0;\n    return NULL;\n}\n\nvoid sentinel_ref_store_clear(void)\n{\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&ref_mu);\n    for (int i = 0; Each call adds exactly one\n * value to the stack on success; on failure the stack is wound back\n * to where this call started so partial decodes don't pollute it. */\nstatic int decode_node(lua_State *L, const json_node_t *node)\n{\n    int baseline = lua_gettop(L);\n    switch (json_kind(node)) {\n    case JSON_NULL:\n        lua_pushnil(L);\n        return 0;\n    case JSON_BOOL:\n        lua_pushboolean(L, json_bool_value(node));\n        return 0;\n    case JSON_NUMBER:\n        lua_pushnumber(L, json_number_value(node));\n        return 0;\n    case JSON_STRING:\n        lua_pushstring(L, json_string_value(node));\n        return 0;\n    case JSON_ARRAY: {\n        /* Push as `{n = N, [1] = ..., [2] = ..., ...}` so the\n         * encoder's n-field path can reconstruct the array\n         * faithfully on the way out, including any embedded or\n         * trailing nulls. `lua_rawseti` on a JSON `null` (which\n         * decode_node pushed as Lua nil) is effectively a key\n         * deletion — which is precisely the right representation\n         * for \"missing slot, fill with null at encode time.\" */\n        int n = json_array_size(node);\n        lua_createtable(L, n, 1);\n        lua_pushinteger(L, n);\n        lua_setfield(L, -2, \"n\");\n        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {\n            if (decode_node(L, json_array_at(node, i)) != 0) {\n                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            lua_rawseti(L, -2, i + 1);\n        }\n        return 0;\n    }\n    case JSON_OBJECT: {\n        int n = json_object_size(node);\n        lua_createtable(L, 0, n);\n        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {\n            if (decode_node(L, json_object_value(node, i)) != 0) {\n                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            lua_setfield(L, -2, json_object_key(node, i));\n        }\n        return 0;\n    }\n    }\n    fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: decode_node: unknown JSON kind\\n\");\n    lua_settop(L, baseline);\n    return -1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"    case JSON_OBJECT: {\n        /* Issue 318: sentinel detection. A single-key object matching\n         * one of the reserved sentinel keys gets routed through the\n         * reconstruct path for that kind instead of materialising as\n         * a plain Lua table with `$ref` / `$lang_opaque` /\n         * `$function_pointer` as a literal key. */\n        sentinel_kind_t skind = sentinel_detect(node);\n        if (skind == SENTINEL_LANG_OPAQUE) {\n            const json_node_t *inner = json_object_value(node, 0);\n            const json_node_t *lang_n = inner ? json_object_get(inner, \"lang\") : NULL;\n            const json_node_t *tag_n  = inner ? json_object_get(inner, \"tag\")  : NULL;\n            if (!lang_n || json_kind((json_node_t *)lang_n) != JSON_STRING ||\n                !tag_n  || json_kind((json_node_t *)tag_n)  != JSON_NUMBER) {\n                fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: malformed $lang_opaque\\n\");\n                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            const char *lang = json_string_value(lang_n);\n            if (strcmp(lang, \"lua\") != 0) {\n                fprintf(stderr,\n                    \"lua spec: $lang_opaque lang='%s' is not reconstructable \"\n                    \"by the Lua spec (cross-language opaque values require \"\n                    \"matching producer/consumer language)\\n\", lang);\n                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            int ref = (int)json_number_value(tag_n);\n            lua_rawgeti(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, ref);\n            if (lua_isnil(L, -1)) {\n                fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: $lang_opaque tag %d not in registry\\n\", ref);\n                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            return 0;\n        }\n        if (skind == SENTINEL_REF) {\n            const json_node_t *inner = json_object_value(node, 0);\n            const json_node_t *ptr_n = inner ? json_object_get(inner, \"chunk_ptr\") : NULL;\n            if (!ptr_n || json_kind((json_node_t *)ptr_n) != JSON_STRING) {\n                fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: malformed $ref\\n\");\n                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            uintptr_t ptr = (uintptr_t)strtoull(json_string_value(ptr_n), NULL, 0);\n            int len = 0;\n            const void *bytes = sentinel_ref_lookup(ptr, &len);\n            if (!bytes) {\n                fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: $ref chunk_ptr=0x%lx not in store\\n\",\n                        (unsigned long)ptr);\n                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            lua_pushlstring(L, (const char *)bytes, (size_t)len);\n            return 0;\n        }\n        if (skind == SENTINEL_FUNCTION_POINTER) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: $function_pointer reconstruction needs \"\n                            \"the wrapper-binary subsystem (issue 318 amendment), \"\n                            \"not yet implemented\\n\");\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        /* Plain object — fall through to the existing table path. */\n        int n = json_object_size(node);\n        lua_createtable(L, 0, n);\n        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {\n            if (decode_node(L, json_object_value(node, i)) != 0) {\n                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n                return -1;\n            }\n            lua_setfield(L, -2, json_object_key(node, i));\n        }\n        return 0;\n    }\n    }",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/langs/lua/spec.c"

{
  "uuid":"b60fef96-24b5-43c8-ae98-93290c39d8e8",

  "toolUseResult":{
    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    # Per-map env opt-in: a map may set SORAMECH_TEST_WORKERS to\n    # pin worker count for tests that depend on per-worker state\n    # (e.g. issue 318's $lang_opaque, which lives in the producer's\n    # Lua registry and can only be reconstructed by a consumer on\n    # the same worker).\n    local workers_env=\"\"\n    if [[ -f \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers\" ]]; then\n        workers_env=$(cat \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers\")\n    fi\n    if [[ -n \"$workers_env\" ]]; then\n        output=$(SORAMECH_WORKERS=\"$workers_env\" \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    else\n        output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    fi\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\ncheck_map \"read-literal\" \\\n    \"echo → hello, world!\"\n\ncheck_map \"319a-many-inputs\" \\\n    \"combine → count=20 sum=210\"\n\ncheck_map \"319d-runtime-create\" \\\n    \"trigger → trigger-fired:auto_\" \\\n    \"auto_\" \\\n    \"echo_dyn-received:trigger-fired:auto_\"\n\ncheck_map \"319e-c-create\" \\\n    \"trigger → c-trigger-fired:auto_\" \\\n    \"c-echo-received:c-trigger-fired:auto_\"\n\ncheck_map \"246-c-shim\" \\\n    \"echo → seen:HELLO-FROM-SEED\"\n\ncheck_map \"246-lua-shim\" \\\n    \"echo → seen:REV-fedcba\"\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; produce parseable JSON whose round-trip detects\n *    as the expected kind\n *  - $ref store: alloc / lookup / clear\n *  - capability validation: gap detection across emit / reconstruct\n *    masks\n */\n#include \"020-sentinels.h\"\n#include \"json.h\"\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* {{{ Tiny test harness */\n#define ASSERT(cond) do { \\\n    if (!(cond)) { \\\n        printf(\"FAIL %s:%d  %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond); \\\n        return 0; \\\n    } \\\n} while (0)\n\nstatic int tests_run = 0, tests_passed = 0;\n#define RUN(name) do { }}} */\n\n/* {{{ detect_round_trip — emit then re-detect */\nstatic int test_detect_round_trip_ref(void)\n{\n    char buf[256];\n    json_writer_t w;\n    json_writer_init(&w, buf, sizeof buf);\n    sentinel_write_ref(&w, 0xCAFEBABE, 1024);\n    int n = json_writer_finish(&w);\n    ASSERT(n > 0);\n\n    json_arena_t *a = json_arena_create();\n    int eo; const char *em;\n    json_node_t *root = json_parse(a, buf, &eo, &em);\n    ASSERT(root != NULL);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_detect(root) == SENTINEL_REF);\n    json_arena_destroy(a);\n    return 1;\n}\n\nstatic int test_detect_round_trip_lang_opaque(void)\n{\n    char buf[256];\n    json_writer_t w;\n    json_writer_init(&w, buf, sizeof buf);\n    sentinel_write_lang_opaque(&w, \"lua\", 42, \"function\");\n    int n = json_writer_finish(&w);\n    ASSERT(n > 0);\n\n    json_arena_t *a = json_arena_create();\n    int eo; const char *em;\n    json_node_t *root = json_parse(a, buf, &eo, &em);\n    ASSERT(root != NULL);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_detect(root) == SENTINEL_LANG_OPAQUE);\n    json_arena_destroy(a);\n    return 1;\n}\n\nstatic int test_detect_round_trip_function_pointer_stub(void)\n{\n    char buf[256];\n    json_writer_t w;\n    json_writer_init(&w, buf, sizeof buf);\n    sentinel_write_function_pointer_stub(&w, \"int(int,int)\");\n    int n = json_writer_finish(&w);\n    ASSERT(n > 0);\n\n    json_arena_t *a = json_arena_create();\n    int eo; const char *em;\n    json_node_t *root = json_parse(a, buf, &eo, &em);\n    ASSERT(root != NULL);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_detect(root) == SENTINEL_FUNCTION_POINTER);\n    json_arena_destroy(a);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Non-sentinel objects don't false-positive */\nstatic int test_detect_skips_plain_objects(void)\n{\n    json_arena_t *a = json_arena_create();\n    int eo; const char *em;\n\n    /* Plain object — multiple keys. */\n    json_node_t *n1 = json_parse(a, \"{\\\"a\\\":1,\\\"b\\\":2}\", &eo, &em);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_detect(n1) == SENTINEL_NONE);\n\n    /* Single-key object whose key isn't a sentinel name. */\n    json_node_t *n2 = json_parse(a, \"{\\\"foo\\\":1}\", &eo, &em);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_detect(n2) == SENTINEL_NONE);\n\n    /* Arrays / scalars / null. */\n    json_node_t *n3 = json_parse(a, \"[1,2,3]\", &eo, &em);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_detect(n3) == SENTINEL_NONE);\n    json_node_t *n4 = json_parse(a, \"42\", &eo, &em);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_detect(n4) == SENTINEL_NONE);\n    json_node_t *n5 = json_parse(a, \"null\", &eo, &em);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_detect(n5) == SENTINEL_NONE);\n\n    json_arena_destroy(a);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ $ref store round-trip */\nstatic int test_ref_store(void)\n{\n    sentinel_ref_store_clear();\n    const char *payload = \"0123456789ABCDEF\";\n    int len = (int)strlen(payload);\n    uintptr_t p = sentinel_ref_alloc(payload, len);\n    ASSERT(p != 0);\n    int got_len = 0;\n    const void *got = sentinel_ref_lookup(p, &got_len);\n    ASSERT(got != NULL);\n    ASSERT(got_len == len);\n    ASSERT(memcmp(got, payload, (size_t)len) == 0);\n\n    /* Lookup with a wrong pointer returns NULL. */\n    int dummy = 0;\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p + 1, &dummy) == NULL);\n\n    sentinel_ref_store_clear();\n    /* After clear, the pointer is no longer valid (and may be freed\n     * memory — we only assert lookup miss, not dereferencing). */\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p, &dummy) == NULL);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Capability validation */\nstatic int test_validate(void)\n{\n    /* No emission → no gap. */\n    ASSERT(sentinel_validate(0, 0) == 0);\n\n    /* Identical capabilities → no gap. */\n    ASSERT(sentinel_validate(\n        SENTINEL_MASK_REF | SENTINEL_MASK_LANG_OPAQUE,\n        SENTINEL_MASK_REF | SENTINEL_MASK_LANG_OPAQUE) == 0);\n\n    /* Consumer covers producer's emit set → no gap. */\n    ASSERT(sentinel_validate(\n        SENTINEL_MASK_REF,\n        SENTINEL_MASK_REF | SENTINEL_MASK_LANG_OPAQUE) == 0);\n\n    /* Producer emits something consumer can't reconstruct → gap. */\n
