```json
    "stdout":"## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: \"map\"`, the `ref` field, and\n   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a\n   clear error if any field is missing where required.\n2. **External-binding toggles**: inspector toggle on data boxes\n   (externally-supplied) and write boxes (externally-consumed);\n   kind / name / index selectors when on. Same visual idiom for\n   both.\n3. **File browser \"Encapsulate\" action**: adds a `kind: \"map\"`\n   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's\n   marked data boxes and marked write boxes to populate the new\n   box's `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.\n4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's\n   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and\n   marked-output lists on the parent box record.\n5. **Multi-output slot allocation**: the encapsulated box gets\n   one output slot per externally-consumed write box (the\n   documented exception to issue 218). Graph loader and slot\n   store accept this shape only for `lang: \"map\"` boxes.\n6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph\n   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a\n   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).\n7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at\n   compile (or load) time.\n8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for\n   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent\n  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later\n  renames or moves `<sub>`? The reference path is brittle.\n  Options: store a stable id in the sub-map's `meta.json` and\n  reference that, plus a path hint; or require the sub-map to\n  live inside the parent's map directory tree.\n- **Re-sync behaviour when the sub-map changes**: if the user\n  edits the sub-map and changes its marked inputs, the parent's\n  encapsulating box's `inputs` array drifts out of date. Likely\n  resolution: on parent map load, the loader re-derives the\n  inputs from the sub-map and warns the user if wiring needs\n  fixing.\n- **`.map` packaging format**: this issue assumes sub-maps are\n  directories. A single-file `.map` archive (tarball / zip)\n  would be more portable for distribution. Out of scope here;\n  separate ticket if it becomes relevant.\n- **Output naming consistency**: outputs use the same\n  positional / numbered / named binding kinds as inputs. The\n  question is whether a single encapsulated box can mix kinds\n  across outputs (e.g. two named, one positional), or whether\n  all outputs must share a kind. Inputs already allow mixing —\n  preferable to keep outputs symmetric.\n- **Side-effect ordering**: the sub-map's write boxes run as\n  part of the sub-graph and write to disk. The encapsulating\n  box's output emits *after* those side effects complete. If\n  the parent wires the encapsulating box's output forward, the\n  downstream task can rely on the writes having happened. Worth\n  documenting; not a design choice so much as a consequence of\n  the existing dispatch model.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe original 2026-05-21 design packed all write-box outputs into\na single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, and\nthe encapsulated box had a single output wire carrying that blob:\n\n> \"the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of\n> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null\n> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index\n> of data...\" — 2026-05-21\n\nThat design was reconsidered on 2026-05-23 while specifying the\nself-construction built-ins (issue 319). The reconsideration:\nboxes never \"return\" values to the outside world under the\nexisting model — they push values onto wires that other boxes\nconsume, and `write` boxes specifically terminate values to\nfiles. Repurposing the file-writing destination to emit strings\ninto wires would have been a substitution of one mechanism for\nanother. The symmetric design — mark write boxes\nexternally-consumed, surface each as its own output port —",
```

```json
{
  "attachment":{
    "filename":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/langs/bash/bash-server.sh",
    "content":{
      "type":"text",
      "file":{
        "numLines":102,
        "startLine":1,
        "totalLines":102,
        "content":"#!/bin/bash\n# langs/bash/bash-server.sh — persistent bash subprocess, one per\n# worker thread, that talks to the C spec over a Unix-domain\n# socketpair connected to stdin/stdout.\n#\n# Designed in issue 308. Replaces the fork+exec-per-call model\n# with a long-lived process: process startup happens once at\n# pool init, every box invocation reuses the same bash state\n# (and the sourced module cache).\n#\n# Protocol — line-oriented, all values UTF-8:\n#\n#   Request:\n#     <n_args>\\n            (or \"QUIT\" to terminate)\n#     <file_path>\\n\n#     <fn_name>\\n\n#     <arg1>\\n              (n_args of these)\n#     <arg2>\\n\n#     ...\n#\n#   Response:\n#     <exit_status>\\n        (0 on success)\n#     <output_length>\\n      (decimal byte count, no newline at end of payload)\n#     <output_bytes>         (output_length bytes, NOT followed by \\n)\n#\n# Limitations of this iteration:\n#   - Arguments cannot contain literal newlines (line-oriented protocol).\n#   - Output is read as bytes — newlines inside the payload are fine,\n#     but trailing newlines from bash builtins like `echo` are part\n#     of the output. Box functions use `printf '%s' \"$x\"` to avoid them.\n#\n# Caching: each box file is sourced on first use and remembered in\n# the `sourced` associative array; subsequent invocations skip the\n# `source` and reuse the loaded functions. Per-worker, no locking.\n\nset -u\n\ndeclare -A sourced\n\n# {{{ Pre-source files listed in SORAMECH_BASH_PRESOURCE_FILES\n# Issue 313 follow-on (Bash merge): the runner publishes a\n# colon-separated list of every distinct bash box ref at pool\n# startup. Sourcing them here moves the cost out of the request\n# loop (which previously did a lazy `source` on first call). The\n# `sourced` cache still tracks file paths so subsequent per-call\n# checks short-circuit immediately. Function-name collisions\n# across files remain last-write-wins; sourcing eagerly doesn't\n# change those semantics, so user code that wants per-box\n# uniqueness should namespace its function names.\nif [[ -n \"${SORAMECH_BASH_PRESOURCE_FILES:-}\" ]]; then\n    IFS=':' read -ra _presource <<< \"$SORAMECH_BASH_PRESOURCE_FILES\"\n    for _f in \"${_presource[@]}\"; do\n        [[ -z \"$_f\" || ! -f \"$_f\" ]] && continue\n        # shellcheck disable=SC1090\n        if source \"$_f\" 2>/dev/null; then\n            sourced[$_f]=1\n        fi\n    done\n    unset _presource _f\nfi\n# }}}\n\nwhile IFS= read -r n_args; do\n    [[ \"$n_args\" == \"QUIT\" ]] && break\n\n    IFS= read -r file_path\n    IFS= read -r fn_name\n\n    args=()\n    for ((i = 0; i < n_args; i++)); do\n        IFS= read -r a\n        args+=(\"$a\")\n    done\n\n    if [[ ! -f \"$file_path\" ]]; then\n        printf '127\\n0\\n'\n        continue\n    fi\n\n    if [[ -z \"${sourced[$file_path]:-}\" ]]; then\n        # shellcheck disable=SC1090\n        if ! source \"$file_path\" 2>/dev/null; then\n            printf '126\\n0\\n'\n            continue\n        fi\n        sourced[$file_path]=1\n    fi\n\n    # Capture function output and exit status. The function name\n    # itself failing (not a callable) surfaces as exit 127.\n    if ! declare -F \"$fn_name\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf '127\\n0\\n'\n        continue\n    fi\n\n    out=$(\"$fn_name\" \"${args[@]}\" 2>/dev/null)\n    status=$?\n    n=${#out}\n    printf '%d\\n%d\\n' \"$status\" \"$n\"\n    printf '%s' \"$out\"\ndone\n",
        "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/langs/bash/bash-server.sh"
      }
    },
    "type":"file",
    "displayPath":"langs/bash/bash-server.sh"
  },
```

```json
{
  "attachment":{
    "type":"invoked_skills",
    "skills":[{
        "name":"loop",
        "content":"# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt\n\nParse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.\n\n## Parsing (in priority order)\n\n1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.\n2. **Trailing \"every\" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows \"every\" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.\n3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see \"Dynamic mode\" below).\n\nIf the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.\n\nExamples:\n- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)\n- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)\n- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)\n- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)\n- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — \"every\" not followed by time)\n- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage\n\n## Offer cloud first\n\nBefore any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:\n- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or\n- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing (\"every morning\", \"daily\", \"every day\", \"each night\", \"every weekday\")\n\nIf either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:\n- `question`: \"This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?\"\n- `header`: \"Schedule\"\n- `options`: `[{label: \"Cloud schedule (recommended)\", description: \"Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session\"}, {label: \"This session only\", description: \"Runs in this terminal until you exit\"}]`\n\nIf they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: \"schedule\", args: \"every morning tell me a joke\"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no \"execute the prompt now\").\nIf they pick **This session only**:\n- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.\n- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.\nIf neither trigger condition was met: continue below.\n\n## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)\n\nConvert the interval to a cron expression:\n\n| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |\n|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|\n| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |\n| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|\n| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |\n| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |\n| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |\n\n**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.\n\nThen:\n1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.\n2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.\n3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.\n\n## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)\n\nThe user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.\n\n1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.\n2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. Arm once; on later iterations call TaskList first and skip this step if a monitor is already running.\n3. **At the end of this turn, call ScheduleWakeup** with:\n   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks past the 5-minute cache window are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.\n   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.\n   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.\n4. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 3 — the Monitor remains the wake signal; this only resets the safety net.\n5. **To stop the loop**, omit the ScheduleWakeup call and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context).\n6. Briefly confirm: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you picked.\n\n## Input\n\ncontinue with 319b implementation flow — check exporter status, then commit 313 + refreshed transcripts, then move on to 319b",
```

```json
{
  "slug":"optimized-skipping-umbrella",
  "uuid":"6037fdd9-087c-4dc1-98d7-42adb5bbb84b",
  "type":"user",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-24T04:11:42.247Z",
  "parentUuid":"50beeb57-4379-45f0-b5a4-f84cbf6b59dd",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "numLines":363,
      "startLine":1,
      "totalLines":363,
      "content":"/* src/010-graph-loader.h — C graph loader (phase 3), public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: reads a map directory off disk, parses\n * every JSON file in it, and produces an in-memory graph_t that the\n * dispatch layer (issue 304) and the pool runner (issue 301) walk\n * to drive a run.\n *\n * Designed in issue 305. Aligned to the unified routing schema\n * from issue 233 — every call box carries a routing.kind, and the\n * legacy `comparand` / `iterator_outputs` fields are gone. The data\n * and file_write box kinds from issue 229 are dispatch-layer\n * primitives — they have no function to invoke.\n *\n * Memory model: every string the graph_t holds (box ids, refs,\n * function names, branch tags, paths, input port names) lives in a\n * single json_arena_t owned by the graph_t. graph_destroy frees the\n * arena, the box / connection / input arrays, and the graph_t in\n * one call.\n *\n * Errors: graph_load returns NULL on failure and sets *err to a\n * malloc'd diagnostic of the form \"<file>:<line>: <message>\". The\n * caller frees *err. The hard-crash policy of the rest of phase 3\n * (issue 303) applies upstream — graph_load's caller decides\n * whether to abort or surface the error.\n *\n * Pipeline: directory walk, JSON parse, per-box schema validation,\n * topology resolution (string refs → integer indices), non-iterator\n * cycle rejection, per-edge same-language classification (issue 312),\n * entry-box detection. graph_attach_runtime then allocates input\n * slots sized per the feeders' declared output_capacity, resolves\n * each call box's language spec, and enumerates the distinct\n * languages and slot size classes the map uses.\n *\n * Errors out of any phase abort the load and return NULL with a\n * diagnostic via *err.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H\n#define SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n#include <stdatomic.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Box kinds */\ntypedef enum {\n    BOX_CALL,        /* runs a function via a language spec                */\n    BOX_READ,        /* value source — inline literal or file at `path`    */\n    BOX_WRITE,       /* file sink — writes one input, emits \"true\" downstream */\n    /* Runtime self-construction (issue 319, design-correction follow-on\n     * to 319d/319e). These are language-agnostic box kinds — the same\n     * shape as read/write boxes, no `lang` field. Their `do_*`\n     * implementations live in the dispatch layer and call\n     * runtime_create_box / runtime_connect internally.\n     *\n     * The per-language wrappers (langs/lua/spec.c's\n     * `soramech.create_box`, langs/c/soramech.h's\n     * `soramech_create_box`) remain as backwards-compatible\n     * convenience entry points; the box-kind path is the new idiomatic\n     * way and the only path that works uniformly across every\n     * language (including Bash, which has no per-language wrapper). */\n    BOX_CREATE_BOX,  /* construct a new box from a spec on the input wire  */\n    BOX_CONNECT,     /* attach a wire described by a connection-entry input */\n    /* Issue 248: encapsulated map. A box of this kind names a\n     * sub-map directory via `ref`; at graph load the loader\n     * recursively loads the sub-map's boxes, splices them into\n     * the parent with id prefixes, and rewires the parent's\n     * wires that reach this box to instead reach the sub-map's\n     * externally-marked data / write boxes. After inlining the\n     * box itself becomes inert — it never dispatches. */\n    BOX_MAP,\n} box_kind_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Routing kinds (issue 233 unified schema) */\ntypedef enum {\n    ROUTING_PLAIN,\n    ROUTING_COMPARATOR,\n    ROUTING_ITERATOR,\n    ROUTING_RANDOMIZER,\n    ROUTING_WEIGHTED,\n    ROUTING_DISTRIBUTOR,\n} routing_kind_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    routing_kind_t kind;\n    int            n_outputs;   /* iterator / randomizer / weighted / distributor */\n    double         comparand;   /* comparator */\n    /* Weighted routing: arena-owned double array of n_outputs\n     * entries. Normalised at runtime. NULL for other kinds. */\n    const double  *weights;\n} routing_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Input port declaration */\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;       /* port name; arena-owned     */\n    const char *type;       /* \"string\" by convention     */\n    const char *literal;    /* NULL or arena-owned value  */\n    int         optional;   /* issue 230 optional flag    */\n    /* Per-port custom translation shim (issue 246). When non-NULL,\n     * names a file relative to the map dir that contains a\n     * user-written shim. The shim runs at the start of the\n     * consumer's task and replaces the default decode for THIS\n     * port only — other ports keep the default path. The shim's\n     * language is implied by the box's `lang` field; the file is\n     * compiled / loaded by the appropriate spec's machinery. */\n    const char *custom_translation;\n} input_decl_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Outgoing connection */\n/* String refs are preserved for diagnostics; resolved integer\n * indices are filled in by the topology pass and let the dispatch\n * layer (issue 304) avoid string lookups at runtime. */\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *to_box;       /* destination box id (arena-owned)        */\n    const char *to_input;     /* destination port name                   */\n    const char *from_branch;  /* NULL for plain output; else branch name */\n    int         to_box_idx;   /* resolved index into graph->boxes        */\n    int         to_input_idx; /* resolved index into target's inputs[]   */\n} connection_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ External binding (issue 248)\n *\n * A `data` box marked externally-supplied OR a `write` box marked\n * externally-consumed carries one of these. The kind picks how the\n * box's port maps to the encapsulating BOX_MAP's input/output\n * port list: `positional` by argument order, `numbered` by an\n * explicit index, `named` by a string. */\ntypedef enum {\n    EXTERNAL_NONE = 0,\n    EXTERNAL_POSITIONAL,\n    EXTERNAL_NUMBERED,\n    EXTERNAL_NAMED,\n} external_kind_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    external_kind_t kind;\n    int             index;     /* positional / numbered */\n    const char     *name;      /* named; arena-owned */\n} external_binding_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Box */\n/* Tagged so the forward declaration `typedef struct box box_t;` in\n * langs/lang-spec.h matches and the compile callback can accept a\n * `const box_t *` parameter. */\ntypedef struct box {\n    const char    *id;\n    box_kind_t     kind;\n\n    /* Call boxes */\n    const char    *lang;          /* \"lua\" / \"c\" / \"bash\" / NULL    */\n    const char    *ref;           /* source file (call only)        */\n    const char    *fn;            /* function name (call only)      */\n    const char    *returns;       /* declared output type: \"string\"/\"int\"/\n                                   * \"double\"/\"bool\"/\"bytes\"/\"json\"/\"void\"\n                                   * or NULL when the user hasn't said.\n                                   * Read by specs on the JSON-output\n                                   * path (issue 307 item 2). */\n    routing_t      routing;       /* call only                      */\n    int            output_capacity; /* 0 means variable-size        */\n\n    /* Per-box compile hints, optional, currently used by the C spec\n     * (issue 307). Lua / Bash boxes leave these at NULL / 0. All\n     * point into the graph's arena; no separate ownership. */\n    const char    *cflags;        /* extra flags appended to `cc`   */\n    int            n_link_libs;\n    const char   **link_libs;     /* each becomes `-l<name>`        */\n    int            n_headers;\n    const char   **headers;       /* `#include`d by generated wrappers */\n\n    /* Read boxes */\n    const char    *path;          /* file path (read only; ignored if value set) */\n    const char    *value;         /* inline literal; if set, read emits this directly */\n\n    /* Issue 248 — externally-supplied / externally-consumed binding.\n     * Present on `data` boxes inside a sub-map that should source\n     * their value from the parent's encapsulating box's input, OR\n     * on `write` boxes whose `value` should also surface back to\n     * the parent. EXTERNAL_NONE means \"not bound to the parent.\"\n     * The loader's encapsulation pass reads this to rewire wires;\n     * the dispatch never looks at it (the rewiring happens\n     * entirely at load time). */\n    external_binding_t external;\n\n    /* Read-box value cache (issue 244): the bytes a downstream consumer\n     * pulls when it needs this read box's value. Populated at graph\n     * load — inline `value` is strdup'd; file `path` is read and the\n     * file's bytes are owned here. Always present on BOX_READ; NULL on\n     * call / write boxes. Freed by graph_destroy. */\n    char          *cached_value;\n    int            cached_size;\n\n    /* Common */\n    int            n_inputs;\n    input_decl_t  *inputs;\n    /* Connections grow at runtime via runtime_connect (issue 319d).\n     * Writers allocate a new array, copy + append, atomic-store the\n     * new connections pointer, then atomic-store the new count;\n     * old arrays are parked on the graph's stale list and freed at\n     * graph_destroy. Readers see either (old, old) / (new, old) /\n     * (new, new) — never (old, new) — so iteration is always safe\n     * against a concurrent grow. Implicit atomic loads via C11\n     * cover the common access patterns. */\n    _Atomic int                n_connections;\n    _Atomic(connection_t *)    connections;\n\n    /* Runtime state — populated by graph_attach_runtime, left at\n     * defaults (-1 / NULL / 0) by graph_load alone. */\n    int            spec_idx;       /* index into the spec registry; -1 if no spec  */\n    int           *input_slot_ids; /* n_inputs entries; -1 if not allocated yet    */\n    int           *input_slot_modes;/* 0 = PEEK (1-cell), 1 = POP (N-cell)         */\n    int            counter_slot_id;/* atomic-counter slot for iterator routing; -1 */\n    int            multi_spawn;    /* 1 if the box may fire many times in one run  */\n\n    /* 312 per-edge fast-path classification.\n     *\n     * One bit per input port: true iff the producer feeding that\n     * port shares this box's language. Drives the consumer's\n     * decoder choice on single-ring slots and seeds the\n     * `input_native[i]` flag that the spec's invoke consults.\n     *\n     * One bit per outgoing connection (not per output port — a\n     * single output may fan to consumers of different languages):\n     * true iff the consumer on the other end of that connection\n     * shares this box's language. When set, the producer pushes\n     * native bytes to the consumer slot's `ring_native`; when\n     * cleared, the producer calls `native_to_json` first and\n     * pushes JSON to `ring_json`. */\n    int           *input_edge_native;   /* n_inputs entries, or NULL              */\n    int           *output_edge_native;  /* n_connections entries, or NULL         */\n\n    /* 244 per-port read-box predecessor lists.\n     *\n     * A consumer's input port may be fed by one or more BOX_READ\n     * value sources. Under the pull-on-demand model these don't push\n     * at startup; instead, when the consumer fires and finds the\n     * slot empty, the dispatch layer pulls the next read box's\n     * cached value into the input buffer directly. With more than\n     * one predecessor on the same port the dispatch rotates via the\n     * counter slot (atomic increment, mod count).\n     *\n     * Allocated by graph_load: n_inputs entries each; entries with\n     * zero read predecessors hold NULL / 0 / -1. Returns the\n * new box's index (>= 0) or -1 on allocation failure.\n *\n * box_add_connection appends a connection entry to the given box's\n * `connections` array via atomic copy-and-publish: a new array is\n * allocated at current_n+1 entries, the old entries are copied in,\n * the new entry is appended, and the new array pointer is published\n * before the new count.         "content":"1\t/* src/010-graph-loader.h — C graph loader (phase 3), public API.\n2\t *\n3\t * What it is, in a sentence: reads a map directory off disk, parses\n4\t * every JSON file in it, and produces an in-memory graph_t that the\n5\t * dispatch layer (issue 304) and the pool runner (issue 301) walk\n6\t * to drive a run.\n7\t *\n8\t * Designed in issue 305. After this call,\n338\t * the dispatch layer can read inputs via `box->input_slot_ids[i]` and\n339\t * invoke the spec via `spec_registry_at(r, box->spec_idx)`.\n340\t *\n341\t * Per-port slot sizing: cell_capacity = max(declared output_capacity\n342\t * across feeders, default_cell_bytes). The LARGE_VALUE flag is set if\n343\t * any feeder has output_capacity == 0 (variable-size). Multi-spawn\n344\t * boxes (any box reachable from an iterator-routing call box) get an\n345\t * N-cell pop ring; single-spawn boxes get a 1-cell peek slot.\n346\t *\n347\t * Returns 0 on success, -1 with *err set on the first resolution or\n348\t * allocation failure. */\n349\tstruct slot_store;        /* opaque forward decl */\n350\tstruct spec_registry;     /* opaque forward decl */\n351\tint graph_attach_runtime(graph_t *g,\n352\t                         struct slot_store    *slots,\n353\t                         struct spec_registry *specs,\n354\t                         int                   default_cell_bytes,\n355\t                         char                **err);\n356\t/* }}} */\n357\t\n358\t#ifdef __cplusplus\n359\t}\n360\t#endif\n361\t\n362\t#endif /* SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H */\n363\t"
```

```json
      "content":"    if (err) *err = NULL;\n    if (!map_dir) {\n        if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"graph_load: NULL map_dir\");\n        return NULL;\n    }\n\n    graph_t *g = calloc(1, sizeof *g);\n    if (!g) { if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"out of memory\"); return NULL; }\n    pthread_mutex_init(&g->graph_mu, NULL);\n    atomic_init(&g->boxes,        NULL);\n    atomic_init(&g->n_boxes,      0u);\n    atomic_init(&g->box_capacity, 0u);\n    g->stale_box_arrs = NULL;\n\n    g->arena = json_arena_create();\n    if (!g->arena) {\n        if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"out of memory\");\n        free(g);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n\n    g->map_dir = strdup(map_dir);\n    if (!g->map_dir) {\n        if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"out of memory\");\n        graph_destroy(g);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n\n    if (load_meta(g, map_dir, err)            != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }\n    if (load_boxes(g, map_dir, err)           != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }\n    if (resolve_topology(g, err)              != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }\n    if (detect_cycles(g, err)                 != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }\n    if (cache_read_box_values(g, err)         != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }\n    if (build_read_predecessor_lists(g, err)  != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }\n    if (detect_entry_boxes(g, err)            != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }\n\n    /* Compute the same-language fast path flag per call box (issue\n     * 312). A box is \"native-eligible\" iff every adjacent call box —\n     * any producer feeding its inputs AND any consumer reading its\n     * output — shares the box's language. Read boxes and\n     * write boxes don't constrain (they emit/consume JSON-shaped\n     * bytes that any spec interprets through its bridges).\n     *\n     * Computed in graph_load (not graph_attach_runtime) because\n     * it's purely topology-derived and doesn't need the slot\n     * store or registry. The dispatch reads these per-cell to\n     * pick the producer's push ring (native vs JSON) and to set\n     * the consumer's `input_native[i]` flag at read time. */\n    for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) {\n        box_t *b = g->boxes[i];\n        b->input_edge_native  = NULL;\n        b->output_edge_native = NULL;\n        if (b->kind != BOX_CALL || !b->lang) continue;\n\n        /* Allocate per-port input bits and per-connection output\n         * bits. malloc rather than calloc — we fill every entry\n         * explicitly below. */\n        if (b->n_inputs > 0) {\n            b->input_edge_native = malloc((size_t)b->n_inputs * sizeof(int));\n            if (!b->input_edge_native) { if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"oom\"); return NULL; }\n            for (int j = 0; j < b->n_inputs; j++) b->input_edge_native[j] = 0;\n        }\n        if (b->n_connections > 0) {\n            b->output_edge_native = malloc((size_t)b->n_connections * sizeof(int));\n            if (!b->output_edge_native) { if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"oom\"); return NULL; }\n            for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) b->output_edge_native[j] = 0;\n        }\n\n        /* Outgoing edges: for each connection, the consumer's lang\n         * is native iff it's also a call box in this box's\n         * language. Read / write consumers are not native\n         * (they don't carry a language). */\n        int all_outs_native = 1;\n        for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {\n            int dst = b->connections[j].to_box_idx;\n            if (dst < 0) { all_outs_native = 0; continue; }\n            const box_t *c = g->boxes[dst];\n            int native = (c->kind == BOX_CALL && c->lang\n                          && strcmp(c->lang, b->lang) == 0);\n            b->output_edge_native[j] = native;\n            if (!native) all_outs_native = 0;\n        }\n\n        (void)all_outs_native;   /* slice 5 of 312 removed the per-box bit */\n\n        /* Incoming edges: for each input port the port is native iff\n         * it has at least one feeder AND every feeder is a call box\n         * sharing this box's language. A mixed-language fan-in\n         * downgrades the port to JSON — the slot can carry only one\n         * format and JSON is the common denominator.\n         *\n         * NOTE (issue 318 follow-on): this per-edge classification is\n         * the FALLBACK on single-ring slots. For dual-ring slots\n         * (issue 312), the consumer's read path uses the per-cell\n         * which_ring tag returned by slot_pop_ordered instead. The\n         * dual-ring path is what makes intra-Lua $lang_opaque survive\n         * a producer that was forced to JSON by a cross-language\n         * sibling consumer — each cell carries its own format flag,\n         * so the consumer doesn't have to trust a per-edge\n         * approximation that lies when the producer's per-call\n         * output_native is 0. */\n        for (int port = 0; port < b->n_inputs; port++) {\n            input_feeders_t f = scan_input_feeders(g, i, port, b->lang);\n            b->input_edge_native[port] = (f.n_feeders > 0 &&\n                                          f.n_native == f.n_feeders) ? 1 : 0;\n        }\n    }\n    return g;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ graph_destroy() */\nvoid graph_destroy(graph_t *g)\n{\n    if (!g) return;\n    box_t **boxes = atomic_load_explicit(&g->boxes, memory_order_relaxed);\n    uint32_t n    = atomic_load_explicit(&g->n_boxes, memory_order_relaxed);\n    if (boxes) {\n        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {\n            box_t *b = boxes[i];\n            if (!b) continue;\n            free(b->inputs);\n            free(b->connections);\n            free(b->input_slot_ids);\n            free(b->input_slot_modes);\n            free(b->input_edge_native);\n            free(b->output_edge_native);\n            free((double *)b->routing.weights);\n            /* per-box compile hint pointer arrays (strings inside\n             * are arena-owned; only the array itself is heap) */",
```

```json
{
  "slug":"optimized-skipping-umbrella",
  "uuid":"b0225d2f-f181-46ff-9105-ec7166387aa9",

      "content":"# 248 — Encapsulated map as box\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nA map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the\ntop-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to\nopen a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*\non the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a\nsingle box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from `data`\nboxes inside the sub-map that have been marked\n**externally-supplied**; its outputs come from `write` boxes\ninside the sub-map that have been marked **externally-consumed**.\nThe two markings are symmetric: one redirects an input from \"file\non disk\" to \"wire from parent,\" the other redirects an output\nfrom \"file on disk\" to \"wire to parent.\"\n\nEncapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.\nThe parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box\nwith declared input ports, declared output ports, and known\nsemantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across\nparent maps, and packaged once for distribution.\n\n**Encapsulated boxes are the documented exception to issue 218's\n\"single output per box\" rule.** Every other box kind has exactly\none output (with fan-out via multiple wires leaving that one\noutput). An encapsulated map has *N* distinct output ports, one\nper `write` box marked externally-consumed. *N* may be zero (the\nmap is a pure side-effect sink), one (matches the common case),\nor many. The exception exists because an encapsulated map's\noutputs are independent values produced by independent\n`write` boxes — packing them into a single blob (the earlier\ndesign in this issue) would have repurposed file-writing\nmachinery to emit strings into wires, which is the wrong shape:\n`write` boxes should keep their semantics (\"terminate a value\")\nand the destination kind (\"file vs. parent wire\") should be a\nmode toggle, not a substitution.\n\n## Marked input ports inside the sub-map\n\nA **data** box inside the sub-map (kind: `data`, the existing\nlanguage-agnostic file-IO source) can be marked as\n**externally-supplied** via a small toggle on the box's\ninspector. Toggling declares: \"this data box's value comes from\nthe encapsulating context, not from its `path` or `value`\nfield.\"\n\nThe toggle is intentionally scoped to `data` boxes — those are\nthe natural entry points for external values into a map. Call\nboxes / read boxes / write boxes don't carry the toggle, which\nkeeps the inspector uncluttered for the common cases. Each\nexternal input becomes a small shared-memory chunk seeded by\nthe encapsulating call's invoke; the marked data box reads from\nthat chunk on each fire, treating it identically to a value\nloaded from disk.\n\nThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"sum_input\",\n    \"kind\": \"data\",\n    \"external\": {\n        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n        \"name\": \"count\",            // for named\n        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n    },\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nThree binding kinds capture how the encapsulating box's input\nmaps to this internal port:\n\n- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating\n  box has N input ports; the *k*th port's value flows to the\n  internal box whose `external.index` is *k*. Conceptually\n  matches positional function arguments.\n- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index. Same shape\n  as positional but the user picks the number (so they can leave\n  gaps, reorder freely, etc.).\n- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's\n  input port has a label; the matching internal box's\n  `external.name` is the same string.\n\nA single sub-map can mix kinds across its marked boxes — some\npositional, some named — and the parent map's encapsulated box\nexposes the union as its input ports.\n\n## Marked output ports inside the sub-map\n\nA **write** box inside the sub-map (kind: `write`, issue 229's\nfile-write kind) can be marked as **externally-consumed** via a\nsmall toggle on the box's inspector — the mirror of the\nexternally-supplied toggle on data boxes. Toggling declares:\n\"this write box's value goes to the encapsulating context, not\nto its `path` field.\"\n\nThe toggle is intentionally scoped to `write` boxes — those are\nthe natural exit points for values out of a map. Each\nexternally-consumed write box surfaces as one **distinct output\nport** on the encapsulating box. The port carries that one\nvalue, on its own wire, to whichever downstream box(es) the\nparent wires it to.\n\nThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON, in\nthe same shape as the input-side toggle:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"result_value\",\n    \"kind\": \"write\",\n    \"external\": {\n        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n        \"name\": \"result\",           // for named\n        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n    },\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nThree binding kinds — same vocabulary as the input side:\n\n- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating\n  box's *k*th output port is the externally-consumed write box\n  whose `external.index` is *k*.\n- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index, allowing\n  gaps and reordering.\n- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's\n  output port carries that label.\n\nA write box marked externally-consumed **also** writes to its\n`path` if one is set — the two destinations are independent. The\nwrite box can opt out of the file write (set `path: null`) if it\nexists solely to surface a value to the parent.\n\nEach externally-consumed write box's emitted value becomes an\nindependent output wire on the encapsulating box. The earlier\ndesign in this issue packed all write-box outputs into a single\nbyte-blob with a leading size index; that design is rejected —\nsee the \"Concept\" section for why. No packing, no unpacking\nlibrary; the wire format is the same per-port wire format every\nother box uses.\n\n## File layout in the parent map\n\n**The encapsulating box is a normal `call` box.** From the\neditor's perspective it has the same JSON shape as any other\ncall box — `kind: \"call\"`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`,\n`connections`, `routing`. What makes it an encapsulation is\nthat its `lang` is `map` and its `ref` points to a sub-map\ndirectory rather than a source file. The map-language spec\n(`langs/map/spec.so`) is responsible for the \"behind the\nscenes\" processing — running the sub-graph and packing the\noutputs.\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"stats_pipeline\",\n    \"kind\": \"call\",\n    \"lang\": \"map\",\n    \"ref\": \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",\n    \"fn\": null,                                  // unused for map kind\n    \"inputs\": [\n        { \"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"int\" },\n        { \"name\": \"label\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n    ],\n    \"outputs\": [\n        { \"name\": \"mean\",  \"type\": \"float\" },\n        { \"name\": \"stdev\", \"type\": \"float\" },\n        { \"name\": \"n\",     \"type\": \"int\" }\n    ],\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nThe `outputs` array on the encapsulating box JSON is the\ndocumented exception to the single-output-per-box rule. The\ngraph loader treats each entry as a distinct output slot,\nallocates one ring buffer per output port (same machinery as\ninput slots, but on the producer side), and lets the parent\nwire each output independently.\n\nThe map-language spec is registered in the spec registry the\nsame way `lua` / `c` / `bash` are. Its `file_ext` is `.map`\n(or no extension if the ref points to a directory). The graph\nloader resolves the `ref`, the map spec's `init` (per worker)\nloads the sub-graph, and its `invoke` runs the sub-graph and\npacks the outputs. From the dispatch layer's view, an\nencapsulating call is just another spec invocation.\n\nThe sub-map's input ports (derived from its marked data boxes)\nand output ports (derived from its marked write boxes) are\nexposed on the encapsulating box's JSON as `inputs` and `outputs`\narrays. The user doesn't write either array themselves — the\neditor generates them from the sub-map on first encapsulation\nand re-syncs them when the sub-map changes.\n\n## Editor UI\n\n### File browser\n\nThe file browser (issue 207's source-file-browser, or its\ndescendant) shows map directories with a distinct icon — a\nfolder-like glyph annotated to suggest \"this is a runnable\ngraph, not a source file.\" Clicking opens a small menu:\n\n- **Edit this map** — switches the editor's active map (the\n  existing map-select behaviour).\n- **Encapsulate** — adds the map as a `kind: \"map\"` box to the\n  currently-edited parent map. The new box appears on the\n  canvas at the cursor position; the user wires it in like any\n  other box.\n\n### External-binding toggle (inputs and outputs)\n\nThe inspector for a `data` box's value-input grows a small\ntoggle that marks it externally-supplied; the inspector for a\n`write` box's value-input grows the same toggle that marks it\nexternally-consumed. Both surface in the same visual idiom:\n\n```\n  ┌─────────────────────────────┐\n  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound\n  │   kind:    named            │\n  │   name:    \"count\"          │\n  └─────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nWhen the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector\n(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.\nWhen off, the port behaves normally (wires-in / literal value on\nthe data box; `path` write on the write box).\n\nA map with no marked data boxes encapsulates to a no-input box\n(just a source of values). A map with no externally-consumed\nwrite boxes encapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting\nonly — legal but unusual; useful for \"fire and forget\"\nsub-pipelines).\n\n### Visual on the canvas\n\nThe encapsulating box renders distinctly — different border,\nmaybe a small \"sub-map\" badge — so the user sees at a glance\nthat this isn't a leaf call. Hovering shows the sub-map's name\nand a small thumbnail of its graph.\n\n## Runtime model — two paths, needs a decision\n\nTwo implementation paths exist. The encapsulating box being a\nnormal `call` box from the editor's perspective doesn't pick\nbetween them; the choice lives in what the map-language spec\ndoes behind the scenes and what (if anything) the compile\npipeline does at build time.\n\n### Path A — Compile-time inlining\n\nThe compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call\nboxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.\nSteps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:\n\n1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.\n2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:\n   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.\n3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.\n4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with\n   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input\n   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.\n5. For each externally-consumed write box inside the sub-map:\n   route its emitted value to the matching output port on the\n   encapsulating box (so downstream consumers in the parent map\n   see the value on a distinct wire per write box). The write\n   box still performs its disk-write if `path` is set.\n6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph.\n\nAfter expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.\nThe runtime never sees `lang: \"map\"`. The map-language spec\nexists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing\nthe sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector).\n\n**Pros:**\n\n- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec\n  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.\n- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no\n  nested dispatch.\n- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-\n  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions\n  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.\n- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to\n  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.\n\n**Cons:**\n\n- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit\n  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.\n- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to\n  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the\n  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.\n- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of\n  encapsulations.\n- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)\n  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.\n- The multi-output exception to issue 218 has to be carried\n  through compile-time inlining as well: after expansion, the\n  parent's flat graph has wires going from internal sub-graph\n  boxes directly to whichever parent consumers were wired to\n  the encapsulating box's output ports. The compile-time\n  artifact loses the \"encapsulated box\" identity entirely but\n  preserves the per-output routing.\n\n### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch\n\nThe encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat\ngraph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at\ncall time:\n\n1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced\n   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each\n   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,\n   dispatch context).\n2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., outputs, ...)`** —\n   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk\n   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the\n   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch\n   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished\n   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk each\n   externally-consumed write box and push its emitted value onto\n   the matching output port of the encapsulating box. Each output\n   port surfaces on its own wire to the parent — no packing.\n\nThe sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the\nparent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the\nparent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is\njust box-id prefix.\n\n**Pros:**\n\n- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent\n  invocations and across many parent maps.\n- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the\n  new version on next run (no parent recompile).\n- The multi-output boundary is clean — each externally-consumed\n  write box pushes onto its own output port wire as it would\n  if it were a leaf box in the parent graph, no packing or\n  unpacking required.\n- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the\n  task's namespace says \"this came from `stats-pipeline`\").\n- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its\n  own spec for a sub-sub-map.\n\n**Cons:**\n\n- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested\n  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy\n  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch\n  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.\n- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —\n  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous\n  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.\n- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the\n  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at\n  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be\n  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's\n  a separate design.)\n- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset\n  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get\n  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a\n  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).\n\n### What to weigh\n\nThe choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time\nabstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**\nor **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared\nlibrary)**.\n\nPath A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is\nhow the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one\nflat program. Best for raw performance and integration with\nthe existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.\n\nPath B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a\nreal boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output\nas the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,\nhot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and\nloss of cross-boundary optimization.\n\nA third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating\nbox** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: \"inline\" |\n\"runtime\"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;\nruntime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per\nencapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost\nbut maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it\nfor later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.\n\nRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under\neither path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or\nload-time, under B) error.\n\n## Relationship to existing issues\n\n- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the\n  entry point for the \"encapsulate\" action.\n- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the\n  external-input slider reuses the same visual idiom on the\n  input-port row.\n- **Issue 229 (data box as language-agnostic file IO)** —\n  encapsulation adds an \"externally-supplied\" toggle to data\n  boxes and an \"externally-consumed\" toggle to write boxes. The\n  boxes' default behaviour (read from / write to disk) is\n  unchanged; the toggles route the value through a parent-wire\n  instead of (or in addition to) the disk file.\n\n- **Issue 218 (single output per box)** — the encapsulated\n  `kind: \"map\"` box is the documented exception. Every other box\n  has exactly one output; an encapsulated box has one per\n  externally-consumed write box (zero or more).\n- **Issue 309 (build system / compile pipeline)** — the\n  compile-time inlining path (option A above) extends the\n  pipeline with an \"encapsulation expansion\" step.\n- **Issue 313 (whole-program same-language merge)** — composes\n  with compile-time inlining; the inlined sub-graph's same-\n  language regions merge into the parent's merge as if they\n  were always part of one map.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, the `kind: \"map\"` box,\n  the per-input-port external-binding state.\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — file browser; menu with Edit /\n  Encapsulate actions.\n- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI for the external-binding\n  toggle.\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend; resolving sub-map\n  paths, validating bindings.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — graph loader; recognise\n  `kind: \"map\"`, resolve the sub-map, build the encapsulated\n  shape.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — encapsulating-box dispatch (runtime\n  path) or compile-time expansion (compile path).\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — encapsulation expansion if the\n  compile-time path wins.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: \"map\"`, the `ref` field, and\n   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a\n   clear error if any field is missing where required.\n2. **External-binding toggles**: inspector toggle on data boxes\n   (externally-supplied) and write boxes (externally-consumed);\n   kind / name / index selectors when on. Same visual idiom for\n   both.\n3. **File browser \"Encapsulate\" action**: adds a `kind: \"map\"`\n   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's\n   marked data boxes and marked write boxes to populate the new\n   box's `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.\n4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's\n   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and\n   marked-output lists on the parent box record.\n5. **Multi-output slot allocation**: the encapsulated box gets\n   one output slot per externally-consumed write box (the\n   documented exception to issue 218). Graph loader and slot\n   store accept this shape only for `lang: \"map\"` boxes.\n6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph\n   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a\n   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).\n7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at\n   compile (or load) time.\n8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for\n   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent\n  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later\n  renames or moves `<sub>`? The reference path is brittle.\n  Options: store a stable id in the sub-map's `meta.json` and\n  reference that, plus a path hint; or require the sub-map to\n  live inside the parent's map directory tree.\n- **Re-sync behaviour when the sub-map changes**: if the user\n  edits the sub-map and changes its marked inputs, the parent's\n  encapsulating box's `inputs` array drifts out of date. Likely\n  resolution: on parent map load, the loader re-derives the\n  inputs from the sub-map and warns the user if wiring needs\n  fixing.\n- **`.map` packaging format**: this issue assumes sub-maps are\n  directories. A single-file `.map` archive (tarball / zip)\n  would be more portable for distribution. Out of scope here;\n  separate ticket if it becomes relevant.\n- **Output naming consistency**: outputs use the same\n  positional / numbered / named binding kinds as inputs. The\n  question is whether a single encapsulated box can mix kinds\n  across outputs (e.g. two named, one positional), or whether\n  all outputs must share a kind. Inputs already allow mixing —\n  preferable to keep outputs symmetric.\n- **Side-effect ordering**: the sub-map's write boxes run as\n  part of the sub-graph and write to disk. The encapsulating\n  box's output emits *after* those side effects complete. If\n  the parent wires the encapsulating box's output forward, the\n  downstream task can rely on the writes having happened. Worth\n  documenting; not a design choice so much as a consequence of\n  the existing dispatch model.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe original 2026-05-21 design packed all write-box outputs into\na single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, and\nthe encapsulated box had a single output wire carrying that blob:\n\n> \"the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of\n> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null\n> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index\n> of data...\" — 2026-05-21\n\nThat design was reconsidered on 2026-05-23 while specifying the\nself-construction built-ins (issue 319). The reconsideration:\nboxes never \"return\" values to the outside world under the\nexisting model — they push values onto wires that other boxes\nconsume, and `write` boxes specifically terminate values to\nfiles. Repurposing the file-writing destination to emit strings\ninto wires would have been a substitution of one mechanism for\nanother. The symmetric design — mark write boxes\nexternally-consumed, surface each as its own output port —\npreserves the `write` box's semantics (\"terminate a value\") and\ntreats the destination as a mode toggle. Cost: multi-output boxes\nexist for this kind alone; benefit: one mechanism does both jobs\ncleanly.\n",

The opened map becomes a\n12\tsingle box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from `data`\n13\tboxes inside the sub-map that have been marked\n14\t**externally-supplied**; its outputs come from `write` boxes\n15\tinside the sub-map that have been marked **externally-consumed**.\n16\tThe two markings are symmetric: one redirects an input from \"file\n17\ton disk\" to \"wire from parent,\" the other redirects an output\n18\tfrom \"file on disk\" to \"wire to parent.\"\n19\t\n20\tEncapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.\n21\tThe parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box\n22\twith declared input ports, declared output ports, and known\n23\tsemantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across\n24\tparent maps, and packaged once for distribution.\n25\t\n26\t**Encapsulated boxes are the documented exception to issue 218's\n27\t\"single output per box\" rule.** Every other box kind has exactly\n28\tone output (with fan-out via multiple wires leaving that one\n29\toutput). An encapsulated map has *N* distinct output ports, one\n30\tper `write` box marked externally-consumed. *N* may be zero (the\n31\tmap is a pure side-effect sink), one (matches the common case),\n32\tor many. The exception exists because an encapsulated map's\n33\toutputs are independent values produced by independent\n34\t`write` boxes — packing them into a single blob (the earlier\n35\tdesign in this issue) would have repurposed file-writing\n36\tmachinery to emit strings into wires, which is the wrong shape:\n37\t`write` boxes should keep their semantics (\"terminate a value\")\n38\tand the destination kind (\"file vs. parent wire\") should be a\n39\tmode toggle, not a substitution.\n40\t\n41\t## Marked input ports inside the sub-map\n42\t\n43\tA **data** box inside the sub-map (kind: `data`, the existing\n44\tlanguage-agnostic file-IO source) can be marked as\n45\t**externally-supplied** via a small toggle on the box's\n46\tinspector. The user doesn't write either array themselves — the\n198\teditor generates them from the sub-map on first encapsulation\n199\tand re-syncs them when the sub-map changes.\n200\t\n201\t## Editor UI\n202\t\n203\t### File browser\n204\t\n205\tThe file browser (issue 207's source-file-browser, or its\n206\tdescendant) shows map directories with a distinct icon — a\n207\tfolder-like glyph annotated to suggest \"this is a runnable\n208\tgraph, not a source file.\" Clicking opens a small menu:\n209\t\n210\t- **Edit this map** — switches the editor's active map (the\n211\t  existing map-select behaviour).\n212\t- **Encapsulate** — adds the map as a `kind: \"map\"` box to the\n213\t  currently-edited parent map. The new box appears on the\n214\t  canvas at the cursor position; the user wires it in like any\n215\t  other box.\n216\t\n217\t### External-binding toggle (inputs and outputs)\n218\t\n219\tThe inspector for a `data` box's value-input grows a small\n220\ttoggle that marks it externally-supplied; the inspector for a\n221\t`write` box's value-input grows the same toggle that marks it\n222\texternally-consumed. Both surface in the same visual idiom:\n223\t\n224\t```\n225\t  ┌─────────────────────────────┐\n226\t  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound\n227\t  │   kind:    named            │\n228\t  │   name:    \"count\"          │\n229\t  └─────────────────────────────┘\n230\t```\n231\t\n232\tWhen the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector\n233\t(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.\n234\tWhen off, the port behaves normally (wires-in / literal value on\n235\tthe data box; `path` write on the write box).\n236\t\n237\tA map with no marked data boxes encapsulates to a no-input box\n238\t(just a source of values). A map with no externally-consumed\n239\twrite boxes encapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting\n240\tonly — legal but unusual; useful for \"fire and forget\"\n241\tsub-pipelines).\n242\t\n243\t### Visual on the canvas\n244\t\n245\tThe encapsulating box renders distinctly — different border,\n246\tmaybe a small \"sub-map\" badge — so the user sees at a glance\n247\tthat this isn't a leaf call. Hovering shows the sub-map's name\n248\tand a small thumbnail of its graph.\n249\t\n250\t## Runtime model — two paths, needs a decision\n251\t\n252\tTwo implementation paths exist. The encapsulating box being a\n253\tnormal `call` box from the editor's perspective doesn't pick\n254\tbetween them; the choice lives in what the map-language spec\n255\tdoes behind the scenes and what (if anything) the compile\n256\tpipeline does at build time.\n257\t\n258\t### Path A — Compile-time inlining\n259\t\n260\tThe compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call\n261\tboxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.\n262\tSteps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:\n263\t\n264\t1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.\n265\t2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:\n266\t   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.\n267\t3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.\n268\t4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with\n269\t   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input\n270\t   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.\n271\t5. For each externally-consumed write box inside the sub-map:\n272\t   route its emitted value to the matching output port on the\n273\t   encapsulating box (so downstream consumers in the parent map\n274\t   see the value on a distinct wire per write box). The write\n275\t   box still performs its disk-write if `path` is set.\n276\t6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph.\n277\t\n278\tAfter expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.\n279\tThe runtime never sees `lang: \"map\"`. The map-language spec\n280\texists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing\n281\tthe sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector).\n282\t\n283\t**Pros:**\n284\t\n285\t- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec\n286\t  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.\n287\t- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no\n288\t  nested dispatch.\n289\t- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-\n290\t  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions\n291\t  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.\n292\t- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to\n293\t  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.\n294\t\n295\t**Cons:**\n296\t\n297\t- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit\n298\t  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.\n299\t- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to\n300\t  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the\n301\t  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.\n302\t- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of\n303\t  encapsulations.\n304\t- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)\n305\t  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.\n306\t- The multi-output exception to issue 218 has to be carried\n307\t  through compile-time inlining as well: after expansion, the\n308\t  parent's flat graph has wires going from internal sub-graph\n309\t  boxes directly to whichever parent consumers were wired to\n310\t  the encapsulating box's output ports. The compile-time\n311\t  artifact loses the \"encapsulated box\" identity entirely but\n312\t  preserves the per-output routing.\n313\t\n314\t### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch\n315\t\n316\tThe encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat\n317\tgraph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at\n318\tcall time:\n319\t\n320\t1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced\n321\t   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each\n322\t   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,\n323\t   dispatch context).\n324\t2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., outputs, ...)`** —\n325\t   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk\n326\t   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the\n327\t   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch\n328\t   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished\n329\t   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk each\n330\t   externally-consumed write box and push its emitted value onto\n331\t   the matching output port of the encapsulating box. Each output\n332\t   port surfaces on its own wire to the parent — no packing.\n333\t\n334\tThe sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the\n335\tparent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the\n336\tparent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is\n337\tjust box-id prefix.\n338\t\n339\t**Pros:**\n340\t\n341\t- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent\n342\t  invocations and across many parent maps.\n343\t- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the\n344\t  new version on next run (no parent recompile).\n345\t- The multi-output boundary is clean — each externally-consumed\n346\t  write box pushes onto its own output port wire as it would\n347\t  if it were a leaf box in the parent graph, no packing or\n348\t  unpacking required.\n349\t- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the\n350\t  task's namespace says \"this came from `stats-pipeline`\").\n351\t- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its\n352\t  own spec for a sub-sub-map.\n353\t\n354\t**Cons:**\n355\t\n356\t- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested\n357\t  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy\n358\t  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch\n359\t  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.\n360\t- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —\n361\t  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous\n362\t  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.\n363\t- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the\n364\t  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at\n365\t  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be\n366\t  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's\n367\t  a separate design.)\n368\t- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset\n369\t  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get\n370\t  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a\n371\t  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).\n372\t\n373\t### What to weigh\n374\t\n375\tThe choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time\n376\tabstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**\n377\tor **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared\n378\tlibrary)**.\n379\t\n380\tPath A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is\n381\thow the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one\n382\tflat program. Best for raw performance and integration with\n383\tthe existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.\n384\t\n385\tPath B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a\n386\treal boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output\n387\tas the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,\n388\thot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and\n389\tloss of cross-boundary optimization.\n390\t\n391\tA third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating\n392\tbox** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: \"inline\" |\n393\t\"runtime\"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;\n394\truntime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per\n395\tencapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost\n396\tbut maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it\n397\tfor later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.\n398\t\n399\tRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under\n400\teither path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or\n401\tload-time, under B) error.\n402\t\n403\t## Relationship to existing issues\n404\t\n405\t- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the\n406\t  entry point for the \"encapsulate\" action.\n407\t- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the\n408\t  external-input slider reuses the same visual idiom on the\n409\t  input-port row.\n410\t- **Issue 229 (data box as language-agnostic file IO)** —\n411\t  encapsulation adds an \"externally-supplied\" toggle to data\n412\t  boxes and an \"externally-consumed\" toggle to write boxes. The\n413\t  boxes' default behaviour (read from / write to disk) is\n414\t  unchanged; the toggles route the value through a parent-wire\n415\t  instead of (or in addition to) the disk file.\n416\t\n417\t- **Issue 218 (single output per box)** — the encapsulated\n418\t  `kind: \"map\"` box is the documented exception. Every other box\n419\t  has exactly one output; an encapsulated box has one per\n420\t  externally-consumed write box (zero or more).\n421\t- **Issue 309 (build system / compile pipeline)** — the\n422\t  compile-time inlining path (option A above) extends the\n423\t  pipeline with an \"encapsulation expansion\" step.\n424\t- **Issue 313 (whole-program same-language merge)** — composes\n425\t  with compile-time inlining; the inlined sub-graph's same-\n426\t  language regions merge into the parent's merge as if they\n427\t  were always part of one map.\n428\t\n429\t## Relevant files\n430\t\n431\t- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, the `kind: \"map\"` box,\n432\t  the per-input-port external-binding state.\n433\t- `assets/js/005-app.js` — file browser; menu with Edit /\n434\t  Encapsulate actions.\n435\t- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI for the external-binding\n436\t  toggle.\n437\t- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend; resolving sub-map\n438\t  paths, validating bindings.\n439\t- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — graph loader; recognise\n440\t  `kind: \"map\"`, resolve the sub-map, build the encapsulated\n441\t  shape.\n442\t- `src/012-dispatch.c` — encapsulating-box dispatch (runtime\n443\t  path) or compile-time expansion (compile path).\n444\t- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — encapsulation expansion if the\n445\t  compile-time path wins.\n446\t\n447\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n448\t\n449\t1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: \"map\"`, the `ref` field, and\n450\t   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a\n451\t   clear error if any field is missing where required.\n452\t2. **External-binding toggles**: inspector toggle on data boxes\n453\t   (externally-supplied) and write boxes (externally-consumed);\n454\t   kind / name / index selectors when on. Same visual idiom for\n455\t   both.\n456\t3. **File browser \"Encapsulate\" action**: adds a `kind: \"map\"`\n457\t   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's\n458\t   marked data boxes and marked write boxes to populate the new\n459\t   box's `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.\n460\t4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's\n461\t   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and\n462\t   marked-output lists on the parent box record.\n463\t5. **Multi-output slot allocation**: the encapsulated box gets\n464\t   one output slot per externally-consumed write box (the\n465\t   documented exception to issue 218). Graph loader and slot\n466\t   store accept this shape only for `lang: \"map\"` boxes.\n467\t6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph\n468\t   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a\n469\t   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).\n470\t7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at\n471\t   compile (or load) time.\n472\t8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for\n473\t   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.\n474\t\n475\t## Open questions\n476\t\n477\t- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent\n478\t  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later\n479\t  renames or moves `<sub>`? The reference path is brittle.\n480\t  Options: store a stable id in the sub-map's `meta.json` and\n481\t  reference that, plus a path hint; or require the sub-map to\n482\t  live inside the parent's map directory tree.\n483\t- **Re-sync behaviour when the sub-map changes**: if the user\n484\t  edits the sub-map and changes its marked inputs, the parent's\n485\t  encapsulating box's `inputs` array drifts out of date. Likely\n486\t  resolution: on parent map load, the loader re-derives the\n487\t  inputs from the sub-map and warns the user if wiring needs\n488\t  fixing.\n489\t- **`.map` packaging format**: this issue assumes sub-maps are\n490\t  directories. A single-file `.map` archive (tarball / zip)\n491\t  would be more portable for distribution. Out of scope here;\n492\t  separate ticket if it becomes relevant.\n493\t- **Output naming consistency**: outputs use the same\n494\t  positional / numbered / named binding kinds as inputs. The\n495\t  question is whether a single encapsulated box can mix kinds\n496\t  across outputs (e.g. two named, one positional), or whether\n497\t  all outputs must share a kind. Inputs already allow mixing —\n498\t  preferable to keep outputs symmetric.\n499\t- **Side-effect ordering**: the sub-map's write boxes run as\n500\t  part of the sub-graph and write to disk. The encapsulating\n501\t  box's output emits *after* those side effects complete. If\n502\t  the parent wires the encapsulating box's output forward, the\n503\t  downstream task can rely on the writes having happened. Worth\n504\t  documenting; not a design choice so much as a consequence of\n505\t  the existing dispatch model.\n506\t\n507\t## Design history\n508\t\n509\tThe original 2026-05-21 design packed all write-box outputs into\n510\ta single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, and\n511\tthe encapsulated box had a single output wire carrying that blob:\n512\t\n513\t> \"the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of\n514\t> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null\n515\t> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index\n516\t> of data...\" — 2026-05-21\n517\t\n518\tThat design was reconsidered on 2026-05-23 while specifying the\n519\tself-construction built-ins (issue 319). The reconsideration:\n520\tboxes never \"return\" values to the outside world under the\n521\texisting model — they push values onto wires that other boxes\n522\tconsume, and `write` boxes specifically terminate values to\n523\tfiles. Repurposing the file-writing destination to emit strings\n524\tinto wires would have been a substitution of one mechanism for\n525\tanother. The symmetric design — mark write boxes\n526\texternally-consumed, surface each as its own output port —\n527\tpreserves the `write` box's semantics (\"terminate a value\") and\n528\ttreats the destination as a mode toggle. Cost: multi-output boxes\n529\texist for this kind alone; benefit: one mechanism does both jobs\n530\tcleanly.\n531\t"
      }],

  },
```
